items.description: A Crucible review packet for one binary-search thesis that keeps claims, measurements, verdicts and unmeasured claims apart, so another reviewer can check each.

items.body_html:
MATCH 1 The measured bound matches the claim.
DRIFT 1 The claim says 3 comparisons; the record shows the worst case is 11.
UNVERIFIABLE 1 The claim has no falsification condition, so the packet refuses to pretend.

What This Is

Captured. Recorded on 9 July 2026 and shown as recorded. Nothing on this page runs the tool. The record is crucible-cleanroom-demo.zip, SHA-256 2d4e819e4032f07e.

This is a small review packet for one binary-search thesis. The point is not binary search. The point is the review boundary: the packet keeps claims, measurements, verdicts, and unmeasured claims separate enough for another reviewer to inspect.

The verifier boundary excludes worker context, reasoning trace, intermediate steps, prior chat, and notes. If the packet cannot support a claim, the result stays UNVERIFIABLE.

Included Records

FileRole
spec.jsonOriginal claims and falsification conditions.
run.jsonWitnessed run record, verdicts, seals, and integrity checks.
report.mdHuman-readable summary of verdicts and evidence.
review.mdCleanroom review boundary and excluded context.

Verify Locally

From a fresh clone of HarperZ9/crucible:

pip install -e ".[dev]"
python -m crucible review path/to/crucible-cleanroom-demo/bundle

Expected result:

cleanroom bundle PASS

Download Hash

SHA-256: 2D4E819E4032F07E3A54D35AF2DC78161C1D2F04C43F89C26B56878D6377D1F1

What To Critique

  • Does the packet include enough to re-check the verdict?
  • What fields imply more trust than they should?
  • Where should signatures, attestations, or provenance anchors fit?
  • What should stay outside this packet?
  • Is UNVERIFIABLE represented clearly enough for reviewers?

Non-Claims

This does not certify code, safety, compliance, or correctness beyond the tiny demo. It is a small example of a review packet that can say MATCH, DRIFT, or UNVERIFIABLE.

items.body_html:
The 30-second proof

Captured. Recorded on 12 July 2026 and shown as recorded. Nothing on this page runs the tool. The record is transcript.txt, SHA-256 70e41be8880f9dd9.

A draft release brief satisfies one of three measured claims. Crucible records the two concrete drifts, the worker artifact is refined without moving the criterion, and the same thesis reaches three measured matches.

Your browser cannot play this video. Open the MP4 directly.

Silent, captioned on screen. The exact sanitized transcript, thesis, artifact receipts, and machine-readable evidence are linked below.

The observed conversion

3claims measured
1 / 2draft MATCH / DRIFT
3 / 0refined MATCH / DRIFT
2 PASScleanroom reviews
  • Register: one three-claim thesis defines the release criterion before either artifact is judged.
  • Measure the draft: one claim holds; two measured axes return DRIFT rather than an invented pass.
  • Hold the boundary: the cleanroom reviewer receives the spec and artifact packet, not worker context or reasoning traces.
  • Refine: the artifact changes while the thesis stays fixed.
  • Re-check: the refined run returns 3 MATCH / 0 DRIFT, and the verdict is re-derived from disk.

The full 94-second workflow

The long cut preserves all seven successful commands: build draft evidence, run and review the draft, build refined evidence, run and review the refined artifact, then verify the recorded verdicts. Every displayed count, receipt, seal, return code, and verdict comes from the captured evidence package.

Your browser cannot play this video. Open the MP4 directly.

Run path

python make_substrate.py worker-draft.md substrate-draft.json artifact-evidence-draft.json
python -m crucible run thesis.json --substrate substrate-draft.json --registry registry-draft --bundle bundle-draft
python -m crucible review bundle-draft
python make_substrate.py worker-refined.md substrate-refined.json artifact-evidence-refined.json
python -m crucible run thesis.json --substrate substrate-refined.json --registry registry-refined --bundle bundle-refined
python -m crucible review bundle-refined
python -m crucible verdicts registry-refined --verify

Claim boundary

This is a local, sanitized fixture built to make the measurement loop inspectable. It demonstrates the register, run, cleanroom review, refinement, witnessed assessment, and disk re-verification paths shown here. It does not claim that an evaluation criterion is automatically well-designed, that all claims can be reduced to numeric measures, or that a passing fixture proves production fitness.

items.title: Demo: the byte witness (emet)
items.description: A live in-browser demo of the one move emet makes: re-derive a file's bytes, compare against a stored target, and report MATCH, DRIFT, or UNVERIFIABLE.
headings: Why this is the real move
items.excerpt: Skip to content Demo · the byte witness About emetLive demoSample reportResearch What this demo does emet checks a file by re-deriving its fingerprint and comparing that to a fingerprint it saved earlier. This page does the real version of that move, right here, with no server in the loop. You give it some text or a small file. It computes the actual SHA-256
items.body_html:
What this demo does

emet checks a file by re-deriving its fingerprint and comparing that to a fingerprint it saved earlier. This page does the real version of that move, right here, with no server in the loop. You give it some text or a small file. It computes the actual SHA-256 of those exact bytes using your browser's own cryptography (window.crypto.subtle.digest), then compares the result to a stored target. It reports one of three honest answers and nothing else.

The fingerprint is a SHA-256 digest: a short code that is unique to those exact bytes. Move a single character and the whole code changes. There is no fourth answer that just means trust me. The verdict you see below is driven entirely by the hash this page actually computed, never by anything written into the markup.

The three answers

  • MATCH. The fingerprint of your input equals the stored target. It means nothing moved, not that the input is good or safe.
  • DRIFT. The fingerprint differs from the target. Something changed. The tool reports that and does not decide whose fault it is.
  • UNVERIFIABLE. There is nothing to check yet, or your browser cannot run the cryptography (for example on an insecure origin where crypto.subtle is unavailable). It says so plainly, with a reason, rather than guessing.

Try it

Live. This runs in your browser now, on what you give it.

Type or paste below, or pick a small file. Set what you have as the target, then change a single character and witness again. The verdict will flip from MATCH to DRIFT, because it follows the bytes and nothing else.

Your input (text)

Whatever you type here is hashed exactly as written. A file, if you choose one below, takes the place of this text.

Or a small file (optional)

Read locally and hashed in your browser. Nothing is uploaded. Keep it small, since the whole file is held in memory to hash it.

Witness Set this as the target Clear
Source
no input yet
Computed
SHA-256 of your input appears here
Target
no target set yet
UNVERIFIABLE No input yet. Type or pick a file, then press Witness.

Why this is the real move

A witness is not a judge. It re-derives the bytes itself and tells you what it compared. It never speaks for the thing it is checking, and it never hands out a verdict of trusted, because it was never given any trust to pass along. That is the whole discipline, in your browser, with no backend to take on faith.

The stored target here is just a number you choose by pressing set the target. In the real tool, that saved fingerprint comes from an earlier known-good state, and the file is read straight off the disk. The shape of the check is the same: compute the fingerprint again from scratch, compare, and report MATCH, DRIFT, or UNVERIFIABLE.

Honest limits

  • This page proves the move, not the product. It witnesses input you give it in the browser. It does not read your filesystem on its own, and it keeps no history.
  • SHA-256 detects change. It does not tell you whether a change was intended or whether the content is correct. MATCH means unchanged, never approved.
  • If your browser does not expose crypto.subtle (some insecure origins withhold it), the demo reports UNVERIFIABLE rather than faking a result. That is the honest answer when it cannot check.
  • The full tool lives at github.com/HarperZ9/flywheel/tree/main/packages/emet (v1.0, on PyPI: pip install emet): one spec, four independent language implementations, run yourself and checked on every push. The one claim it still owes is an implementation built by a hand with no tie to mine, a different author.

No data leaves your machine. The verdict is computed from the actual SHA-256 of your input and compared to a target you set; it is never hardcoded. Updated 2026-06-30.

items.body_html:
The surface

Captured. Shown as recorded. Nothing on this page runs the tool. The full record of the run (date, command, file and hash) is not published with it yet.

The gateway serves one page on one local origin. Below, captured 2026-08-04: the endpoint table reads 34 endpoints with 11 usable right now and records credential presence only, never a value. The prompt routes to a local model (telos-coder-14b through ollama) and the answer comes back with the sealed receipt's identifier beside it.

The tamper demonstration

Captured. Recorded on 4 August 2026 and shown as recorded. Nothing on this page runs the tool. The record is flywheel-tamper-demo-2026-08-04.txt, SHA-256 47cc1e7fda31e803.

Recorded terminal transcript, 2026-08-04, from the public repository at its default branch. Two chained tool-call receipts are sealed and verified, one byte of the second receipt's admission decision is corrupted, and the verifier answers TAMPERED / SEAL_MISMATCH with the recomputed hash named. The chain check refuses too. The verifier is Python standard library only: no key, no network, no dependency on the runtime that emitted the receipt.

$ tamper-demo (flywheel harness, stdlib only, offline) STEP 1 -- seal two chained tool-call receipts receipt 1: seal e4cb1ba6daf5e1c3... (read_file, builtin-read, allow) receipt 2: seal 63a2f2d838e693ae... (run_tests, builtin-exec, allow, chained to 1) STEP 2 -- verify both, untouched (recomputes every seal from the record alone) receipt 1: verdict MATCH seal e4cb1ba6daf5e1c30701860bbd440b6e2fb3fe7b7a4e4d6d9af68279fdcd196d receipt 2: verdict MATCH seal 63a2f2d838e693ae2077792d08f76ab5abb73f027301cf11c208898932aa8819 chain: verdict MATCH n=2 STEP 3 -- corrupt ONE byte: receipt 2's admission 'allow' -> 'aIlow' tampered receipt 2: verdict TAMPERED failure_class: SEAL_MISMATCH detail: seal sha256:63a2f2d838e6, recomputed sha256:6885189a7439 STEP 4 -- the chain refuses too chain: verdict TAMPERED n=2 (receipt 1 MATCH, receipt 2 TAMPERED)

Raw transcript: artifacts/flywheel-tamper-demo-2026-08-04.txt

METR count_odds reviewer packet

A public-safe packet for Flywheel PR234 preserves one METR count_odds task-image interoperability check, with source pins, runner receipts, and bounded limits.

Open the METR count_odds reviewer packet. It is interop evidence, not METR endorsement, a model benchmark, or a Flywheel 1.0 release claim.

Run it yourself

One line from PyPI, or from a clone of github.com/HarperZ9/flywheel:

pip install flywheel-verify # the PyPI name; the command is `flywheel`
flywheel up # the surface above # or, from a clone:
git clone https://github.com/HarperZ9/flywheel
cd flywheel
pip install -e .
python scripts/run_harness_cli.py app --port 8799 # the surface above
python -m harness.cli tasks/example_pass # ends in FAIL, deliberately: # the default proposer offers a # wrong candidate and the engine # refuses to accept it

The rejection is the feature: acceptance you cannot forge is what makes the acceptance worth having.

Claim boundary

This page demonstrates that a sealed receipt refuses tampering and that the gateway routes and seals on one surface. It does not demonstrate model quality, capability uplift, or that a verified answer is true in the world; a passing check proves the check passed, and each verdict says so.

Captured and verified 2026-08-04. The screenshot was reviewed for private paths and credential-shaped strings before publication; the endpoint table records presence labels only.

items.body_html:
The 27-second proof

Captured. Recorded on 12 July 2026 and shown as recorded. Nothing on this page runs the tool. The record is transcript.txt, SHA-256 507a167629f1ce7c.

Forum routes a backend-and-documentation request, turns it into three dependent waves, validates each result, and leaves behind a content-addressed ledger that can be independently rechecked.

Your browser cannot play this video. Open the MP4 directly.

Silent, captioned on screen. The exact sanitized transcript, raw ledger, structured evidence, and capture verification are linked below.

The observed run

3dependency waves
3validator passes
19ledger entries
3checkpoints
  • Route: the request selects the backend track without escalation.
  • Plan: backend design, code review, and technical writing become three dependency-ordered waves.
  • Run: upstream results cross typed data edges into the next task, and every wave closes with a checkpoint.
  • Validate: 3 task results receive 3 validator passes and zero failures.
  • Prove: 19 ledger entries, 3 checkpoints, and their content-addressed bodies pass both chain and deep-payload verification.

The full 105-second workflow

The long cut shows the original request, route, dependency plan, each task result, synthesized answer, causal ledger, summary, independent ledger verification, and the operator-room projection. The commands, counts, verdicts, checkpoints, hashes, and success state come from the captured run.

Your browser cannot play this video. Open the MP4 directly.

python -m forum ledger show --ledger "<DEMO_DIR>/ledger" --limit 30

python -m forum ledger verify --ledger "<DEMO_DIR>/ledger"

items.title: Attention: how a language model decides what matters
items.description: Watch Tallow show how attention lets a word use the words before it, then train a tiny transformer in your browser and watch its heads learn.
headings: Attention. How a language model decides what matters.
The old way: a whisper down the line
items.excerpt: Skip to content Zain Dana Harpernight school / L10 Attention. How a language model decides what matters. A word in a sentence often needs another word from much earlier. Attention is how a transformer goes and gets it. Tallow shows you in his lamp room, and then you train one yourself. The film About 6:19, hosted by Tallow. It asks you two questions and wait
items.body_html:
The film

About 6:19, hosted by Tallow. It asks you two questions and waits for your answer before it shows you. The narrated cut runs 5:08, voiced by Tallow in a synthesized voice made from the author's own voice; the author approved these cuts for publishing. Captions are on by default. The live version under it draws the same film in your browser, waits for your answer at each question, and runs a little longer; the full words are also below.

Play the film

Nothing loads until you press play.

The lab: Tallow's lamp room

Train the same kind of model the film uses: 2 layers, 2 heads each, 20,864 numbers, starting from random. It learns from sentences about the coast, such as "rerun found a kettle . pylon put a cone on the", where the last word can only be guessed by looking back. Pick a head to light the sentence with, change the test sentence, or turn the lamp off and train again.

The film's own runs of 2,000 steps filled 99% of the copy holes with attention on, 17% when each word could see only itself, and 64% with even light and no choosing. Your run is a new one, so its numbers will differ a little.

Open the lamp room

The model trains on your computer, in this page. Nothing is sent anywhere.

A circuit, switched off

A second, short film: a different small model, trained on a computer's main processor to continue random strings with one repeated stretch. One head in its first layer moves each character one place forward; a head in its second layer finds the earlier copy and reads what came next. Switch the heads off and the model loses the repeat. That is a causal test, which a picture of attention weights alone is not.

About 73 seconds, with captions. The narration is a synthesized voice made from the author's own voice, and the author listened to this cut before it was published. Every number on screen comes from the model's data file in raw-native.

Everything the film says

Attention

Attention. How a language model decides what matters.

I keep the lamp at Night School. Tonight the lamp is the lesson.

A hole at the end

Here is a sentence with a hole at the end.

Rerun found a kettle. Pylon put a cone on the...

What word goes in the hole? (the film pauses here)

You said kettle. And you did not read the sentence again. You glanced back, past the full stop, to one word near the start, and took it.

The old way: a whisper down the line

A language model like this one does one job. It reads the words so far and guesses the next one.

The first neural translation models squeezed the whole sentence into one fixed-length list of numbers, and worked from that.

Think of a message whispered down a line of people. By the end of a long line, the message has worn thin.

In 2014, Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio let a translation model look at every word of the sentence while it wrote each new word, and weigh how much each one counts. They called it an alignment model. Today we call the idea attention.

Question, label, cargo

Here is how the looking works. Every word does three things.

It asks a question. It holds up a label. And it carries some cargo.

The word at the end shines its question back along the sentence. Each earlier word answers with its label.

A good match gets a high score. The scores are turned into shares that add up to one hundred percent.

Then the word takes a blend of the cargo of every word so far, itself included, in those shares. That blend is what it carries forward.

Inside the lamp

Let's go inside the lamp.

Every word here is a list of 32 numbers. One dot is one number.

A match is a dot product: multiply the two lists number by number, and add it all up.

Each head works on a shorter list of its own, 16 numbers here, and the score is divided by the square root of that length. Without it, long lists give huge scores, the shares go all or nothing, and the model learns slowly.

This is a real model, trained on sentences from our coast. It has 20,864 numbers in total, and nothing in it was set by hand.

Which earlier word will get most of the light? (the film pauses here)

On this sentence, the word at the end gives more than 99 percent of its light to kettle.

One beam, several heads

One beam asks one kind of question. A transformer runs several at once, and calls each one a head.

The base transformer in the 2017 paper had eight heads in every attention layer. The larger one had sixteen.

Ours has 2 heads in each of 2 layers. Nobody told them what to look for.

After training, a head in the second layer puts 71 percent of its light on the word to be copied.

In small attention-only models, researchers at Anthropic found pairs of heads, in different layers, that work together to copy. The first writes into each word a note about the word before it. The second uses that note to find an earlier copy of the current word, and reads the word that followed it. They called them induction heads.

Turn the lamp off

Here is the test that matters. We trained the same model again with the lamp turned off, so each word could see only itself.

With attention, it filled the copy holes correctly 99 percent of the time.

With each word seeing only itself, 17 percent.

Then one more run. Every word got an even share of light over everything before it, with no choosing. That run reached 64 percent.

Knowing which words came before helps. Choosing where to look is what finishes the job.

What the light costs

There's a bill. Every word compares itself with every word before it.

In each head, a thousand words means about half a million comparisons. Double the text, and the attention work goes up about four times.

That's why people build special machinery to do this fast. We take it apart in the cannery, in a later lesson.

What the light does not tell you

One warning before you go.

The light shows where a head is reading from. It does not, on its own, tell you why the model answered what it did.

In 2019, researchers showed that in some text classifiers, very different attention patterns can give almost the same answer. Others replied that it depends on what you mean by explain, and proposed tests. Treat the light as a clue, and check it.

Your turn

The lamp room is open below this film. Train the model yourself, and watch the heads learn where to look.

My voice is synthesized, made from the author's voice.

Sources

Every claim in the film, with the paper it comes from and what that paper does not prove. The numbers about our model come from its weights file, which you can load and check: model.json and facts.json.

  • Vaswani and others 2017, Attention Is All You Need. Vaswani, A., Shazeer, N., Parmar, N., Uszkoreit, J., Jones, L., Gomez, A. N., Kaiser, L., Polosukhin, I. (2017). Attention Is All You Need. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 30. https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762

    Used for: Scaled dot-product attention computes softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d_k)) V: queries are compared with keys by dot products, the scores are divided by the square root of the key dimension, turned into weights by a softmax, and used to average the values (section 3.2.1). The authors suspect that for large d_k the dot products grow large, pushing the softmax into regions with extremely small gradients, and scale by 1/sqrt(d_k) to counteract it (section 3.2.1). Multi-head attention runs several attention functions in parallel on learned projections; the base model uses h = 8 heads and the big model h = 16 (section 3.2.2, Table 3). The decoder's self-attention masks later positions, so a position can attend only to itself and earlier positions (section 3.2.3). Self-attention's cost per layer grows with the square of the sequence length (Table 1, O(n^2 d)).

    Does not prove: Anything about how attention behaves inside a particular trained model; the paper defines the mechanism.

  • Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio 2015, neural machine translation by jointly learning to align and translate. Bahdanau, D., Cho, K., Bengio, Y. (2015). Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate. ICLR 2015 (oral). arXiv:1409.0473, first posted 1 September 2014. https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0473

    Used for: Neural encoder-decoder translation models encoded a source sentence into a fixed-length vector, which the authors conjecture is a bottleneck for long sentences; the baseline's score drops sharply with sentence length (sections 1 and 5.1). Their model searches the source positions and weighs them for each output word; they call it an alignment model, and section 3.1 says it implements a mechanism of attention in the decoder.

    Does not prove: That early words in particular fade; the paper shows degradation with sentence length.

  • Olsson and others 2022, In-context Learning and Induction Heads. Olsson, C., Elhage, N., Nanda, N., Joseph, N., DasSarma, N., Henighan, T., and others (2022). In-context Learning and Induction Heads. Transformer Circuits Thread, Anthropic. arXiv:2209.11895. https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.11895

    Used for: An induction head attends to the token that followed an earlier occurrence of the current token and copies it ([A][B] ... [A] -> [B]). It works with a previous-token head in an earlier layer (K-composition), first described for two-layer attention-only models in Elhage and others 2021.

    Does not prove: That the heads in our tiny model are induction heads; that is measured on our own model, separately.

  • Jain and Wallace 2019, Attention is not Explanation. Jain, S., Wallace, B. C. (2019). Attention is not Explanation. NAACL-HLT 2019. arXiv:1902.10186. https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.10186

    Used for: In the recurrent text-classification and question-answering models studied, attention weights often correlate weakly with gradient-based importance, and very different attention distributions can give equivalent predictions; simpler averaging encoders behaved better.

    Does not prove: That attention never explains a prediction, or anything about transformer language models in particular.

  • Wiegreffe and Pinter 2019, Attention is not not Explanation. Wiegreffe, S., Pinter, Y. (2019). Attention is not not Explanation. EMNLP-IJCNLP 2019. arXiv:1908.04626. https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.04626

    Used for: Argues that whether attention is an explanation depends on the definition of explanation, and that the earlier experiments do not settle it; proposes tests for when attention can serve as one.

    Does not prove: That attention is an explanation; it argues the earlier experiments do not settle the question.

  • Dao and others 2022, FlashAttention. Dao, T., Fu, D. Y., Ermon, S., Rudra, A., Re, C. (2022). FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness. arXiv:2205.14135. https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135

    Used for: Standard attention's time and memory grow quadratically with sequence length; FlashAttention computes exact attention in tiles to cut reads and writes to GPU memory. FlashAttention keeps the exact result and the quadratic arithmetic; it cuts memory traffic and makes memory use linear in sequence length.

    Does not prove: Anything about this lesson's model, which runs on a CPU.

  • Night School's tiny transformer, trained for this film. media/school/attention/model.json, written by tools/school/train_film_weights.mjs from system/school/tinyformer.mjs at a fixed seed; the same code the lab runs in the browser. https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/attention

    Used for: Every number the film states about 'our model' (size, heads, the probe's attention share, copy accuracy with and without attention) is read from model.json by tools/school/fill_film.mjs.

    Does not prove: Anything about large language models' attention; it is a two-layer model on a toy language.

  • Counting comparisons. A causal attention head compares each of n positions with itself and every earlier one: n (n + 1) / 2 scores, 500,500 for n = 1,000, or n (n - 1) / 2 = 499,500 counting only earlier words. Doubling n multiplies either by about four.

    Used for: In each head, a thousand words means about half a million comparisons; doubling the text multiplies the attention work by about four (3.998).

    Does not prove: Wall-clock time, which also depends on memory traffic (see dao2022).

  • Elhage and others 2021, A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits. Elhage, N., Nanda, N., Olsson, C., Henighan, T., Joseph, N., Mann, B., and others (2021). A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits. Transformer Circuits Thread, Anthropic. https://transformer-circuits.pub/2021/framework/index.html

    Used for: Induction heads were first described in two-layer attention-only models, working with a previous-token head through K-composition. An attention pattern can be very informative and also misleading about what a head does.

    Does not prove: Anything about models with MLP layers, such as ours, without measuring them.

What this lesson leaves out

The model here is tiny: two layers on a made-up language of 46 words, so it can train in your browser in about a minute. Large models have dozens of layers and many heads, and their heads do jobs that are much harder to name. Where a head puts its light tells you where it reads from; on its own it does not tell you why the model answered as it did.

Next along the coast: the transformer block that attention sits in (L11), and attention rebuilt as one fast trip through the GPU (K23). Both are planned, not made yet.

items.title: Backpropagation: blame, passed backwards
items.description: A chain of buckets down the hill: how a network gets every number's slope in one walk back, checked number by number, then trained in your browser.
items.excerpt: Skip to content Zain Dana Harpernight school / F4 Backpropagation. Blame, passed backwards. A model needs the slope for every one of its numbers. Nudging each one costs a whole run apiece. Pylon's bucket chain shows the trick that gets them all in one walk back. The film About 4:59, hosted by Pylon. It asks you one question and waits for your answer before i
items.body_html:
The film

About 4:59, hosted by Pylon. It asks you one question and waits for your answer before it shows you. The narrated cut runs 3:50, voiced by Pylon in a synthesized voice made from the author's own voice; the author approved these cuts for publishing. Captions are on by default. The live version under it draws the same film in your browser, waits for your answer at each question, and runs a little longer; the full words are also below.

Play the film

Nothing loads until you press play.

The lab: Pylon's bucket chain

Train a 2-8-8-2 network (114 numbers) on two spirals, in your browser. Click any point to see its chain: the value in every bucket and the blame arriving at it. Check the walk back against nudging every number, then break one link on purpose and watch the check point at it. In the film's run, one walk back cost 208 multiply-adds against 98 for the forward pass, and the network was right on 99.8% of new points after 4,000 steps.

Fill the buckets

Everything is computed on your computer, in this page. Nothing is sent anywhere.

Everything the film says

Backpropagation

Backpropagation. Blame, passed backwards.

Last time I could feel the slope for two numbers. A model has thousands. Tonight, how it gets all their slopes in one go.

A chain of buckets

Here is a small network. It looks at a point on a map and says which of two spirals the point belongs to.

It has 114 numbers. Two go in at the top, pass through two layers of 8 buckets each, and come out as two guesses at the bottom.

Every bucket in the middle takes what the buckets above hand it, weighs it, adds it up, and squashes the total through a smooth curve. The last two turn their totals into two guesses that add up to one. That's the forward pass.

Feeling every slope by hand

At the bottom we measure how wrong it was: the loss. Now we want each of the 114 slopes.

The slow way: nudge one number, run the whole chain again, see how the loss moved. That's one extra run for every number. For the model from the attention lesson, that's 20,864 runs, for every single step of training.

Pass the blame back

The fast way runs the chain once, then walks it backwards.

How many backward walks does it take to get all the slopes? (the film pauses here)

Each bucket at the bottom knows how much the loss changes when its own output changes. It hands that blame up to each bucket that fed it, multiplied by how much its own output moved when that input moved. A bucket that fed several adds up the blame from all of them, then does the same, all the way to the top.

That's the chain rule from school, done in reverse order. Seppo Linnainmaa worked out this reverse order in 1970, and in 1986 Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams showed what it could do for training networks.

One walk back

One. A single walk back hands every number its slope.

Counting multiply-adds for one point, and leaving the curves aside: the forward pass takes 98, the backward pass 208, about 2.12 times as many. Not 114 extra runs. About two runs' worth.

Checking the chain

A walk back like this is easy to get slightly wrong, so we check it the slow way. Nudge every number, compare.

After training, they agree layer by layer to about one part in a billion, and the worst single number is off by about three parts in a hundred million.

Now I break one link on purpose: in the second layer, the curve's slope is written wrong. The check fails in that layer and every layer above it, and still passes in the last layer, below the break. The check doesn't just say something is wrong. It points to where.

Downhill, every number at once

Now put it together with last time: walk forward, walk back, step every number a little downhill, repeat.

On points it never trained on, the network starts out right 36 percent of the time. It is past 95 percent by step 2,000, and after 4,000 steps it gets 99.8 percent right.

The same walk, inside the language model

The model from the attention lesson walks forward and back the same way, with a backward pass written out by hand for every part: the attention, the layer norms, the bends. It steps downhill a little more cleverly, and that's next time.

We checked it the slow way too, on 36 of its numbers. In full precision the worst disagreement is a few parts in ten million.

Goodnight

Run forward once, pass the blame back once, and every number knows its slope.

Next along the hill: better ways to step than straight downhill. Goodnight.

Sources

Every claim in the film, with where it comes from and what that source does not prove. The numbers about the model are computed from its weights, which you can load and check: facts.json.

  • Night School's small network, built for this film. media/school/backprop/facts.json, written by tools/school/fill_backprop.mjs from system/school/backprop.mjs: a 2, 8, 8, 2 tanh network (114 numbers) on seeded two spirals, with a hand-written forward and backward pass and a finite-difference check of every number. https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/backprop

    Used for: Counted multiply-adds for one point: forward 98, backward 208 (ratio 2.12); tanh, exp and log calls counted apart. Finite-difference check of every number: worst tensor error 1.2e-9 after training; worst single entry 3.3e-8. With the second hidden layer's local slope written as 1 - a instead of 1 - a^2, the check fails for W1, b1, W2 and b2 and passes for W3 and b3. Held-out accuracy on 400 points, measured every 100 steps: 0.355 at the start, 0.95 reached by step 2,000, 0.9975 after 4,000 steps.

    Does not prove: Anything about large networks; one seed, one task.

  • Linnainmaa 1970, reverse-mode accumulation of rounding errors. Linnainmaa, S. (1970). The representation of the cumulative rounding error of an algorithm as a Taylor expansion of the local rounding errors. Master's thesis, University of Helsinki. https://people.idsia.ch/~juergen/who-invented-backpropagation.html

    Used for: Linnainmaa's 1970 thesis described what is now called reverse-mode automatic differentiation, for the accumulated rounding error of an algorithm; it was published in English in 1976, and the idea was also found independently by others, among them Werbos (1982) for networks.

    Does not prove: That the method was then used to train neural networks.

  • Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams 1986, Learning representations by back-propagating errors. Rumelhart, D. E., Hinton, G. E., Williams, R. J. (1986). Learning representations by back-propagating errors. Nature 323, 533-536. https://doi.org/10.1038/323533a0

    Used for: The paper describes back-propagation for networks of neuron-like units and shows that hidden units come to represent useful features of the task.

    Does not prove: That it was the first description of reverse-mode differentiation.

  • Griewank and Walther 2008, Evaluating Derivatives. Griewank, A., Walther, A. (2008). Evaluating Derivatives: Principles and Techniques of Algorithmic Differentiation, 2nd edition. SIAM. https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898717761

    Used for: Reverse mode computes the gradient of a scalar function at a cost bounded by a small constant times the cost of the function, whatever the number of inputs. Our count of 2.12 is the backward pass alone; forward plus backward is 3.12 times the forward pass.

    Does not prove: The exact constant for a given program; we measured ours.

  • Night School's tiny transformer, the attention lesson's trained weights. media/school/attention/model.json; system/school/backprop-attention.mjs checks tinyformer's hand-written backward pass by central differences. https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/backprop

    Used for: On 36 entries over 9 tensors, two held-out rows: worst relative error 2.9e-7 in float64; a control that drops the softmax Jacobian term fails 18 of 36. This model trains with AdamW, a warmup and gradient clipping, not plain gradient descent.

    Does not prove: That every entry is right; 36 of 20,864 were checked here (the lab's own test checks every tensor on a small model).

What this lesson leaves out

The network is tiny and the spirals are a toy task, so it trains in well under a second. Large models are trained the same way in principle, by software that writes the backward pass automatically rather than by hand.

The count of multiply-adds leaves out the curves (tanh, exp and log) and is for one point. The general bound for reverse mode is a small constant times the cost of the function; our measured 2.12 is one network, not that bound.

Before this: Gradients (F3). Next along the hill: optimisers (F5), planned.

items.title: Case study: a score that carries its receipt
items.description: Re-derive a published score from its receipt in your browser, flip any byte and watch the check fail, and see the one lie a receipt cannot catch.
headings: A score that carries its receipt.
16 October 2026: Flywheel closed the gap this lesson found
A score that carries its receipt
items.excerpt: Skip to content Zain Dana Harpernight school / E25 A score that carries its receipt. Flywheel's demonstration receipt says 40 of 50 and carries the fingerprints to prove its rows were not changed. Rerun recounts the rows, recomputes every fingerprint in this page, tampers with every byte, and finds the edit that only the true answers can catch. The film Abou
items.body_html:
The film

About 4:42, hosted by Rerun. It asks you one question and waits for your answer before it shows you. The guide's voice is not recorded yet, so for now the film plays with captions; the full words are also below.

Play the film

Nothing loads until you press play.

Since this lesson was made

16 October 2026: Flywheel closed the gap this lesson found

The film says Flywheel's verifier never recomputes the receipt's own identifier, and that it never reads the envelope's schema name or the signature's key name. That was true of the version this lesson checked (Flywheel at f04ef26). On 16 October 2026 Flywheel merged a fix, pull request 419 (commit 21d4669): its verifier now recomputes the identifier, checks the key name against the pinned key, and checks the schema name.

We reran the one-byte sweep of the receipt against both versions. Of 5,744 flipped copies, 1,315 no longer parse. The old verifier says the receipt still matches on 81 of the rest; the fixed one, on none. The signed lie in the film still passes any check that trusts the liar's key, and only the true answers catch it; the fix does not change that. The film, its numbers and the lab are left as measured against f04ef26.

The lab: the receipt

The real bundle, checked from scratch in this page. Flip any byte of any file and check again, or try a cheater's edits. In the film's sweep, all 2,892 flips of the rows file were caught, and 5,663 of 5,744 in the receipt.

Open the shell

The bundle is checked on your computer, in this page, with your browser's own SHA-256 and Ed25519. Nothing is sent anywhere.

Everything the film says

A score that carries its receipt

Case study: a score that carries its receipt.

In lesson E24 we saw a check that could be fooled. Tonight Rerun opens a score that comes with its own evidence, checks it from scratch, and finds out exactly what that evidence proves.

A claim and its receipt

Flywheel is our evaluation tool. In this demonstration a data owner runs an approved job on private questions, and the job writes one row per question: the answer given and whether it was right.

The result says 40 of 50. Beside it sits a receipt: a hash of the rows, a tree of hashes over every row, the hash of the approved job, a hash of the approval record, and a signature over the whole body.

Check it yourself

A hash is a fingerprint of bytes: change one byte and the fingerprint changes completely.

So we counted the rows ourselves: 40 of 50. Then we recomputed, in this page's own code, every fingerprint the files let us check, nine in all. Each matched the published value exactly. The approval record's hash and the model and data commitments cannot be recomputed from the bundle.

Flip any one byte of the rows file. Does the check catch every flip, most of them, or few? (the film pauses here)

One byte at a time

We flipped every byte of every file, one at a time, 10,960 tampered copies in all. In the rows file, all 2,892 of 2,892 were caught.

In the receipt itself, 5,663 of 5,744. The 81 missed bytes sit in two fields outside the signed body, the envelope's schema name and the signature's key name, which Flywheel's verifier never reads. The permissions file was caught 0 times in 108: the job's hash leaves it out on purpose.

Same score, different rows

A sneakier edit: swap the right and wrong marks on two rows. The count is still 40, so a check on the score alone passes.

The fingerprints do not. The rows' hash and the tree both change, and the receipt no longer matches.

What the receipt cannot see

Now the hard case. Someone signs a lie: they mark one wrong row as right, rebuild every fingerprint and sign again.

If we accept their key, every hash check passes, and the receipt is perfectly consistent. If we insist on a key we trusted before, the signature check catches the swap. But if the liar holds that trusted key, only the true answers, revealed afterwards, catch it.

A receipt proves the bytes have not changed since they were signed, and which key signed them. It cannot prove the rows were true when they were written. That needs a check against the truth, like the exact checker in lesson E24.

Found while checking

One more thing turned up. Flywheel's verifier never recomputes the receipt's own identifier. Flywheel's own test of a consistent lie rebuilds and signs everything except that identifier, and its verifier still says the receipt matches until the answers are revealed.

Our page checks the identifier too. That is a gap worth closing in Flywheel's verifier, and it is the point of a receipt anyone can recheck: an outside check found it.

Goodnight

Recount the rows, recompute the fingerprints, and remember what a signature cannot see.

Goodnight.

Sources

Every claim in the film, with where it comes from and what that source does not prove. The numbers about the model are computed from its weights, which you can load and check: facts.json, receipt.json, results.jsonl.

  • Flywheel: the PySyft result receipt. HarperZ9/flywheel at f04ef26, docs/features/pysyft-result-receipt.md. https://github.com/HarperZ9/flywheel/blob/f04ef26fda8e36e3f73521ebbc5e03c4220da72d/docs/features/pysyft-result-receipt.md

    Used for: What the receipt binds (rows by hash and Merkle root, the approved job by its hash, an Ed25519 signature over the canonical body) and what a stranger can and cannot check.

    Does not prove: That the hidden model or data were what the parties said (attestation is UNVERIFIABLE in the fixture).

  • Flywheel: the PySyft receipt fixture. HarperZ9/flywheel at f04ef26, tests/fixtures/pysyft_receipt/ (last changed at 7d47b8f), copied unchanged to media/school/receipts/. https://github.com/HarperZ9/flywheel/blob/f04ef26fda8e36e3f73521ebbc5e03c4220da72d/tests/fixtures/pysyft_receipt

    Used for: A demonstration job: 50 questions, 40 marked correct; the receipt's published hashes and signature.

    Does not prove: Anything about a real model; the job is a demonstration with a toy adder.

  • Flywheel's verifier. HarperZ9/flywheel at f04ef26, harness/job_result_verify.py. https://github.com/HarperZ9/flywheel/blob/f04ef26fda8e36e3f73521ebbc5e03c4220da72d/harness/job_result_verify.py

    Used for: Which checks the verifier runs; it does not recompute receipt_id.

    Does not prove: How the verifier behaves on other receipt types.

  • Night School's re-derivation and tamper sweep. media/school/receipts/facts.json, written by tools/school/fill_receipts.mjs from system/school/receipts*.mjs: every derived field recomputed with WebCrypto SHA-256, canonical JSON and an RFC 6962 Merkle tree; every byte of every file flipped once; four false-success controls; verdicts compared with Flywheel's own verifier on 8,636 tampers. https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/receipts

    Used for: All derived fields reproduce byte for byte; 40 of 50 re-derived; sweep counts per file; the consistent cheater passes every hash check and fails only against the revealed answers or a pinned honest key.

    Does not prove: Resistance to multi-byte edits by someone without the key beyond what hashes and signatures give by construction.

What this lesson leaves out

The receipt is Flywheel's demonstration fixture with a toy job, not a real model's evaluation.

A receipt proves the bytes have not changed since they were signed and which key signed them; it does not prove the rows were true, or that the run was the only one.

The sweep flips one byte at a time; edits by someone who holds the key are the signed lie the film shows.

Before this: When the check can be fooled (E24) and Evaluating a language model (L16). Earlier on this beach: The denoiser's tensor-core parity (K25).

items.title: Case study: our MMBU Challenge entry
items.description: Two weeks of fine-tuning a small model for a biomedical image contest: every bar written first, the misses kept, and what the logbook cannot prove.
headings: Our MMBU Challenge entry. The logbook, misses included.
The lab: redo the logbooks intervals
Between a guess and a cheat
Better at picking than at saying
items.excerpt: Skip to content Zain Dana Harpernight school / S20 Our MMBU Challenge entry. The logbook, misses included. For the MMBU Challenge we fine-tuned two small open models on 86 disclosed sources and wrote down every bar before the result it judged. Tallow opens the logbook: the runs that missed, the rule that turned away its own champion, a score that flipped sig
items.body_html:
The film

About 7:15, hosted by Tallow. It asks you one question and waits for your answer before it shows you. The guide's voice is not recorded yet, so for now the film plays with captions; the full words are also below.

Play the film

Nothing loads until you press play.

The lab: redo the logbook's intervals

Pick a comparison and the lab reruns the scorer's bootstrap on the published per-row scores, in this page, with numpy's own random stream ported to JavaScript. With the scorer's seed, 8 intervals come out to the logbook's printed digits, among them the candidacy bar, +0.0425 [0.0354, 0.0498], and both readings of the held-out context score. Another seed moves the bounds in the third or fourth decimal.

Open the logbook

The scores are loaded from this site and resampled on your computer. Nothing is sent anywhere.

Everything the film says

Our MMBU Challenge entry

Case study: our MMBU Challenge entry.

For two weeks this boatyard fine-tuned a small model for a public contest, writing down every bar before the result it would judge.

The contest

MMBU is a biomedical image benchmark from Stanford MARVL, built from 410 public datasets. A model answers each question about an image once, with no tools, and is scored on the answer and on context, such as what kind of image it is.

We trained small LoRA strips on two open Qwen 3.5 models, of 2.3 and 4.7 billion numbers, from 86 sources across all the runs, every one listed in our disclosure. This is benchmark work, not a medical tool, and every score tonight is from our own scorers, not the contest's judge.

The bar comes first

Before each result, we wrote down the comparison that would decide it and the bar it had to clear: usually, new model minus old on about 3,100 practice questions, with a bootstrap interval whose lower end sits above zero.

The fourth run added 20 public datasets, 17 of them ones we believe the benchmark draws on.

Seventeen of the benchmark's likely sources. Did the practice answers go up? (the film pauses here)

A miss, kept

No. The difference was -0.007, interval -0.018 to 0.004. Zero sits inside, so by the rule those rows did not go forward.

The fifth run gave the champion a second pass over its own rows: up 0.001, interval -0.007 to 0.009. Another miss, written down the same way a win is.

Between a guess and a cheat

Then a worrying number. The champion got 21.6 percent of the practice answers right. A guesser who could see the judge's options, which our model never sees, would average 20.7. A cheat giving each kind of question its most common answer, 23.7.

Was it even looking? Given blank pictures, the fourth run fell from 20.9 percent right to 8.2. It uses the picture. And 51 percent of its answers named none of the options at all.

Better at picking than at saying

So, for our eyes only, we showed the fifth run's model each option and measured how likely it found each one. Its favourite option was right 41 percent of the time; its written answer, 20.

Picking from a list is easier than writing, but much of the loss is in the words it writes. The rule chose the next step, training on the labels' own words, and on region questions the sixth run beat the fifth by 0.026, interval 0.008 to 0.044.

The rule that turned away its own champion

The sixth run cleared every answer bar but missed a format bar: valid replies 99.8 percent of the time, against a bar of 99.9. The champion it would replace scored only 99.6. As written, the bar turned away its own champion.

The verdict stood. For later runs we signed a new rule, while the seventh run was at step 20: replace the champion when every answer bar is met and the format is no worse. The seventh run met it, up 0.043 on our size-adjusted score, interval 0.035 to 0.050.

Whose words count

One number went the wrong way. On our held-out sources, the seventh run's context score fell 0.089 below the sixth run's.

It now answered in the benchmark paper's words, X-ray rather than X-ray imaging, while our answer key kept each source's old words. With the key rewritten in the paper's words, the same replies scored 0.152 higher. Neither key is neutral, and this re-score came after we saw the fall: a measurement, not a test.

Keeping the lamp lit

Each run takes a lock on the shared graphics card, saves every 50 steps, and has a watchdog. A shutdown mid-run lost nothing. Code that had never run idled the card for about 10 hours, and two trainers on one run cost 40 steps; now, when a check cannot tell if a trainer is alive, it counts it as alive.

What the logbook can prove

Every bar was fingerprinted into a ledger, and all 19 rule files still match it, 16 by full fingerprint and 3 by the short prefix it kept. But the ledger was meant to be pushed to GitHub, which stamps the time, before each result. Only entries up to 27 were, the last on 4 October.

Entries 28 to 89, every run tonight, were first pushed on 18 October, after the results; the ledger is now public. So the claim that each bar came before its score rests on our word. A fingerprint proves the bytes, not the hour.

Goodnight

The seventh run is the candidate; nothing has been submitted. The eighth stopped at step 500 of 1,918 when the author paused the work. The contest runs to 31 December 2026.

In the lab, redo eight of the logbook's intervals, digit for digit. Goodnight.

Sources

Every claim in the film, with where it comes from and what that source does not prove. The numbers about the model are computed from its weights, which you can load and check: facts.json, published.json, dev_per_row.json, heldout_context_per_row.json, heldout_task_per_row.json.

  • The MMBU benchmark paper. D'Cunha et al., MMBU: A Massive Multi-modal Biomedical Understanding Benchmark to Probe the Perception Capabilities of Vision-Language Models, arXiv 2606.06696, 4 June 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06696

    Used for: The benchmark curates 410 public datasets; each question pairs a biomedical image with a task; the paper's words for context fields (for example X-ray, Light Microscopy, specimen Human).

    Does not prove: Anything about our models, or the hidden test set's contents.

  • The MMBU Challenge site and brief. MMBU Challenge, organized by Stanford MARVL: challenge site and participant brief, read 2 to 9 October 2026. https://akiranishii.github.io/mmbu-challenge/

    Used for: One model, one pass per question, no tools or retrieval; answer (T) and context (C) scored, S = 0.8T + 0.2C; Track 3 for small models (the web page: at most 4B active and 12B total parameters; the brief of 9 October: a 4B model, counted as 4.66 billion total parameters), scaled by (4.66e9 / P)^0.1; training sources disclosed; deadline 31 December 2026, 23:30 Pacific (the organisers' Discord answer of 3 October).

    Does not prove: How the organisers' judge scores a given reply, or the final leaderboard.

  • Organiser rulings. MMBU organiser answers on the challenge Discord, 3 to 14 October 2026, as recorded in our run notes.

    Used for: "All datasets are acceptable as long as disclosed" (9 October); the public dev questions are for evaluation only; the 4B limit counts the vision tower and the embeddings.

    Does not prove: Rulings after 14 October.

  • Our preregistrations. MMBU run records: train/PREREG.md and train/ft2 to ft8 PREREG-*.md, each fingerprinted into the prereg ledger.

    Used for: Each run names its comparison and bar before its result: a paired bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed 20261002, percentile) on the public dev questions, lower bound above zero unless a non-inferiority margin is stated. Our answer scorer JP1 agreed with a blind re-grade of 180 earlier dev answers on 175, with no false accepts; the re-grade was done by the Claude session leading the work, the same model family as the official judge.

    Does not prove: That the files were written before the results; see the ledger source.

  • FT4 results. MMBU run records, train/ft4/bars_ft4_excl12.json (SHA-256 ca54d77a73c6); the run's preregistration, train/ft4/PREREG-FT4.md.

    Used for: FT4 added 20 public sources, 17 of them inferred MMBU sources (tier Q2) and 3 more (RIVA_PAP, DERM12345, FDG_PET_CT), plus 1,039 format copies: 29,421 rows. H1, dev answers FT4_4B minus FT3A_4B: -0.007 [-0.018, 0.004], not met (decided on 3,102 rows; the same verdict on 3,091 after the 12-row exclusion). The format copies arrived with the new sources, so the result cannot separate them.

    Does not prove: That those sources could not help with a different recipe.

  • FT5 results. MMBU run records, train/ft5/bars_ft5.json (SHA-256 b367b9703d49).

    Used for: K1, one more epoch from FT3A_4B over FT3A's rows plus the format copies: +0.001 [-0.007, 0.009], not met.

    Does not prove: Anything about longer schedules or other learning rates.

  • Baselines. MMBU run records, diag/baselines.json (SHA-256 d135ae4f7f0a); FT7_4B's dev answer score from train/ft7/bars_ft7.json (SHA-256 221bd716e8c9).

    Used for: Chance among the judge's options 0.2074; the most common answer per question family, left one out (an oracle the model cannot use), 0.2368; FT7_4B 0.2294 (JP1).

    Does not prove: What the official judge would score.

  • Blank-image audit. MMBU run records, diag/image_audit.json (SHA-256 6944a2c19847) (FT4_4B).

    Used for: Real images 0.2087; mean-colour blank images 0.0819; real minus blank +0.127 [0.113, 0.141]; 74.7% of answers change.

    Does not prove: That the model uses the image well, only that it uses it.

  • Where the model loses to the oracle. MMBU run records, diag/prior_gap.json (SHA-256 fcf37e9b3fd6) (FT4_4B).

    Used for: 51% of answers name no option; chest radiograph regions, 82 rows: model right 2 times, the oracle 40; surgical instrument tips, 54 rows: 7 against 31.

    Does not prove: Why the model words its answers off the option list.

  • Option-scoring readout. MMBU run records, diag/option_readout_FT5_4B.json (SHA-256 6aca907696fe); the rule was fixed in ledger entry 64 before the run.

    Used for: FT5_4B on 2,654 single-label rows: its top-scored option right 0.414, its generated answer right 0.197, difference +0.217 [0.198, 0.236]; the rule chose answer-vocabulary rows. The readout calls the gap wording and label recall, partly inferred, since picking from a closed list is easier than open generation.

    Does not prove: That option scoring could be used in the contest; it is an evaluation-only readout, since the rules allow one generated reply.

  • FT6 results. MMBU run records, train/ft6/bars_ft6.json (SHA-256 5fc665673356).

    Used for: M2, region-question answers, FT6_4B minus FT5_4B on 860 rows: +0.026 [0.008, 0.044], met; M5, Pass 2 replies valid 0.9984 against a bar of 0.999, not met; M6, 3,090 of 3,091 Pass 1 replies hold an answer, not met.

    Does not prove: Held-out behaviour beyond bar M4.

  • FT7 amendment 2. MMBU run records, train/ft7/PREREG-FT7-AMENDMENT-2.md (SHA-256 a8663983c53b), ledger entry 79: signed 07:13:43Z on 16 October 2026, while FT7 was at step 20 and no FT7 output existed.

    Used for: The absolute format bars also rejected the standing candidate, FT3A_4B (Pass 2 valid 0.9958, 3,089 of 3,091). The new rule, for later runs: replace the candidate when every answer bar is met and the format is no worse than the candidate's.

    Does not prove: The signing time, beyond our own record; see the ledger source.

  • FT7 results. MMBU run records, train/ft7/bars_ft7.json (SHA-256 221bd716e8c9).

    Used for: N4, adjusted S, FT7_4B minus FT3A_4B: +0.043 [0.035, 0.050], met; N5, held-out answers: +0.021 [0.007, 0.036] (non-inferiority, margin 0.02), met; FT7_4B became the candidate.

    Does not prove: The hidden test set's result.

  • Held-out vocabulary re-score. MMBU run records, train/heldout_vocab/heldout_vocab_ft7.json (SHA-256 6cb68387f23b); preregistration train/heldout_vocab/PREREG-HELDOUT-VOCAB.md; ledger entries 87 and 88.

    Used for: FT7 minus FT6 held-out context: -0.089 [-0.103, -0.076] under the sources' own labels, +0.152 [0.135, 0.172] under labels rewritten to the paper's words (light microscopy 400 rows, X-ray 150, ultrasound 101, specimen 250). Post hoc for FT6 and FT7; preregistered for FT8 only.

    Does not prove: Which key is right; neither is neutral.

  • The survival record. MMBU status notes (STATUS-2026-10-15.md) and ledger entries 54, 73 to 76 and 84.

    Used for: Checkpoints every 50 steps; FT7 saved step 665 in 0.53 s on a shutdown and resumed about 6.2 hours later with no step lost; the FT5_4B init_lora crash idled the GPU about 10 hours; a duplicate trainer after an app restart cost 40 steps and about 30 minutes; the liveness check now fails closed; FT8 stopped at step 500 of 1,918 when the author paused the work on 16 October 2026.

    Does not prove: That no other failure mode remains.

  • The prereg ledger. HarperZ9/prereg-ledger, ATTESTATIONS.md, read with git on 17 October 2026: entries to 89 in the local file; the remote holds entries to 27, last pushed 4 October 2026; the repository is private.

    Used for: All 19 preregistration and amendment files match the ledger, 16 to a full SHA-256 and 3 to the 8-character prefix the ledger recorded (re-hashed 17 October 2026). Entries 28 to 89 were never committed or pushed, so no outside timestamp backs their order, and a file and its local fingerprint line could have been changed together.

    Does not prove: When entries 28 to 89 were written.

  • Night School's re-derivation. media/school/mmbu/facts.json, written by tools/school/fill_mmbu.mjs: numpy's SeedSequence, PCG64 and integers ported to JavaScript (system/school/mmbu-rng.mjs, checked against numpy), and the scorers' bootstraps re-run on the published per-row scores (media/school/mmbu/data/). https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/mmbu

    Used for: K1, M1, N1, N3, N4, N5 and both held-out vocabulary intervals reproduce to the printed digits.

    Does not prove: That the per-row scores are right; they come from our local scorers.

What this lesson leaves out

Every score here comes from our own local scorers. The contest's judge was never called, and dev scores will not match the final leaderboard. Nothing has been submitted.

This is benchmark work. The images are benchmark data, and nothing here is a medical tool or a clinical claim.

The ledger's fingerprints still match the rule files, but only entries up to 27 were pushed to GitHub before the results, the last on 2026-10-04; entries 28 to 89, which cover every run in the film, were first pushed on 2026-10-18, after the results, and the ledger is now public. So the claim that each bar came before its result has no outside timestamp before that date for those runs.

The held-out vocabulary re-score (FT7 minus FT6: -0.08946 under the sources' words, +0.15225 under the paper's) was made after the fall was seen, so for these runs it is a measurement, not a test. The eighth run's reading was preregistered, but that run was paused before it was scored.

MMBU work is paused: the eighth run stopped at step 500 of 1,918 when the author paused it on 16 October 2026. The contest runs to 31 December 2026.

The lab re-derives the arithmetic from the published per-row scores. It does not check that those scores are right; they come from our scorers.

Before this: LoRA and fine-tuning (S19), Evaluating a language model (L16) and When the check can be fooled (E24). The same lesson about fingerprints, from the other side: A score that carries its receipt (E25).

items.title: Case study: the denoiser's tensor-core parity
items.description: A parity check that failed: 16-bit tensor-core arithmetic against a fixed bound, the sun glint that broke it, fixes that fell short, and a bound that stayed.
items.excerpt: Skip to content Zain Dana Harpernight school / K25 The denoiser's tensor-core parity. raw-native's neural denoiser runs on the tensor cores with 16-bit inputs and weights, or in plain 32-bit. On an RTX 4090 the tensor-core path missed its parity bound of 0.01 by ten times, at one sun glint. Rerun follows the search for why, and the fix that was not made: mov
items.body_html:
The film

About 6:37, hosted by Rerun. It asks you one question and waits for your answer before it shows you. The guide's voice is not recorded yet, so for now the film plays with captions; the full words are also below.

Play the film

Nothing loads until you press play.

The lab: the parity check

Pick a version of the arithmetic, a seed and whether the image has its glint, and run every pixel against the exact value with raw-native's own bound and measure. The image is a small synthetic stand-in built to the note's magnitudes: with the glint, the tensor-core arithmetic missed on 18 of 576 pixels at seed 1. The real chip's figure was 0.106689.

Raise the prism

Everything is computed on your computer, in this page. Nothing is sent anywhere.

Everything the film says

The denoiser's tensor-core parity

Case study: the denoiser's tensor-core parity.

Last lesson measured where 16-bit numbers run out. Tonight Rerun follows a real case where they did: a check that failed, the search for why, and the fix that was not made.

Two paths, one check

raw-native is a renderer with a small neural denoiser. Its network runs two ways on the graphics chip: one on the tensor cores, with 16-bit inputs and weights and 32-bit sums, and one in plain 32-bit arithmetic.

Before either ships, a parity check compares every output value with a reference. The rule is fixed in advance: no value may differ by more than 0.01.

On an RTX 4090, over 64 frames, the 32-bit path's worst difference was 0.0029. The tensor-core path's was 0.1067, at frame 48.

The tensor-core path missed by ten times the bound. Wrong everywhere, or in a few places? (the film pauses here)

A few places

In a few places. Out of 24,883,200 values, the average difference was about six millionths, and 99.99 percent were under 0.0018.

A check on the average would have passed. This one asks for the worst value, so one bad pixel is enough to fail it.

Reproduce before fixing

Before trying any fix, the note on this miss wrote down its predictions, then ran the network on the main processor with the same 16-bit rounding.

The emulation missed by 0.1085, at the same frame and the same pixel as the chip. So 16-bit arithmetic alone reproduces the miss; no fault in the chip is needed to explain it.

The note had set out two guesses: the weights alone, or the inputs alone. Both were refuted as stated. Rounding only the weights gave 0.1370, and rounding only the inputs gave 0.1041, so either rounding by itself misses the bound.

A sun glint

The bad pixels were single sun glints. At frame 48, one sample on a glossy surface carried 1,087 units of light beside neighbours near 0.1.

The denoiser first divides by the surface's specular reflectance, 0.04 plus a small 0.01, which turns that sample into about 21,700. Its five by five filter then weighs it down to around a hundred: the note gives 105, against a reference of 110.

The arithmetic

Now the bound. Missing by no more than 0.01 on a value of 110 asks for about one part in ten thousand. Near 110, 16-bit marks are 0.0625 apart, as we measured last lesson.

The filter itself runs in 32-bit. The rounding happens earlier, in the 16-bit layers that compute the filter's weights. 16-bit numbers hold about one part in a thousand, and any error that size feeding the filter, times a value of 110, moves the answer by about a tenth.

We rebuilt that step at small scale, with a made-up glint of the same size. In our seeded case the stand-in misses by 0.0789 with 16-bit inputs and weights, and differs by only 0.00002289 in 32-bit; across 200 seeds it misses in 180. Take the glint away and every version passes. These are the stand-in's numbers, not the real network's.

Fixes that fell short

The natural fix is mixed precision: keep the most sensitive layers in 32-bit and the rest on the tensor cores.

In the emulation, with the full-resolution head in 32-bit, the worst difference fell to 0.0512. With three layers, 0.0341. With six, 0.0340, on 4 pixels. Still over.

None of the mixed splits tried met the bound; 32-bit throughout did.

The bound stays

So the tensor-core path stays unchanged this round, and its parity check still fails. The options named are 32-bit throughout, which costs speed, or a model change that keeps the filter away from values that large, for example filtering a squeezed range and expanding it after, which also affects image quality.

And the note says plainly that the bound is not loosened. In our view that is the lesson: a bound loosened after the miss is seen no longer tests the result. It is fitted to it.

Goodnight

Reproduce the miss, find the arithmetic, and leave the post where you planted it.

Goodnight.

Sources

Every claim in the film, with where it comes from and what that source does not prove. The numbers about the model are computed from its weights, which you can load and check: facts.json.

  • raw-native parity run on an RTX 4090. HarperZ9/raw-native at 9de6582, evidence/rr-h2-v4/rtx4090/v4-parity-raw_hero-validation.json. https://github.com/HarperZ9/raw-native/blob/9de6582e822c6eb1eca63de39f857e1be8913b5d/evidence/rr-h2-v4/rtx4090/v4-parity-raw_hero-validation.json

    Used for: Tensor-core path max absolute difference 0.106689 at frame 48, pixel 64580; scalar fp32 path 0.00290298; 64 frames, 24,883,200 values each; p99.99 upper 0.00176668 for the tensor-core path; the perturbed-weights control fails as required.

    Does not prove: Behaviour on other GPUs, other scenes or other network versions.

  • raw-native inference bounds. HarperZ9/raw-native at 9de6582, evidence/rr-inference-bounds.json and the parity measure in vk_rrnet.cpp. https://github.com/HarperZ9/raw-native/blob/9de6582e822c6eb1eca63de39f857e1be8913b5d/evidence/rr-inference-bounds.json

    Used for: The parity bound: maximum absolute difference at most 1e-2, measured per value in double over every value.

    Does not prove: That 1e-2 is the right bound for image quality; it is the bound set in advance.

  • raw-native evidence note on the tensor-core parity miss, 15 October 2026. HarperZ9/raw-native at 9de6582, evidence/rr-tc-note-2026-10-15.json (last changed at 6c06e62). https://github.com/HarperZ9/raw-native/blob/9de6582e822c6eb1eca63de39f857e1be8913b5d/evidence/rr-tc-note-2026-10-15.json

    Used for: Predictions written before the emulation; weights-only hypothesis refuted; single-sample specular fireflies (radiance 1,087 beside neighbours near 0.1, demodulated by 0.05 to about 21,700, filtered to about 105 against a reference of 110); per-layer and mixed-precision results; decision: no change this round and the bound is not loosened.

    Does not prove: That PyTorch's emulation reproduces the tensor cores' summation order.

  • raw-native CPU emulations W, A and WA. HarperZ9/raw-native at 9de6582, evidence/rr-tc-2026-10-15/emu-W.json, emu-A.json, emu-WA.json (commit a0e2cc0). https://github.com/HarperZ9/raw-native/blob/9de6582e822c6eb1eca63de39f857e1be8913b5d/evidence/rr-tc-2026-10-15/emu-WA.json

    Used for: WA max 0.108489990234375 at frame 48, pixel 64580; W 0.13702392578125; A 0.104095458984375.

    Does not prove: The GPU's exact arithmetic; it agrees on the worst location and the order of the miss.

  • raw-native mixed-precision runs. HarperZ9/raw-native at 9de6582, evidence/rr-tc-2026-10-15/keep-10.json, keep-10_1_9.json, keep-10_1_9_8_0_3.json. https://github.com/HarperZ9/raw-native/blob/9de6582e822c6eb1eca63de39f857e1be8913b5d/evidence/rr-tc-2026-10-15/keep-10.json

    Used for: Layer 10 in fp32: 0.0512 (25 pixels over); layers 10, 1, 9: 0.0341 (12); layers 10, 1, 9, 8, 0, 3: 0.0340 (4).

    Does not prove: That no other mixed-precision split would pass.

  • Night School's small re-creation of the denoiser's arithmetic. media/school/denoiser/facts.json, written by tools/school/fill_denoiser.mjs from system/school/denoiser.mjs: one convolution step and the 5 x 5 softmax filter with a synthetic glint of the note's magnitudes, in fp32, fp16 and bf16 variants, against raw-native's own bound and measure. https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/denoiser

    Used for: The re-created tensor-core arithmetic misses at the glint pixel and the fp32 path passes; without the glint every variant passes.

    Does not prove: Anything numeric about raw-native's network: the real frame, weights and 12 layers are not in its evidence, so every re-created number is synthetic.

  • Night School's precision measurements (lesson K24). media/school/precision/facts.json, written by tools/school/fill_precision.mjs. https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/precision

    Used for: Near 110, fp16 values are 0.0625 apart.

    Does not prove: Anything about the denoiser by itself.

What this lesson leaves out

The film's figures for the real denoiser come from raw-native's published evidence; the re-creation is synthetic, because the frame's pixel values and the network's weights are not in that evidence.

The emulations ran on a processor, not the tensor cores, so their summation order may differ from the chip's; they agree with it on the worst frame and pixel.

Three mixed-precision splits were tried, down to 0.0340; other splits were not, so the film says none of those tried met the bound.

Before this: Mixed precision (K24). Next, on the same beach: A score that carries its receipt (E25).

items.title: Data: what goes in comes out
items.description: The same model trained on different crates: how much of a skill's data it needs, what wrong labels and repeated rows do, and what it never saw.
headings: Data. What goes in comes out.
A skill in one frame only
The same rows, over and over
items.excerpt: Skip to content Zain Dana Harpernight school / L13 Data. What goes in comes out. A model learns whatever is in its training crates. Pylon changes what goes in, trains the same model the same way, and shows what comes out. The film About 4:26, hosted by Pylon. It asks you two questions and waits for your answer before it shows you. The guide's voice is not re
items.body_html:
The film

About 4:26, hosted by Pylon. It asks you two questions and waits for your answer before it shows you. The guide's voice is not recorded yet, so for now the film plays with captions; the full words are also below.

Play the film

Nothing loads until you press play.

The lab: the crate yard

Choose how many episodes need a look back, how many labels are wrong, and fresh rows or a small repeated pile; train the model in this page and score it on held-out rows. In the film, cutting look-back episodes from 80% to 5% took look-back words from 99% right to 19%.

Open the crate yard

Everything is computed on your computer, in this page. Nothing is sent anywhere.

Everything the film says

Data

Data. What goes in comes out.

The loop from last time learns whatever is in the crates. Tonight we change what goes in, train the same model the same way, and see what comes out.

What is in the crates

The guides' sentences come in three kinds of episode. In copy episodes, a thing found earlier has to come back later. In who episodes, a question has to be answered with the guide who did the deed. Plain episodes need no looking back at all.

In the usual mix, 80 percent of episodes need a look back. Trained on that, the model gets look-back words right 99 percent of the time.

How much is enough

Now cut the look-back episodes down, and keep everything else the same.

Cut the look-back episodes from most of the crates to a twentieth. How much of the skill survives? (the film pauses here)

At 40 percent, it still gets 99 percent right. At 20 percent, 56. At 5 percent, 19.

And with none at all, the model is right 3 percent of the time, less than the untrained model's 7. Its loss on unseen rows is 8.25, worse than before it was trained. It learned to be sure, and wrong.

A skill in one frame only

Take out only the copy episodes, and keep the who episodes, which also need a look back.

On who questions, the model is still right 100 percent of the time. On copy episodes, a kind it never saw in training, 5 percent. The looking back did not carry over to a kind of sentence it had never seen.

Wrong labels

Now swap 10 percent of the training answers for random words.

Ordinary next words barely notice: still right 70 percent of the time. But the look-back skill comes slower: after the same training it gets look-back words right only 76 percent of the time. Copy episodes stay at 100 percent; the who questions take the loss, at 70. At 30 percent noise, look-back words drop to 33.

The same rows, over and over

Last, keep the amount of text the same, but draw it from a small pile of rows, used again and again.

Same amount of text, but only 64 different rows. Better, worse, or the same? (the film pauses here)

With 64 rows, each seen 500 times, the model learns the pile by heart and fails on new rows: a held-out loss of 3.02. Its held-out loss was lowest at the first check, step 100, and only got worse as it learned the pile.

With 1,024 rows: 0.71. With fresh rows every step: 0.69.

Never seen it done

One more crate. Train a model on sentences where Rerun never does the deed in a who episode. Then ask it who did something, when the answer is Rerun.

It names the right guide 0 percent of the time. When the answer is Tallow or Pylon, 100 percent. It has learned its crates faithfully, and its crates never showed Rerun doing it.

Goodnight

A model knows the world through its crates. Whatever is rare in them is weak in the model, and whatever is missing from them is missing from it.

Next in the lighthouse: what happens when the model and the crates get bigger. Goodnight.

Sources

Every claim in the film, with where it comes from and what that source does not prove. The numbers about the model are computed from its weights, which you can load and check: facts.json.

  • Night School's attention model, retrained on altered crates for this film. media/school/data/facts.json, written by tools/school/fill_data.mjs from system/school/data.mjs: the same model, seeds and 2,000 steps on altered training data (look-back share, copy episodes removed, label noise, a small repeated pool, a guide never shown in one role), each scored on the same 256 held-out rows; the default recipe reproduces the lesson's curve exactly. https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/data

    Used for: Look-back accuracy by look-back share of episodes: 0: 0.0316, 0.01: 0.1798, 0.05: 0.1917, 0.2: 0.5593, 0.4: 0.9862, 0.8: 0.9921; with none, held-out loss 8.2495 (untrained 3.84). Copy episodes removed: who look-back 1, copy-only rows 0.0464. Label noise 10% and 30%: look-back 0.7609 and 0.3281; local accuracy 0.7001. Pools of 64, 256 and 1,024 rows at the same tokens: held-out 3.0157, 1.7508, 0.7062; fresh rows 0.6874. Rerun never the doer in training: names Rerun 0 of the time when he is the answer, others 1.

    Does not prove: How much data a skill needs in large models; the removed-copy result could come from the missing sentence frame as much as from the missing skill.

What this lesson leaves out

One small model and one seed per mix (three at two of them): the shapes are clear, the exact thresholds are not general.

Removing copy episodes removes a sentence frame as well as a skill, so the failure to carry over cannot be pinned on one of them alone.

Before this: The training loop (L12). Next: Scaling (L14).

items.title: Decoding: temperature, top-k, top-p
items.description: How a language model's spread of belief becomes text: greedy choice, sampling, temperature, top-k and top-p, measured against the rules.
headings: Top-p: as many as it takes
items.excerpt: Skip to content Zain Dana Harpernight school / L15 Decoding. Turning guesses into sentences. A model's guess is a spread over every word, and a sentence needs one word at a time. Tallow spins the wheel, and shows what each way of cutting it writes. The film About 5:52, hosted by Tallow. It asks you two questions and waits for your answer before it shows you.
items.body_html:
The film

About 5:52, hosted by Tallow. It asks you two questions and waits for your answer before it shows you. The guide's voice is not recorded yet, so for now the film plays with captions; the full words are also below.

Play the film

Nothing loads until you press play.

The lab: the wheel room

Give the model a start, cut the wheel by temperature, top-k or top-p, and spin once or two hundred times; each run is checked against the rules that wrote the guides' sentences. From pylon at temperature 1, 89% of runs follow the rules; at temperature 2, 11%.

Open the wheel room
