Everything is computed on your computer, in this page. Nothing is sent anywhere.

Everything the film says

Decoding

Decoding. Turning guesses into sentences.

In the lesson on next-word prediction, the model's guess was a spread of belief over every word. A sentence needs one word at a time. Tonight, how the choosing is done, and what each way of choosing does.

Always the widest

The simplest way: always take the widest slot. That is called greedy decoding.

Start the model on pylon and let it run. It writes: pylon found a kettle. Pylon put a cone on the kettle. Pylon found a kettle. And again, until the page runs out.

Why the kettle every time? After found a, the rules choose among 10 things equally, but the model leans a little: kettle gets 14 percent. A small lean, taken every time, becomes the only story it tells.

Spin the wheel

The other way: spin a wheel where each word's slot is as wide as its share, and take whatever comes up.

We spun it 1,500 times from the same start. Those runs wrote 1,482 different texts, and 89 percent of the runs could have been written by the rules.

Our check for that is strict. It parses each run with the rules themselves, including the long-range ones: the cone goes on the thing that was found, and the answer to who names the guide who did it.

Temperature

Before the wheel is cut, the scores can be divided by a number called the temperature. Below 1, the wide slots get wider and the thin ones shrink. Above 1, the shares move toward even.

After tallow found a, the kettle's slot is 20 percent of the wheel at temperature 0.5, and 11 percent at temperature 2, where words that make no sense there get bigger slots too.

Turn the temperature up to 2. What share of runs will still follow the rules? (the film pauses here)

At temperature 0.5, 98 percent of runs follow the rules. At 1, 89. At 1.5, 51. At 2, only 11.

And at temperature close to zero, the widest slot takes the whole wheel. In 200 spins at 0.01, every run was the greedy one.

Top-k: only the widest few

Another fix cuts the wheel down to the k widest slots before spinning. Fan and colleagues used ten for writing stories in 2018.

With k at 3, after tallow found a, the wheel keeps 3 slots: kettle, map and crate. The other things that could be found are never written there at all.

The catch is that k never changes. Where only two words make sense, three slots is one too many. Where ten make sense, three is too few.

Top-p: as many as it takes

Holtzman and colleagues, in 2020, cut the wheel by share instead: keep the widest slots until together they reach p, and drop the rest. Where the model is sure, that is one or two words. Where it is torn, it is many.

With p at 0.9, after tallow found a, the wheel keeps 9 slots. Runs that follow the rules: 94 percent.

Push p down to 0.5 and nearly every run follows the rules, 99.7 percent. But its 1,500 runs wrote only 210 different texts. Safe, and samey.

Nearly every run follows the rules. What has it given up? (the film pauses here)

What we did not find

That paper also found that plain spinning, at temperature 1, drifts into nonsense in big models. Thousands of unlikely words each get a sliver of the wheel, and together the slivers add up to far too much.

Ours shows a small version. At temperature 1, 4 percent of runs contain a word pair it never saw in training. Top-p at 0.9 lets none through, and rule-following rises from 89 to 94 percent.

The paper's other warning sign does not show here: scoring its own runs, the model is torn between 1.87 words per step, and scoring the rules' own runs, 1.92. With only 46 words, the tail is short. The full problem needs a bigger model to see.

Goodnight

Greedy tells one story forever. Spinning tells many. Temperature, top-k and top-p decide how wide the wheel's slots are before it spins.

Next in the lighthouse: how to tell whether a language model is any good. Goodnight.

Sources

Every claim in the film, with where it comes from and what that source does not prove. The numbers about the model are computed from its weights, which you can load and check: facts.json.

  • Night School's attention model, sampled for this film. media/school/decoding/facts.json, written by tools/school/fill_decoding.mjs from system/school/decoding.mjs and corpus-grammar.mjs: 1,500 continuations per setting from three prompts with shared random streams, judged by a parser of the corpus generator's own rules. https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/decoding

    Used for: From the prompt 'pylon', greedy decoding writes 'found a kettle . pylon put a cone on the kettle . pylon found a kettle ...'. Grammatical share from 'pylon': temperature 0.5 0.9807, 1 0.8907, 1.5 0.5107, 2 0.106; top-k 3 0.9487; top-p 0.9 0.9447, 0.5 0.9973; uniform 0; generator 1. Distinct continuations per run from 'pylon': temperature 1 0.988, top-p 0.5 0.14. After 'tallow found a': kettle's share is 0.197 at temperature 0.5 and 0.110 at temperature 2; top-k 3 keeps kettle, map and crate; top-p 0.9 keeps 9 words. Temperature 0.01 reproduces greedy in 200 of 200 runs. Model perplexity of its own temperature-1 runs from 'pylon': 1.873; of the generator's runs: 1.921.

    Does not prove: That any setting is best for large models or human text.

  • Fan, Lewis and Dauphin 2018, Hierarchical Neural Story Generation. Fan, A., Lewis, M., Dauphin, Y. (2018). Hierarchical Neural Story Generation. ACL 2018. arXiv:1805.04833. https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.04833

    Used for: Stories are generated by sampling from the k = 10 most likely words (top-k sampling); beam search tends to produce common, repetitive phrases.

    Does not prove: Anything about this model.

  • Holtzman and others 2020, The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration. Holtzman, A., Buys, J., Du, L., Forbes, M., Choi, Y. (2020). The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration. ICLR 2020. arXiv:1904.09751. https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.09751

    Used for: Nucleus (top-p) sampling samples from the smallest set of most likely words whose total probability reaches p. Maximization-based decoding such as greedy and beam search produces repetitive text; pure sampling from the full distribution produces incoherent text through the unreliable low-probability tail.

    Does not prove: Anything about this model.

What this lesson leaves out

One small model and a 46-word grammar: a setting that does well here is not shown to do well on open-ended text, and the papers' main findings are about large models.

Following the rules is a strict check, but not the only one that matters: a run can follow every rule and still say nothing new.

Before this: Next-word prediction (L9). Next: evaluating a language model (L16), planned.

items.title: Distillation: a big teacher, a small student
items.description: Train a small model on a big one's guesses instead of the text alone: when the teacher's soft answers help, and when the text is enough.
headings: Distillation. A big teacher, a small student.
items.excerpt: Skip to content Zain Dana Harpernight school / S17 Distillation. A big teacher, a small student. A big model is costly to run. Tallow trains a student a fifth its size on the attention model's whole wheel of guesses, at several temperatures, and measures when that beats the text's own words. The film About 7:02, hosted by Tallow. It asks you two questions an
items.body_html:
The film

About 7:02, hosted by Tallow. It asks you two questions and waits for your answer before it shows you. The guide's voice is not recorded yet, so for now the film plays with captions; the full words are also below.

Play the film

Nothing loads until you press play.

The lab: two wheels

Choose what the student learns from (the text's words, the teacher's wheel at a temperature, the teacher's top word, or the rules' own odds) and how much text it sees; train it in this page and watch its wheel and held-out loss. In the film, on 32 rows the text's words ended at a held-out loss of 4.80 and the teacher's wheel at 1.64; on fresh text, 0.72 and 0.74.

Light the lamp

Everything is computed on your computer, in this page. Nothing is sent anywhere.

Everything the film says

Distillation

Distillation. A big teacher, a small student.

A big model is slow and costly to run. One way to get a small one is to train it on what the big one says, instead of on the text alone. Tonight the attention model teaches a student a fifth its size, and we find out when that helps.

Two kinds of answer

After "rerun knocked", the rules that write the guides' sentences say "on" half the time and "twice" the other half.

The text itself only ever shows one. A sentence says "on", and that is the answer the model is marked against: a hard label, one word, as if the other had been impossible. Only across many sentences does the split show.

The teacher's own guess keeps the split: 54 percent "twice", 45 percent "on". That is a soft target, the whole wheel instead of one slot.

Open choices like this are common. On 40 percent of the words in our held-out text, the likeliest next word has no more than three quarters of the odds.

Turning up the temperature

Hinton, Vinyals and Dean, in 2015, added one more trick. Before the teacher's scores become shares, divide them by a number they called the temperature.

At a temperature of 1 the wheel is the teacher's own. At 2 and 4 the big slots shrink and the slivers grow, so the student hears more about the words the teacher thinks are unlikely, and how unlikely.

The student matches the softened wheel with its own wheel, softened the same way. The paper multiplies that loss by the temperature squared, so the push stays about the same size whatever the temperature.

Our student has 4,112 numbers, 20 percent of the teacher's 20,864: one floor instead of two, and lists of 16 numbers per word instead of 32.

With plenty of text

First, give the student all the fresh text it wants: 2,000 steps, new sentences every step, three students of each kind with different seeds.

With all the text it wants, does the student learn more from the teacher's wheel than from the text's own words? (the film pauses here)

Trained on the text's own words, the student's held-out loss is 0.72. On the teacher's wheel: 0.70 at temperature 1, 0.74 at 2, 0.72 at 4. None of those differences holds up across the three seeds. Only temperature 8 is clearly different, and it is worse, by 0.04. Some students never learned to look back, whichever way they were taught, and those runs swing the averages.

So with plenty of text, we saw no gain from the teacher that three seeds could confirm. The teacher did make the student more like itself: at temperature 2, students taught by the wheel pick the teacher's top word 92 percent of the time, against 83 for students taught by the text.

With very little text

Hinton and his colleagues made a stronger claim: soft targets carry what the teacher learned to a student that sees very little data.

So give the student only 32 rows of 24 words, and show it the same rows over and over, 1,000 times each.

Now the student gets only 32 rows, over and over. The text's words, or the teacher's wheel? (the film pauses here)

Trained on those rows' own words, the student learns them by heart. Its held-out loss was 1.72 at its best check and 4.80 by the end. On the teacher's wheel for the same rows, its best check was 1.39, and it ended at 1.64. Best against best, every seed agrees.

With 256 rows, the text's words give 0.90 at best and 1.28 by the end, and the teacher's wheel 0.73, close to the teacher's own 0.69.

One caution. The teacher learned from far more text than these rows. What crosses over is what the teacher already knew, carried in its wheel.

Two teachers that fail

A teacher can fail in two ways. Take only the teacher's top word, and train on it as if it were certain. The student copies look-back words well, 95 percent right, but its held-out loss is 3.84, worse than just counting how often each word appears, 3.27. Where the text could go more than one way, it is sure of one word, and pays heavily whenever the text picks another.

Or take a teacher that never trained. Its wheel is close to even, and its student ends at 3.84, worse than counting words too.

And a perfect answer key, the rules' own odds, gives 0.69 with plenty of text, about what the teacher itself scores. It beat the text alone in all three seeds, but by too little for three seeds to settle.

Goodnight

A small model can learn a lot from how a big one hesitates, most of all when there is little else to learn from. For our student, with text that never ran out, the text was enough. With a fixed training set, Hinton's team found a gain even then.

Next in the boatyard: teaching a trained model a new job by fitting a small rudder, instead of rebuilding the hull. Goodnight.

Sources

Every claim in the film, with where it comes from and what that source does not prove. The numbers about the model are computed from its weights, which you can load and check: facts.json.

  • Night School's distillation runs, trained for this film. media/school/distill/facts.json, written by tools/school/fill_distill.mjs from system/school/distill.mjs: the attention lesson's model as teacher; a one-floor student of 4,112 numbers trained 2,000 steps on hard labels, the teacher's soft targets at temperatures 1, 2, 4, 8, a half-and-half mix, the teacher's top word, the generator's exact odds, and an untrained teacher; fresh text and fixed pools of 32 and 256 rows; 3 seeds per arm; paired differences called resolved only when every seed agrees in sign and the mean is over two standard errors. https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/distill

    Used for: Full data: hard 0.7213, soft T1 0.7019, T2 0.7355, T4 0.7229 (none resolved against hard), T8 0.7612 (worse, resolved). 32-row pool: hard 4.801 at the end (best 1.720), soft T2 1.637 (resolved better); 256-row pool: hard 1.276, soft T2 0.727. Top word as certain: held-out 3.843, copy accuracy 0.947; untrained teacher 3.839; word counts 3.273.

    Does not prove: Anything about large models; the teacher learned from far more text than the pools, so the low-data result is transfer through the teacher, not learning from 32 rows.

  • Hinton, Vinyals and Dean 2015, Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network. Hinton, G., Vinyals, O., Dean, J. (2015). Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network. arXiv:1503.02531 (NIPS 2014 Deep Learning Workshop). https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.02531

    Used for: Train a small model on the soft targets of a large one, raising the temperature of the final softmax; the soft-target loss is scaled by T squared to keep gradient magnitudes comparable. Soft targets let a model trained on very little data (3 percent of the speech training set) keep much of the full model's accuracy.

    Does not prove: Anything about this model.

What this lesson leaves out

One teacher of 20,864 numbers and one student of 4,112, three seeds per arm: the results say what happens here, not how much distillation helps a large model.

The teacher learned from far more text than the small pools, so the low-data result is what crosses over through the teacher's wheel, not learning from a few rows alone.

The best checkpoint on a pool is read off the held-out rows themselves, which flatters every arm equally.

Before this: The training loop (L12). Next in the boatyard: LoRA and fine-tuning (S19).

items.title: Dynamic programming: remember what you already worked out
items.description: Edit distance two ways: trying every way, with billions of calls, and the table that solves each smaller question once. Plus a shortcut that fails.
headings: Dynamic programming. Remember what you already worked out.
items.excerpt: Skip to content Zain Dana Harpernight school / A27 Dynamic programming. Remember what you already worked out. How many single-letter edits turn one word into another? Rerun tries every way and counts the calls, then writes each answer down once in a table, the idea Richard Bellman named dynamic programming. The film About 4:15, hosted by Rerun. It asks you o
items.body_html:
The film

About 4:15, hosted by Rerun. It asks you one question and waits for your answer before it shows you. The guide's voice is not recorded yet, so for now the film plays with captions; the full words are also below.

Play the film

Nothing loads until you press play.

The lab: the tide table

Type two strings and fill the table square by square, then trace the edits back from the corner; or try every way, with every call counted, for strings short enough to finish. In the film, kitten and sitting took 29,737 calls the slow way and 56 squares in the table; at 13 characters, 2,114,900,428 calls against 196 squares.

Find the tide table

Everything is computed on your computer, in this page. Nothing is sent anywhere.

Everything the film says

Dynamic programming

Dynamic programming: remember what you already worked out.

Some problems are made of smaller problems that keep coming back. Tonight Rerun learns to solve each one once and write the answer down.

How different are two words

How different are two words? Count the fewest single-letter edits that turn one into the other: put a letter in, take one out, or change one.

Kitten becomes sitting in 3: change the k to an s, the e to an i, and add a g. This count is called the edit distance.

Try every way

The obvious way is to try everything. Look at the last letters: either delete one, insert one, or match or change them, and work out the rest of each case the same way.

That works, but the same smaller questions come up again and again. For kitten and sitting, the recursion made 29,737 calls. For intention and execution, 2,193,844.

Two phrases of thirteen characters. How many calls does trying every way make? (the film pauses here)

Too many calls

For two phrases of 13 characters, it made 2,114,900,428 calls and took 11,327 milliseconds on this computer. Each extra letter multiplies the work by about five and a half, and the factor keeps rising.

Yet there are only 196 different questions in the whole problem, the big one included. The rest is repetition.

The tide table

So write each answer down once, in a table: one row for each letter of the first word plus one for the empty start, and the same for the columns.

Each square needs only three others: the one above, the one to its left, and the one diagonally above and left. Fill them in order and the bottom corner is the answer. For kitten and sitting, 56 squares instead of 29,737 calls.

Robert Wagner and Michael Fischer published this table for strings in 1974, and others found it independently.

Reading the way back

The table also says which edits to make. From the bottom corner, step back to whichever neighbour gave its value, and each step is one edit or one match.

Halve the beach and half the beach are 2 apart: drop the v, and change the e to an f.

A shortcut that fails

Why not just walk along both strings and fix each difference as you meet it? We tried that. It got both classic word pairs right.

It was wrong on all 6 of our guide sentences, and too high on 576 of 1,000 random pairs. A test with only the textbook examples would have passed it.

The idea

Richard Bellman chose the name dynamic programming around 1950, for problems solved in stages. Today it means: when a big problem is built from smaller ones that overlap, solve each smaller one once and keep the answer.

The same idea finds shortest routes and decodes speech.

Goodnight

When the same question keeps coming back, write the answer down.

Goodnight.

Sources

Every claim in the film, with where it comes from and what that source does not prove. The numbers about the model are computed from its weights, which you can load and check: facts.json.

  • Night School's edit-distance measurements. media/school/editdistance/facts.json, written by tools/school/fill_editdistance.mjs from system/school/editdistance.mjs: the table, the naive and memoised recursions with call counters, a breadth-first check, and a greedy control. https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/editdistance

    Used for: Every distance, call count and cell count in the film, and the greedy control.

    Does not prove: Costs under other edit weights.

  • Wagner and Fischer, The string-to-string correction problem (1974). Robert A. Wagner and Michael J. Fischer, J. ACM 21(1):168-173, 1974. https://doi.org/10.1145/321796.321811

    Used for: The dynamic-programming table for edit distance.

    Does not prove: The film's counts.

  • Dreyfus, Richard Bellman on the birth of dynamic programming (2002). Stuart Dreyfus, Operations Research 50(1):48-51, 2002, quoting Bellman, Eye of the Hurricane (1984). https://ideas.repec.org/a/inm/oropre/v50y2002i1p48-51.html

    Used for: Bellman chose the name around 1950 at RAND, for multistage decision processes.

    Does not prove: The modern overlapping-subproblems wording, which is the later textbook framing.

  • Bellman, Dynamic Programming (1957). Richard Bellman, Dynamic Programming, Princeton University Press, 1957.

    Used for: The name and the general idea of dynamic programming.

    Does not prove: Any claim about edit distance.

  • Jurafsky and Martin, Speech and Language Processing, section 2.9 (draft). Daniel Jurafsky and James H. Martin, Speech and Language Processing, 3rd edition draft, section 2.9, Minimum Edit Distance. https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/

    Used for: intention and execution are 5 apart with unit costs; the table was named by Wagner and Fischer and found independently by many; dynamic programming also finds shortest paths, and the Viterbi algorithm for speech extends it.

    Does not prove: The film's call counts.

What this lesson leaves out

Unit costs: inserting, deleting or changing a letter each costs 1.

Call counts for long strings come from the recursion's own formula, checked against the running counter up to 13 characters.

Wagner and Fischer's paper and Bellman's book were checked by their bibliographic records; the naming date comes from Dreyfus's 2002 account.

Before this: Search and sorting (A26).

items.title: Embeddings: every token gets coordinates
items.description: How a list of numbers per word comes to mean something: the skip-gram learns places from the company words keep, measured against a shuffled control.
headings: You are the company you keep
Two ways to the same chart
items.excerpt: Skip to content Zain Dana Harpernight school / L8 Embeddings. Every token gets coordinates. Each piece of text gets a list of numbers, and training moves those lists until words that keep the same company sit close. Tallow hangs the words as cards in her lamp room and lets them drift. The film About 3:38, hosted by Tallow. It asks you one question and waits
items.body_html:
The film

About 3:38, hosted by Tallow. It asks you one question and waits for your answer before it shows you. The narrated cut runs 2:53, voiced by Tallow in a synthesized voice made from the author's own voice; the author approved these cuts for publishing. Captions are on by default. The live version under it draws the same film in your browser, waits for your answer at each question, and runs a little longer; the full words are also below.

Play the film

Nothing loads until you press play.

The lab: the lamp room

Train your own skip-gram on the guides' sentences: choose the seed, the numbers per word, the window and the noise words, then step through its snapshots and pick a word to see its neighbours. The film's run ends with 65% of words beside a word of the same kind, against about 23% shuffled.

Light the lamp

Everything is computed on your computer, in this page. Nothing is sent anywhere.

Everything the film says

Embeddings

Embeddings. Every word gets coordinates.

Pylon showed you that a word in a model is a list of numbers, a place. Tonight, where those places come from.

Before anything is learned

At the start, every word gets a list of 32 small random numbers. The places mean nothing yet.

Check the neighbours: only 26 percent of words sit next to a word of the same kind, about what a shuffle gives.

You are the company you keep

The trick is a guessing game. Take a word in a sentence, and the words around it.

Each word gets two lists: one for when it's the word in the middle, one for when it's a neighbour. Nudge the lists so that the middle word's list and each real neighbour's neighbour-list get a bigger dot product, the measure from the vectors lesson.

And for every real neighbour, pick 5 words at random, common words more often than rare ones, and push those the other way. Tomas Mikolov and his colleagues called it negative sampling, in 2013.

The cards drift

Run the game over the guides' sentences, 5 times through, and watch the places move.

Will the neighbours keep getting tidier all the way through training? (the film pauses here)

Very early, by 5 percent of the way, the neighbours look their tidiest of any checkpoint: 72 percent of words sit next to a word of the same kind. By the end, in this run, it has slipped back to 65, three words fewer out of 46, while the guessing game keeps getting better on sentences it never trained on.

Better at the game is not always tidier on the chart. The game is the goal; the neat neighbours are a side effect.

Another roll of the dice

Start from different random numbers, four more times, and you get different coordinates, but much the same neighbours: against the first run, 75 to 80 percent of each word's three nearest neighbours agree.

Two ways to the same chart

The language model from the attention lesson learned its word lists a different way: as a side effect of guessing the next word, through two layers of attention.

Its lists put 80 percent of words next to a word of the same kind. And between the two tables, about 33 percent of each word's three nearest neighbours agree. By chance it would be about 7 percent.

So the two methods agree on far more than chance, and far less than two runs of the same method agree with each other. Neither one is the true map. Each is a map of what its own game needed.

Goodnight

Nobody draws the chart. A guessing game moves the cards, and words used alike end up close.

Next in the lighthouse: guessing the next word, and keeping score. Goodnight.

Sources

Every claim in the film, with where it comes from and what that source does not prove. The numbers about the model are computed from its weights, which you can load and check: facts.json.

  • Night School's skip-gram, trained for this film. media/school/embeddings/facts.json, written by tools/school/fill_embeddings.mjs from system/school/embeddings.mjs: skip-gram with negative sampling (32 numbers per word, window 1 to 2, 5 noise words, 5 epochs, seed 1) on the guides' corpus; a finite-difference check of the hand-written gradient (worst 5.3e-7). https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/embeddings

    Used for: Same-kind nearest neighbour share: 26% at the start (shuffle control mean 22%, 95% interval 9% to 39%); highest of the 12 snapshots at 5% of training (72%), 65% at the end, from one seed; held-out loss falls at every snapshot (2.14 at 5%, 1.92 at the end). Seed 1 against each of four other seeds: 75% to 80% of each word's three nearest neighbours agree (pairs among seeds 2 to 5 not measured).

    Does not prove: Anything about large embedding tables.

  • Mikolov and others 2013, Distributed Representations of Words and Phrases and their Compositionality. Mikolov, T., Sutskever, I., Chen, K., Corrado, G., Dean, J. (2013). Distributed Representations of Words and Phrases and their Compositionality. NeurIPS 26. arXiv:1310.4546. https://arxiv.org/abs/1310.4546

    Used for: The skip-gram model learns an input and an output vector for every word, trained so a word's vector predicts the words around it (section 2). Negative sampling replaces the full softmax: each real (word, context) pair is pushed together and k words drawn from a noise distribution (the unigram distribution to the 3/4 power) are pushed apart (section 2.2, equation 4).

    Does not prove: That the learned neighbours reflect meaning beyond how words are used in the training text.

  • Night School's tiny transformer, its word table. media/school/attention/model.json (wte), compared in media/school/embeddings/facts.json. https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/embeddings

    Used for: The attention model's word table puts 80% of words next to a same-kind word; its top-3 neighbour lists overlap the skip-gram's by 33% (chance about 7%; shuffled control 2% to 12%).

    Does not prove: Which table is better; they were trained for different games.

What this lesson leaves out

Forty-six words from a made-up corpus are enough to see the effect and far too few to show what large tables learn; the categories used to score neighbours are ours.

The chart shows two directions out of many, so two cards can look close and be far apart; neighbours are measured in all the dimensions.

Before this: Tokens (L7). Next: Next-word prediction (L9).

items.title: Error bars: how sure is the number
items.description: Rerun bootstraps the attention model's score, checks the intervals against a truth known exactly, and shows what to resample: rows, words, or seeds.
headings: Error bars. How sure is the number.
Drawing again from what you have
items.excerpt: Skip to content Zain Dana Harpernight school / E23 Error bars. How sure is the number. Every score in this school came from one set of test rows. Rerun shows how far it could move, checks that the error bars catch the truth as often as they claim, and finds the spread the rows cannot see. The film About 7:02, hosted by Rerun. It asks you one question and wai
items.body_html:
The film

About 7:02, hosted by Rerun. It asks you one question and waits for your answer before it shows you. The guide's voice is not recorded yet, so for now the film plays with captions; the full words are also below.

Play the film

Nothing loads until you press play.

The lab: the bucket

Resample the model's held-out rows or single words and watch the interval form; or draw fresh rows from the rules again and again and count how often the interval holds the true average. In the film, 93.1% of 1,000 row intervals at 64 rows held it.

Open the bucket

Everything is computed on your computer, in this page. Nothing is sent anywhere.

Everything the film says

Error bars

Error bars. How sure is the number.

Every lesson so far has quoted numbers, a loss here, a share of right answers there. Each came from one set of test rows. Tonight Rerun asks how much those numbers would move if the rows had been different.

One number

Score the attention model on 1,024 held-out rows: a loss of 0.6676 and 73 percent of next words right.

Those rows were drawn at random. Another draw of the same size would give a slightly different loss. The question is how different.

Drawing again from what you have

Bradley Efron's answer, in 1979, was the bootstrap. You cannot draw more rows from the world, so draw from the rows you have: pick as many as you have, at random, allowing repeats, and score that pile. Do it thousands of times.

The scores spread out. We take the middle 95 percent of them as the interval.

With 64 rows the loss is 0.7000, and the interval runs from 0.6723 to 0.7282.

Four times as many rows. How much narrower does the interval get? (the film pauses here)

More rows, narrower bars

Its width is 0.0838 with 16 rows, 0.0559 with 64, 0.0311 with 256 and 0.0161 with 1,024.

From 16 to 64 rows it narrows by a third; after that, by nearly half each time. Averaged over a thousand fresh draws, 0.1014, 0.0523 and 0.0264, each fourfold step halves it, as the square root of the number of rows says it should. Four times the rows buys an interval half as wide.

Does it work?

An interval is only worth something if it catches the truth as often as it claims. Usually nobody knows the truth. Here we do: the rules that write the guides' sentences give an exact average loss for their own guesses, 0.6361.

So draw 1,000 fresh sets of 64 rows from the rules, score the rules' own guesses on each, build an interval, and count how many contain 0.6361. The answer: 93.1 percent. With 256 rows, 95.3. Close to the 95 promised, a little short when rows are few.

What to draw again

One choice matters more than it looks: what counts as one draw. Evan Miller's 2024 paper on error bars for evaluations warns that questions which come in clusters must be counted as clusters when the error is worked out, or the interval comes out too narrow.

Our rows are clusters too, but of a kind that steadies the score. Each holds one word at every position, so a row is a balanced sample of easy and hard places. Resampling single words instead gives intervals that are too wide here: they caught the truth 100 percent of the time.

Now make real clusters: 1,000 test sets of 16 rows, each row copied four times. Treated as 64 separate rows, the interval catches the truth only 66.9 percent of the time. Resampling the 16 distinct rows brings it back to 93.3.

Two models, same rows

In the distillation lesson, one student learned from the text and one from the teacher's odds. Score both on the same 1,024 rows. The student taught by the text has the lower loss, by 0.0045.

Resample the rows once for both models, keeping each row's two scores together, and the interval for the difference runs from -0.0081 to -0.0011: it leaves out zero. Resample each model on its own and the interval is 3.27 times as wide, and it contains zero.

Keeping the pairs cancels the rows that are hard for both. Shuffle the pairing and the advantage disappears.

The spread the rows cannot see

But that difference came from one training run of each student. Train each with five seeds, the run we just scored and four more, and score them all on the same rows.

For one student, the spread of loss across seeds is about 12 times the spread the bootstrap found from rows; for the other, about 10. Some runs never learned to look back, and those runs make most of it. Seed by seed, the difference between the two students was -0.0045, 0.0845, -0.0049, 0.0007 and 0.0064.

The first seed's interval was honest about its rows. It said nothing about the next seed.

Goodnight

A number without its spread is half a number. Ask what was drawn at random, the rows, the seeds or both, and draw again from that. Everything tonight came from one small model and a handful of runs; the method carries over, the numbers do not.

Next under the prism: what happens when training pushes a model toward the measure instead of the goal. Goodnight.

Sources

Every claim in the film, with where it comes from and what that source does not prove. The numbers about the model are computed from its weights, which you can load and check: facts.json.

  • Night School's error-bar measurements, computed for this film. media/school/errorbars/facts.json, written by tools/school/fill_errorbars.mjs from system/school/errorbars.mjs and errorbars-truth.mjs: the attention model scored on 1,024 held-out rows; percentile and normal bootstrap intervals by row and by word at 16, 64, 256 and 1,024 rows; the generator's exact expected loss and 1,000-trial coverage checks; a duplicated-row control; a paired comparison of two S17 students; five seeds per student. https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/errorbars

    Used for: Loss 0.6676 and accuracy 0.7332 on 1,024 rows; row-bootstrap widths 0.0838, 0.0559, 0.0311, 0.0161 at 16, 64, 256, 1,024 rows. Exact truth 0.6361; row percentile coverage 0.934, 0.931, 0.953 at 16, 64, 256 rows; word-level 0.998 to 1; 16 rows copied four times 0.669, by distinct row 0.933. Paired difference -0.0045 [-0.0081, -0.0011], unpaired 3.27 times as wide; seed spread 11.8 times the row standard error.

    Does not prove: Anything about large models or other test sets; the rows here are balanced by position, which is why word-level intervals came out too wide.

  • Efron 1979, Bootstrap Methods: Another Look at the Jackknife. Efron, B. (1979). Bootstrap Methods: Another Look at the Jackknife. The Annals of Statistics 7(1), 1-26. https://projecteuclid.org/journals/annals-of-statistics/volume-7/issue-1/Bootstrap-Methods-Another-Look-at-the-Jackknife/10.1214/aos/1176344552.full

    Used for: Introduces the bootstrap: estimate the sampling distribution of a statistic by resampling the observed data with replacement.

    Does not prove: Anything about this model.

  • Miller 2024, Adding Error Bars to Evals. Miller, E. (2024). Adding Error Bars to Evals: A Statistical Approach to Language Model Evaluations. arXiv:2411.00640. https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00640

    Used for: Evaluation questions that come in related groups need clustered standard errors, which can be much larger than the naive ones; paired differences reduce variance when two models answer the same questions.

    Does not prove: Anything about this model.

What this lesson leaves out

One small model and its own test rows: the method carries over, the numbers do not.

Our rows hold one word at every position, which is why single-word intervals came out too wide here; with real clusters of questions, they come out too narrow.

Coverage at 16 and 64 rows ran about 2 standard errors under 95%; percentile intervals are a little short when rows are few.

Before this: The held-out set (F6). Next under the prism: When the check can be fooled (E24).

items.title: Evaluating a language model
items.description: One small model scored by loss, exact match and two judges, with error bars: where the scores agree, where they part, and how a leaked test fools them.
items.excerpt: Skip to content Zain Dana Harpernight school / L16 Evaluating a language model. There is no single number for how good a language model is. Rerun scores one small model three ways as it trains, tests a cheap judge against a perfect one, and leaks the test into training on purpose. The film About 6:07, hosted by Rerun. It asks you one question and waits for y
items.body_html:
The film

About 6:07, hosted by Rerun. It asks you one question and waits for your answer before it shows you. The guide's voice is not recorded yet, so for now the film plays with captions; the full words are also below.

Play the film

Nothing loads until you press play.

The lab: three instruments

Train the model from scratch in this page and score 64 fresh rows at each checkpoint: loss, exact match, a perfect judge and a cheap one. In the film, at step 200 exact match was 18% while the cheap judge passed 97% of the writing.

Set up the instruments

Everything is computed on your computer, in this page. Nothing is sent anywhere.

Everything the film says

Evaluating a language model

Evaluating a language model.

There is no single number for how good a language model is. Tonight Rerun scores the same small model three ways, and watches the three scores tell different stories.

Three ways to score

The first way is the loss: how surprised the model is by every next word of held-out text. Lower is better.

The second is exact match. Some questions have one right answer, like "who painted the rope?" Count how many the model gets exactly right.

The third is a judge: let the model write freely, and have something read what it wrote and say whether it is good.

Watching it learn

Train the same model three times, and score each run as it trains. On average, at step 200, the loss is 0.87 and exact match is 18 percent.

At step 200, exact match is low. What does a judge that reads only neighbouring words say? (the film pauses here)

By step 2,000, the loss is 0.67 and exact match is 99 percent. All three seeds agree on that much.

Two judges

Here we can build a perfect judge, because the rules that write the guides' sentences can say whether they could have written a given text, at least as the start of a longer one. In the real world no such judge exists; people use another model, or people.

So build a cheap judge too. It passes any text where every pair of neighbouring words also turns up in a sample of the same kind of text the model trained on. At step 200 it passes 97 percent of what the model writes. The perfect judge passes 74.

Of the writing the perfect judge rejects, the cheap one still accepts between 86 and 94 percent, depending on the run. It reads each pair of words and never the whole sentence, so a wrong fact in fluent words gets through.

When the scores disagree

Compare checkpoints in pairs, with error bars on each difference. In 6 of 39 pairs, the loss says the later model is better while exact match cannot tell.

In one pair, the scores point opposite ways. Between steps 400 and 600 of the second training run, loss, exact match and the perfect judge all say the model improved. The cheap judge says it got worse.

Each score sees part of the model. Loss sees every word. Exact match sees only the questions with one answer, and stops moving once those are right. A judge sees what it was built to look for.

Who goes first

Judges are often asked which of two answers is better. Give our cheap judge pairs of answers, an early model's and a late one's, then the same pairs with the order swapped.

Where the two answers differ, it keeps its verdict after the swap only 27 percent of the time in our first run. We wrote that habit into its rule, to show what it does: the first answer shown wins.

Lianmin Zheng and colleagues ran a similar test on real model judges in 2023. GPT-4, the most consistent of the three they tried, gave the same verdict after a swap in 65 percent of cases. Most of its flips favoured the answer shown first.

The test that was in the textbook

One more way scores lie: the test questions leak into the training text. Oscar Sainz and colleagues warned in 2023 that this happens with large models trained on the web.

So leak our test rows into training on purpose. Mixed in once, they change nothing we can measure. Even mixed in 16 times, the loss on them improves by only 0.0065 nats more than on fresh rows, and in two of three runs that is within the noise.

But leak a few rows many times, 32 rows 250 times each, and the model starts to learn them by heart: their loss drops below the floor no honest model can beat, and improves by 0.31 nats more than on fresh rows. A leak shows when the same text is seen often.

And some overlap happens by chance: 10 of our 256 test rows already appeared, word for word, in a clean training run.

Goodnight

Ask what a score can see before you trust what it says. Use more than one, put error bars on each, and check that the test was never in the textbook. Apart from the 65 percent, all of tonight's numbers come from one small model, trained a few times over; the questions carry over.

Next, in the cannery: how a graphics chip does thousands of small sums at once. Goodnight.

Sources

Every claim in the film, with where it comes from and what that source does not prove. The numbers about the model are computed from its weights, which you can load and check: facts.json.

  • Night School's evaluation runs, computed for this film. media/school/evaluate/facts.json, written by tools/school/fill_evaluate.mjs from system/school/evaluate*.mjs: the attention model retrained at three seeds and scored at eight checkpoints by held-out loss, exact match on one-answer questions, a perfect grammar judge and a cheap word-pair judge, all with bootstrap intervals; judge agreement and order tests; contamination runs with test rows leaked into training. https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/evaluate

    Used for: Step 200: loss 0.873, exact 0.179, perfect judge 0.743, cheap judge 0.973; step 2000: loss 0.673, exact 0.990. One of 39 checkpoint pairs gives opposite resolved verdicts; 6 pairs loss better with exact match unresolved. Cheap judge keeps its verdict after a swap on 0.274 of differing pairs; leaking 256 rows 16 times moves loss by 0.0065 on average; 32 rows 250 times by 0.305.

    Does not prove: Anything about large models, LLM judges or web-scale contamination; the cheap judge's biases are written into its rule.

  • Zheng and others 2023, Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena. Zheng, L., Chiang, W.-L., Sheng, Y., and others (2023). Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena. arXiv:2306.05685; NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks. https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05685

    Used for: LLM judges show position bias; GPT-4 was consistent under swapped order in 65.0 percent of cases.

    Does not prove: Anything about this model.

  • Sainz and others 2023, NLP Evaluation in trouble. Sainz, O., Campos, J. A., Garcia-Ferrero, I., Etxaniz, J., Lopez de Lacalle, O., Agirre, E. (2023). NLP Evaluation in trouble: On the Need to Measure LLM Data Contamination for each Benchmark. Findings of EMNLP 2023. arXiv:2310.18018. https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.18018

    Used for: Benchmark test data in the pretraining corpus inflates reported scores; contamination should be measured per benchmark.

    Does not prove: Anything about this model.

What this lesson leaves out

One small model trained three times: the questions carry over to large models, the numbers do not.

The perfect judge exists only because the rules that write this text are known; real evaluations use people or other models, which are not perfect.

The cheap judge's preference for the first-shown and longer answer is written into its rule, to show the effect; it measures nothing about real model judges.

Before this: When the check can be fooled (E24). Next, in the cannery: Threads, workgroups and memory (K21).

items.title: Fused attention
items.description: Attention without writing its table of scores: a running largest score and total, the bytes it saves, and the overflow the running largest prevents.
items.excerpt: Skip to content Zain Dana Harpernight school / K23 Fused attention. The plain way writes every head's table of scores to memory and reads it back twice. Pylon's crew keeps a running largest score and a running total instead, never builds the table, and leaves the rescale out on purpose to see the checker catch it. The film About 5:07, hosted by Pylon. It ask
items.body_html:
The film

About 5:07, hosted by Pylon. It asks you one question and waits for your answer before it shows you. The guide's voice is not recorded yet, so for now the film plays with captions; the full words are also below.

Play the film

Nothing loads until you press play.

The lab: the cannery

Pick a kernel and sizes; the emulator counts every byte to and from memory and checks the answer against an exact one; then, if your browser has WebGPU, time the real kernels on your own chip. In the film, at 4,096 words and 16 numbers per head, the plain way moved 285,736,960 bytes and fused 17,301,504; at 64 per head, 538,968,064 against 270,532,608.

Open the cannery

Counting runs in this page. Timing runs the kernels on your own graphics chip, only when you press Time. Nothing is sent anywhere.

Everything the film says

Fused attention

Fused attention.

Attention, the step where each word looks back at the words before it, is where the lighthouse meets the cannery. Tonight Pylon shows how to do it in one trip, without ever writing the whole table of scores to the warehouse.

The table of scores

For every word, attention scores that word and every earlier one, turns the scores into shares, and mixes the words by those shares.

Done the plain way on a graphics chip, that takes three passes, and the table crosses the warehouse door four times. Write the scores. Read them back and write the shares. Read the shares back to mix. For 4,096 words, one head's scores alone fill 64 mebibytes, in 32-bit numbers.

Shares without the whole row

The trouble is the shares. To turn a score into a share you divide by a total over the whole row, and you seem to need every score before you can start.

Maxim Milakov and Natalia Gimelshein showed in 2018 that the largest score and the total can be built in one pass, as the scores go by. When a bigger score arrives, shrink the total so far to match, and carry on.

On our model's own sentence, the tile-by-tile answer and the plain one both land within float32 rounding of the exact answer, on all four heads.

One trip

Tri Dao and colleagues built FlashAttention on this in 2022. Our kernel follows the same idea. A crew loads a tile of questions and walks tiles of keys and values past it on its bench. It keeps the running largest score and total, and writes only the finished answers. Dao's version loops the other way round, and also saves the running largest and total for training.

Count one head's warehouse traffic for 4,096 words, with 64 numbers per head: 514 mebibytes the plain way, 258 fused. The bench is small, so the keys and values are fetched again for every tile of questions. With 16 numbers per head, more fits on the bench: 272.5 against 16.5.

Four thousand words, sixteen numbers per head. How many times less traffic, fused? (the film pauses here)

Forget one step

The one step that is easy to forget: shrinking the running total when a bigger score arrives.

We left it out on purpose. On our model's sentence, some answers came out wrong on every one of the four heads, and the checker caught it. It is right only when the biggest score happens to arrive in the first tile.

Why keep the largest

The running largest score does a second job. Raising e to a score makes big numbers fast, and fp16, the common 16-bit format, overflows above 65,504.

The largest score in our sentence's last row is 10.32, and e to that is 30,320. That fits, but a score of 11.09 would not. Across the held-out rows, the largest score reaches 23.41, and e to some of those scores would be infinity in fp16. Subtracting the running largest first keeps every term at 1 or below.

What the count leaves out

These are counts of the memory requests our own kernels make, not times, and a chip's caches may serve some of them. Fused attention also does a little more arithmetic, the rescaling, to save the trips.

The lab runs both versions on your own chip, if your browser allows it, and times them beside the count.

Goodnight

Do the whole job on the bench, keep a running largest and a running total, and never build the wall of scores.

Next, with Tallow: what the 16-bit numbers in those trays can and cannot hold. Goodnight.

Sources

Every claim in the film, with where it comes from and what that source does not prove. The numbers about the model are computed from its weights, which you can load and check: facts.json.

  • Night School's attention emulator and kernels, built for this film. media/school/fused/facts.json, written by tools/school/fill_fused.mjs from system/school/fused*.mjs: online softmax and tiled attention checked against a float64 reference on random inputs and the attention model's own Q, K and V; WGSL kernels for the lab; an exact emulator of global memory traffic for unfused and fused attention at N = 64 to 4,096, d = 16 and 64; a broken-rescale control; the overflow arithmetic. https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/fused

    Used for: N 4,096: d 64 unfused 514 MiB against fused 258 MiB; d 16, 272.5 against 16.5. The broken rescale fails on all four probe heads. Probe row largest score 10.32, exp 30,320 in fp16; on held-out rows the largest score is 23.41.

    Does not prove: Any timing; caches and arithmetic cost are not modelled.

  • Dao and others 2022, FlashAttention. Dao, T., Fu, D. Y., Ermon, S., Rudra, A., Re, C. (2022). FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness. NeurIPS 2022. arXiv:2205.14135. https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135

    Used for: Tiling with the online softmax avoids writing the N x N attention matrix to high-bandwidth memory; Theorem 2 gives O(N^2 d^2 / M) memory accesses.

    Does not prove: Anything about this emulator.

  • Milakov and Gimelshein 2018, Online normalizer calculation for softmax. Milakov, M., Gimelshein, N. (2018). Online normalizer calculation for softmax. arXiv:1805.02867. https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.02867

    Used for: The softmax normaliser can be computed in one pass with a running maximum and a rescaled running sum.

    Does not prove: Anything about this model.

What this lesson leaves out

Counts of bytes asked for, not times; caches can serve repeated reads, and the film's kernels were not timed on a graphics chip.

The check tolerance is a first-order float32 error bound derived for this lesson, not a published one.

The model computes in float32 and subtracts the largest score, so it never overflows; 870 of 307,200 held-out scores would overflow fp16 without that subtraction.

Before this: Matmul tiling (K22). Next, in the lamp room: Mixed precision (K24).

items.title: Gradients: which way is downhill
items.description: Pylon feels her way down a hill in fog: the gradient, a step that goes over the edge, a real model's loss, then you walk the hills yourself.
headings: The lab: Pylon in the fog
items.excerpt: Skip to content Zain Dana Harpernight school / F3 Gradients. Which way is downhill. Training a model means walking downhill on a landscape you cannot see. Pylon does it in fog on the hill above the harbour, and then hands you her lantern. The film About 5:45, hosted by Pylon. It asks you two questions and waits for your answer before it shows you. The narrat
items.body_html:
The film

About 5:45, hosted by Pylon. It asks you two questions and waits for your answer before it shows you. The narrated cut runs 4:33, voiced by Pylon in a synthesized voice made from the author's own voice; the author approved these cuts for publishing. Captions are on by default. The live version under it draws the same film in your browser, waits for your answer at each question, and runs a little longer; the full words are also below.

Play the film

Nothing loads until you press play.

The lab: Pylon in the fog

Pick a hill, click the map to place your start, choose a step and walk down by gradient descent, seen from above or as a relief. On the tilted bowl the edge is 2 / 4 = 0.5: try either side of it. Then turn the dial on the attention model's last matrix and step it with the model's own backward pass, on 64 sentences it never trained on. In the film's run, the dial's lowest point was 0.92, and the gradient's length fell from 1.87 before training to 0.12 after.

Into the fog

Everything is computed on your computer, in this page. Nothing is sent anywhere.

Everything the film says

Gradients

Gradients. Which way is downhill.

Tonight the hill is in fog. I can't see the bottom. All I can do is feel the ground under my flippers.

Feel the slope

Put one flipper a little to the east and feel how much higher the ground is there. That's the slope going east.

Do the same going north. Two slopes, written as a list: that list is the gradient.

The gradient points the steepest way up. So to go down, step the opposite way. Feel, step, feel again. That's gradient descent. Augustin Cauchy wrote it down in 1847.

How big a step

Here is a bowl, steep one way and gentle the other: the steep way curves 8 times as sharply as the gentle way.

Bigger steps should get me down faster, so let's double mine.

If I double my step, do I get down twice as fast? (the film pauses here)

Over the edge. On this bowl, any step longer than two divided by the steep way's curvature, 4, overshoots further each time. That edge is 0.5, and running the bowl puts it exactly there.

Half that step gets down smoothly. Just under the edge, I zigzag and crawl. Just over it, I zigzag outwards. At twice it, the loss passes a trillion in just 12 steps.

A long, narrow valley

Now a valley that is steep across and almost flat along. At the bottom, the steep way curves about 2,508 times as sharply as the flat way.

The steep way sets the largest safe step, so along the flat way I creep. It takes 3,925 steps to get the loss under a hundredth, and 15,068 to get it under a millionth.

Which valley

One more hill, with two valleys and a ridge between them. I start just left of the ridge, then just right of it.

Do the two starts end in the same valley? (the film pauses here)

Different valleys. The right one is not even the lower one. Gradient descent finds a bottom near where it starts, not the lowest bottom there is.

The model's own hill

The language model from the attention lesson has 20,864 numbers. Its loss is a hill with 20,864 directions, and its gradient is a list of 20,864 slopes.

Before training, the length of that list was 1.87. After training it is 0.12: the ground under the trained model is much flatter.

To see any of it, we cut a slice through the trained point along two random directions, the way Li and colleagues did in 2018. The loss is 0.70 in the middle and climbs to 13.99 at one corner.

One warning. In a hill with 20,864 directions, two random ones are almost at right angles to the steepest one. This slice shows that the model sits in a dip along these two directions. It cannot show the whole hill.

One number, by hand

So let's follow one direction we choose. Freeze every number, and add one dial that turns the model's last matrix up or down. At one, it's the model as trained.

On sentences it never trained on, the bottom of this one-way slice is at 0.92, not at one, though the loss there is only a hair lower. Turning the dial down makes the model a little less sure of itself, and new text likes that.

Start the dial near zero, feel the slope with the model's own arithmetic, and step. With small steps, forty of them walk the dial up to 0.84. A step too big for the steep ground near zero overshoots to well past one, and has to walk back.

What the fog hides

This model's training never feels the whole hill at once. Each step feels the slope on 16 short stretches of text, so every step is a little off.

And I haven't said how a model with 20,864 numbers works out 20,864 slopes at once without feeling each one separately. That's the bucket chain, next.

Goodnight

The gradient is the list of slopes. Step the other way, not too far, and you go down. Where you end up depends on where you start.

Next along the hill: blame, passed backwards. Goodnight.

Sources

Every claim in the film, with where it comes from and what that source does not prove. The numbers about the model are computed from its weights, which you can load and check: facts.json, model.json.

  • Cauchy 1847, the method of steepest descent. Cauchy, A. (1847). Methode generale pour la resolution des systemes d'equations simultanees. Comptes Rendus de l'Academie des Sciences 25, 536-538. https://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/bpt6k2982c/f540.item

    Used for: Cauchy described moving a point step by step in the direction that most decreases a function, using its partial derivatives (steepest descent), in 1847. Cauchy outlined the method and gave no proof of convergence.

    Does not prove: That the method works well on a given problem; the step size and the shape of the function decide that.

  • Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville 2016, Deep Learning. Goodfellow, I., Bengio, Y., Courville, A. (2016). Deep Learning. MIT Press. Chapter 4.3 (gradient-based optimization) and chapter 8 (minibatch training). https://www.deeplearningbook.org/

    Used for: The gradient points in the direction of steepest increase; gradient descent steps in the negative gradient direction (4.3). With a quadratic approximation, the optimal step along the steepest curvature is 1 divided by the largest Hessian eigenvalue, and a step is uphill once its second-order term outweighs its first-order term (eq. 4.9, 4.10, 8.10). The edge of 2 divided by the largest eigenvalue for a quadratic is our derivation from these, and our runs measure it. Ill-conditioning (very different curvatures in different directions) makes gradient descent slow (8.2.1). Training uses minibatches, so each step uses an estimate of the gradient (8.1.3).

    Does not prove: Anything about a particular trained model.

  • Rosenbrock 1960, the curved valley test function. Rosenbrock, H. H. (1960). An automatic method for finding the greatest or least value of a function. The Computer Journal 3(3), 175-184. https://doi.org/10.1093/comjnl/3.3.175

    Used for: The function f(x, y) = (1 - x)^2 + 100 (y - x^2)^2 has a long, curved, narrow valley with its minimum at (1, 1); it later became a standard hard case for gradient methods.

    Does not prove: How hard real training problems are.

  • Night School's surfaces, computed for this film. media/school/gradients/facts.json, written by tools/school/fill_gradients.mjs from system/school/gradients.mjs: exact gradients, a finite-difference check, curvatures from a finite-difference Hessian, and the stability edge found by bisection on real runs. https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/gradients

    Used for: The bowl's curvatures are 4 and 0.5; the predicted edge 2/4 = 0.5 and the measured edge agree to about 1e-13; runs at 0.5, 0.99 and 1.01 times the edge converge, crawl and diverge over 60 steps, and at 2 times the edge the loss passes the 1e12 cap at step 12; runs at 0.6 and 1.2 times the edge (the film's doubled step) converge and diverge. Rosenbrock from (-1.2, 1) with step 0.001: loss below 1e-2 at step 3,925 and below 1e-6 at step 15,068; curvature ratio at the minimum about 2,508. Two valleys: starts at (-0.3, 0) and (0.3, 0) end in different valleys; the right valley's bottom (0.197) is higher than the left's (-0.202).

    Does not prove: Anything about real models; these are toy surfaces chosen to show one effect each.

  • Li, Xu, Taylor, Studer and Goldstein 2018, Visualizing the Loss Landscape of Neural Nets. Li, H., Xu, Z., Taylor, G., Studer, C., Goldstein, T. (2018). Visualizing the Loss Landscape of Neural Nets. NeurIPS 31. arXiv:1712.09913. https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.09913

    Used for: A loss surface can be viewed by plotting the loss along two random directions through the trained parameters, with each direction normalised filter by filter to the size of the weights. In high dimensions two random directions are nearly orthogonal to any fixed direction (section 7.1 gives an expected cosine of about 0.0055 at this size); ours measure -0.0024 and 0.0079 against the gradient.

    Does not prove: What the full high-dimensional surface looks like; a 2D slice is one view.

  • Night School's tiny transformer, the attention lesson's trained weights. media/school/attention/model.json, read by tools/school/fill_gradients.mjs (system/school/gradients-landscape.mjs uses the model's own backward pass). https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/gradients

    Used for: 20,864 numbers; gradient norm of the mean held-out loss on 256 rows: 1.87 at initialisation, 0.124 trained. A 21 x 21 slice along two filter-normalised random directions on 64 held-out rows: 0.70 at the centre, 13.99 at most; the directions' cosines with the gradient are under 0.01. An added multiplier s on the readout matrix: the loss is lowest at s = 0.92 (0.6988), against 0.69996 at s = 1; descent from s = 0.05 for 40 steps reaches 0.84 with step 0.05; step 0.2 overshoots to about 2.46 and comes back to 1.27. The 0.92 is measured on 64 held-out rows.

    Does not prove: Anything about large models' loss surfaces.

What this lesson leaves out

The bowl, the narrow valley and the two valleys are toy surfaces chosen to show one effect each. Real loss surfaces have thousands or billions of directions, and the slice of the model's loss in the film is one flat view through them along two random directions, which are almost at right angles to the steepest one.

The model's own training uses AdamW with a warmup and gradient clipping, on 16 stretches of text per step, not the plain fixed-step descent shown here. Better ways to step are lesson F5.

Before this: Matrices (F2). Next along the hill: Backpropagation (F4).

items.title: LoRA and fine-tuning
items.description: Teach a trained model a new habit by changing every number, a few, or a pair of thin LoRA strips: what each learns, and what each forgets.
headings: LoRA. A small rudder for a big boat.
items.excerpt: Skip to content Zain Dana Harpernight school / S19 LoRA. A small rudder for a big boat. Tallow teaches the attention model one new habit three ways and measures the new habit, the old skill, and whether the change really needs only a few directions, as the LoRA paper argued. The film About 7:05, hosted by Tallow. It asks you one question and waits for your a
items.body_html:
The film

About 7:05, hosted by Tallow. It asks you one question and waits for your answer before it shows you. The guide's voice is not recorded yet, so for now the film plays with captions; the full words are also below.

Play the film

Nothing loads until you press play.

The lab: the rudder

Pick a method, train it in this page on the new habit, and watch the change it makes to one attention table, the new habit and the old skill. In the film, changing every number got 99% of answers right, rank-1 strips on attention 18%, and rank-8 strips on every table 92%.

Open the boatyard

Everything is computed on your computer, in this page. Nothing is sent anywhere.

Everything the film says

LoRA

LoRA and fine-tuning. A small rudder for a big boat.

A trained model can be taught a new job by training it a little more. That is fine-tuning. Tonight we teach the attention model one new habit, first by changing every number, then by bolting on something small and changing only that.

The new job

The new habit: things keep their look. "The boat was bright." Maybe a sentence or two about something else. Then "the boat was", and the answer is bright again.

In the guides' usual sentences a thing never keeps its look; the adjective is drawn fresh every time. So the trained model gets the answer right only 15 percent of the time, about what guessing among six looks would give.

Our yardstick is the answer word. Once the thing is named again, the right look is certain, so a model that has learned the habit gets it right every time.

Change every number

First, the plain way: train all 20,864 numbers on the new sentences for 1,500 steps.

It learns the habit: 99 percent right.

But look at the old job. Before, the model got look-back words right 99 percent of the time. After, 30 percent. It trained only on the new sentences, and it forgot much of the old skill on the way.

The rudder

LoRA, from Hu and colleagues in 2021, leaves the trained numbers alone. Beside a table of weights it adds two thin strips: one with a number for every input, one with a number for every output. Multiply them together and you get a full-sized table of changes, added to the frozen one.

The table we are looking at is the second floor's query, key and value table, 32 by 96: 3,072 numbers. One pair of strips is 32 plus 96 numbers. That is rank 1. Rank 2 is two pairs, and so on.

One strip starts at zero, so at the first step the model is exactly the trained one, number for number. We checked: every output the same, bit for bit.

How many strips

Fit rank-1 strips to the four attention tables: 384 numbers. Rank 8: 3,072. The answer word comes out right 18 percent of the time at rank 1, hardly better than before, 24 at rank 4, and 61 at rank 8.

Rank-1 strips on the attention tables: 384 numbers out of 20,864. How much of the habit do they learn? (the film pauses here)

Strips on the feed-forward and readout tables too: 36 percent at rank 1, 82 at rank 4, and 92 at rank 8, with 6,768 numbers, 32 percent of the model's.

Something odd happened along the way. Every adapter learned to name the thing again, 98 percent at rank 1. Carrying its look across the sentence was the hard part, and after 1,500 steps the thinner attention strips still had not got it.

And the seeds often disagree. At rank 2, with strips on the feed-forward and readout tables too, the three runs got 14 to 75 percent.

The shape of a change

Why should a few strips be enough? Hu and colleagues guessed that the change fine-tuning makes has a low rank: most of it points in a few directions. We can check that here, on the change a full fine-tune made.

For the readout table, the top direction holds 69 percent of the change. For the attention table on the second floor, 26 percent. A random change of that shape would put only 7 percent there. So the change is lopsided.

But not thin. To hold nine tenths of it, that attention table needs 10 or 11 of its 32 directions. Cut every table's change down to its best rank 1 and the answer is right only 19 percent of the time; at rank 8, 74.

So on this model and this job, the claim is partly true. The change leans toward a few directions, and it still needs more than a few.

What was lost

Every method here trained only on the new sentences, and every one forgot some of the old job.

Rank-1 strips on attention forgot least: look-back words still 70 percent right, against 30 after changing everything. They also learned least. Strips on the feed-forward and readout tables too forgot about as much as changing everything.

Biderman and colleagues found a similar pattern in 2024, on models with billions of numbers: LoRA learned less of a new field than full fine-tuning and forgot less of the old, and more strips meant more forgetting.

We did not try the usual cure, mixing some old sentences into the new training. That is a lesson for another night.

Goodnight

Strips need little memory to train, are small to store and easy to take off again, so one trained model can carry many jobs, one set of strips each. How many strips a job needs, Hu's team expects, depends on the job; we tried only one.

Next, at the prism: how sure we can be of a number like the ones tonight. Goodnight.

Sources

Every claim in the film, with where it comes from and what that source does not prove. The numbers about the model are computed from its weights, which you can load and check: facts.json.

  • Night School's fine-tuning runs, trained for this film. media/school/lora/facts.json, written by tools/school/fill_lora.mjs from system/school/lora.mjs, lora-task.mjs and lora-measure.mjs: the attention lesson's model fine-tuned on a new task (things keep their look) by full fine-tuning, readout only, last layer, and LoRA at ranks 1, 2, 4, 8 on the attention tables and on every dense table; 1,500 steps, 3 seeds each, learning rate picked per method on separate validation rows; forgetting on the original 256 held-out rows; singular values of the full fine-tune's change; controls (step-0 equality, merge equality, gradient check with a wrong-transpose control, rank 0). https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/lora

    Used for: Base answer accuracy 0.149; full fine-tune 0.993; LoRA attention r1/r4/r8 0.178/0.240/0.609; every table r1/r4/r8 0.364/0.821/0.918. Forgetting: original look-back accuracy 0.992 before; 0.295 after full; 0.705 after LoRA attention r1. Full change's top direction: readout 0.694, l1.wqkv 0.264 of energy; random 32 x 96 0.071; l1.wqkv needs 10 of 32 directions for 90 percent.

    Does not prove: Anything about large models; one task, one learning-rate grid, no mixing of old data into fine-tuning.

  • Hu and others 2021, LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. Hu, E. J., Shen, Y., Wallis, P., Allen-Zhu, Z., Li, Y., Wang, S., Wang, L., Chen, W. (2021). LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. arXiv:2106.09685; ICLR 2022. https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685

    Used for: Freeze the pretrained weights and add a trainable low-rank product B A to chosen weight matrices; B starts at zero so training starts from the pretrained model. The update made by adaptation has a low intrinsic rank, which motivates the method.

    Does not prove: Anything about this model.

  • Biderman and others 2024, LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less. Biderman, D., Portes, J., Gonzalez Ortiz, J. J., Paul, M., Greengard, P., Jennings, C., King, D., Havens, S., Chiley, V., Frankle, J., Blakeney, C., Cunningham, J. P. (2024). LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less. Transactions on Machine Learning Research (08/2024). arXiv:2405.09673. https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.09673

    Used for: On code and math, LoRA underperforms full fine-tuning on the target domain and better preserves the base model's performance outside it.

    Does not prove: Anything about this model.

What this lesson leaves out

One small model, one new habit and one learning-rate grid, three seeds per method; at low rank the seeds disagree widely.

Every method trained on the new habit alone; mixing old text into fine-tuning, the usual guard against forgetting, was not tried.

The low-rank test covers this model and this habit only.

Before this: Distillation (S17). Earlier: Matrices move space (F2).

items.title: Matmul tiling
items.description: Multiply two tables on a graphics chip by carrying tiles to fast shared memory: how many reads it saves, why the crew must wait, and what the count leaves out.
items.excerpt: Skip to content Zain Dana Harpernight school / K22 Matmul tiling. Most of the arithmetic in a language model is multiplying tables. Pylon counts every read from memory for the simple kernel and for tiled ones, and breaks the wait on purpose to see the checker catch it. The film About 4:30, hosted by Pylon. It asks you one question and waits for your answer b
items.body_html:
The film

About 4:30, hosted by Pylon. It asks you one question and waits for your answer before it shows you. The guide's voice is not recorded yet, so for now the film plays with captions; the full words are also below.

Play the film

Nothing loads until you press play.

The lab: the trays

Pick a kernel and a size; count every read and check the answer with the emulator; then, if your browser has WebGPU, run the real kernel on your own chip and time it. In the film, at 1,024 wide, tiles of 16 took 134,217,728 reads against 2,147,483,648.

Hand out the trays

Counting runs in this page. Timing runs the kernel on your own graphics chip, only when you press Time. Nothing is sent anywhere.

Everything the film says

Matmul tiling

Matmul tiling.

Most of the arithmetic in a language model is multiplying tables of numbers. Tonight Pylon shows a classic trick for doing that fast on a graphics chip: carry a tray, not one can at a time.

One table times another

Multiplying two square tables, each number of the answer is a row of the first table times a column of the second: multiply pairs, add them up.

For tables 1,024 wide, one answer number needs 2,048 reads from the warehouse, 1,024 from each table.

One can at a time

The simple kernel gives each thread one answer number and lets it fetch everything itself. Every number of each table is then fetched 1,024 times, once for every thread that needs it.

In all, 2,147,483,648 reads from the warehouse, for one multiplication.

A tray to the bench

Now give a crew of threads a square of the answer. Together they carry a square tile of each table to their bench, the chip's small fast shared memory, and wait until every thread has put its part down.

Then each thread works through the tile on the bench. When every thread is done, the crew fetches the next pair of tiles. With tiles 16 wide, each number is fetched 64 times instead of 1,024.

Tiles 16 wide. How many times fewer reads from the warehouse? (the film pauses here)

Counting the reads

Reads from the warehouse: 2,147,483,648 for the simple kernel; 268,435,456 with tiles of 8; 134,217,728 with tiles of 16. The wider the tile, the fewer the trips.

Another way to say it: work done per byte fetched. The simple kernel does 0.25 operations per byte, counting each multiply and each add as one. Tiles of 16 do 3.97. Vasily Volkov and James Demmel used this counting in 2008 when they tuned matrix code for graphics chips.

Wait for the whole tray

The waiting matters. If a thread starts working before the crew has put the whole tile down, it can read a can from the last tile.

We broke the kernel that way on purpose. In our emulator, under the worst timing the missing wait allows, its answers came out wrong at every size we tried, and the checker, which compares each number with a careful answer computed on the main processor, caught it.

What the count leaves out

These are counts of reads asked for, not times. Real chips have caches that can serve repeated reads, so the simple kernel may not be as slow as its count says. How much it gains depends on the chip.

The lab runs both kernels on your own chip, if your browser allows it, and times them beside the count.

Goodnight

Carry a tray once, use it many times. Fast matrix code on graphics chips is built on the same idea.

Next in the cannery: attention itself, done in one trip. Goodnight.

Sources

Every claim in the film, with where it comes from and what that source does not prove. The numbers about the model are computed from its weights, which you can load and check: facts.json.

  • Night School's matmul emulator and kernels, built for this film. media/school/tiling/facts.json, written by tools/school/fill_tiling.mjs from system/school/tiling.mjs: naive and tiled WGSL matmul kernels, an exact emulator of global and shared memory traffic, barriers and arithmetic for n = 64 to 1,024, a float32 tolerance and a missing-barrier control. https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/tiling

    Used for: n = 1,024: global loads 2,147,483,648 (naive), 268,435,456 (tile 8), 134,217,728 (tile 16). Flops per global byte 0.25, 1.99, 3.97. The stale-tile kernel fails at every size.

    Does not prove: Any timing; caches are not modelled.

  • NVIDIA CUDA C++ Programming Guide, release 12.6 (archived), shared memory. NVIDIA (2024). CUDA C++ Programming Guide, release 12.6, section 3.2.4 (shared memory matrix multiplication example). https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/archive/12.6.0/cuda-c-programming-guide/

    Used for: With shared memory tiles, A is read B.width / block_size times from global memory and B is read A.height / block_size times.

    Does not prove: Anything about other vendors' chips.

  • Volkov and Demmel 2008, Benchmarking GPUs to tune dense linear algebra. Volkov, V., Demmel, J. W. (2008). Benchmarking GPUs to tune dense linear algebra. Proceedings of SC08. https://bebop.cs.berkeley.edu/pubs/volkov2008-benchmarking.pdf

    Used for: Blocking reduces global memory traffic for matrix multiply in proportion to the block size.

    Does not prove: Anything about this emulator.

What this lesson leaves out

Counts of reads asked for, not times; caches can serve repeated reads, so the simple kernel may be faster than its count suggests.

The missing-wait failure was shown in the emulator under a worst-case schedule, not on a chip.

The kernels were checked against the main processor within a float32 error bound; they were not timed on a graphics chip for this film.

Before this: Threads, workgroups and memory (K21). Earlier: Quantisation (S18).

items.title: Matrices move space
items.description: Watch Pylon's crane move the whole chart with a matrix, then drive it yourself and rebuild the attention model's question from its trained weights.
headings: Matrices. One move for every place at once.
