items.excerpt: Skip to content Zain Dana Harpernight school / F2 Matrices. One move for every place at once. A matrix is a move that takes every place on a chart somewhere at once. Pylon's crane shows you how to read one, why the order of two moves matters, and how the attention lesson's question was made by one. The film About 5:30, hosted by Pylon. It asks you two questi
items.body_html:
The film

About 5:30, hosted by Pylon. It asks you two questions and waits for your answer before it shows you. The narrated cut runs 4:29, voiced by Pylon in a synthesized voice made from the author's own voice; the author approved these cuts for publishing. Captions are on by default. The live version under it draws the same film in your browser, waits for your answer at each question, and runs a little longer; the full words are also below.

Play the film

Nothing loads until you press play.

The lab: Pylon's crane cab

Type a matrix, or pick a move, and watch the tracing sheet go where it sends it; put two cranes in a row and swap their order. Then the attention question: every earlier word's score, q . k / 4, computed in your browser from the trained query and key matrices (32 x 16 each), with a control that sets the query matrix to zero. In the film's sentence the score of "the" against "kettle" is 41.28 / 4 = 10.32.

Climb into the cab

Everything is computed on your computer, in this page. Nothing is sent anywhere.

Everything the film says

Matrices

Matrices move space.

Last time every crate got a place on my chart. Tonight the crane moves all of them at once.

One move for every place

A crane that lifts one crate is useful. This crane takes the whole chart, and every crate on it, and turns it, or stretches it, or leans it over, in one go.

A matrix is that kind of move written as a grid of numbers. It sends every place on the chart somewhere, it keeps straight lines straight, and it leaves the corner where it is.

Read the columns

Here's how to read one. Forget the crates and watch two short arrows from the corner: one step east, one step north.

The first column of the matrix says where the east step lands. The second column says where the north step lands.

That is all a matrix has to say. Every place on the chart is so many east steps plus so many north steps, so it lands at the same number of the new east steps plus the new north steps.

Turn, stretch, lean

A quarter turn sends east to north, and north to west. Columns: zero, one, and minus one, zero.

A stretch sends east to two steps east and leaves north alone. Every patch of the dock gets twice the area, and that factor has a name: the determinant.

A lean, called a shear, slides the top of the chart sideways. Squares become slanted boxes, and yet the area stays the same: determinant one.

Two cranes in a row

Two cranes, one after the other. The first stretches the dock east, twice as wide. The second turns it a quarter turn.

Does it matter which crane goes first? (the film pauses here)

Stretch then turn sends the east step to 0, 2: two steps north. Turn then stretch sends it to 0, 1: one step north. So yes, the order matters.

Two moves in a row are still one move, and its matrix is the product of the two. Multiplying matrices means doing the moves one after the other, and that is why the order of a product matters.

The corner never moves

Here's a harder one.

Can any matrix move the corner of the chart? (the film pauses here)

No. A matrix times a list of zeros gives a list of zeros, so the corner always stays put. To slide the whole chart over, you add a fixed list after the move.

Many language models do exactly that: a matrix, then a list added on, called a bias. Every layer of the model from the attention lesson does it.

How a word makes its question

Back at the lighthouse, in the attention lesson, the word 'the' asked a question and kettle answered. Tallow skipped how the question was made. A matrix made it.

By the second layer, the list of 32 numbers at each word has been through a step called layer normalisation. It shifts the numbers to average zero and scales them to a standard spread, then applies a learned scale and shift of its own. Then it meets the head's query matrix: 32 rows by 16 columns, plus a bias.

Out comes the question, a list of 16 numbers. Kettle's list goes through a different matrix, the key matrix, and comes out as a label of the same length.

Multiply the question and the label number by number and add it up: 41.28. Divide by 4, the square root of 16: 10.32. That is the score the attention film showed, rebuilt here from the trained weights.

What a matrix cannot do

A matrix can only do moves that keep lines straight. Stack ten of them and you still have one straight-line move: their product.

So a model puts bends between its matrices. In the one from the attention lesson, a smooth curve called GELU sits between the two matrices in the second half of each layer and bends every number that passes through. The softmax and the layer normalisation bend things too.

How a model learns the numbers in its matrices is where the next lessons along the hill go.

Goodnight

A matrix moves every place at once. Read its columns to see where the steps go, multiply two to do one move after another, and mind the order.

Next along the hill, we find out which way is downhill. Goodnight.

Sources

Every claim in the film, with where it comes from and what that source does not prove. The numbers about the model are computed from its weights, which you can load and check: facts.json, model.json.

  • Strang 2016, Introduction to Linear Algebra. Strang, G. (2016). Introduction to Linear Algebra, 5th edition. Wellesley-Cambridge Press. Chapter 1 (vectors, linear combinations, lengths and dot products) and chapters 2 and 8 (matrices, multiplication, linear transformations). https://math.mit.edu/~gs/linearalgebra/

    Used for: A matrix applied to a vector gives a combination of the matrix's columns, weighted by the vector's components; so the first column is where the first unit vector lands and the second column where the second lands (section 2.1). A linear transformation keeps straight lines straight and sends the zero vector to zero (chapter 8). A rotation by 90 degrees has columns (0, 1) and (-1, 0); a stretch along x by 2 has columns (2, 0) and (0, 1); a shear [[1, 1], [0, 1]] slides each row sideways by its height. The determinant of a 2 by 2 matrix is the factor by which it scales areas; a shear has determinant 1. Doing one transformation after another is multiplying their matrices, and matrix multiplication is not commutative in general: AB and BA can differ (section 2.4). A product of linear transformations is again a linear transformation, so stacking matrices without anything between them gives one matrix.

    Does not prove: Anything about language models; it is the mathematics the lesson uses.

  • Night School's tiny transformer, the attention lesson's trained weights. media/school/attention/model.json, read by tools/school/fill_matrices.mjs, which rebuilds the attention film's query, key and score from the layer-norm output and the head's slices of the query-key-value matrix, and refuses to write if they differ from the film's by more than 1e-4. https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/matrices

    Used for: Each layer has biases after its matrices (the query-key-value projection, the output projection and both MLP matrices). At layer 2, head 2, the input (after layer normalisation) is 32 numbers; the head's query and key slices are 32 by 16 with 16 biases each; q . k = 41.28 and q . k / 4 = 10.32, the score the attention film shows. The model's MLP uses GELU between its two matrices.

    Does not prove: Anything about how large models' query matrices behave.

  • Vaswani and others 2017, Attention Is All You Need. Vaswani, A., Shazeer, N., Parmar, N., Uszkoreit, J., Jones, L., Gomez, A. N., Kaiser, L., Polosukhin, I. (2017). Attention Is All You Need. NeurIPS 30. https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762

    Used for: Queries, keys and values are made by multiplying the input by learned projection matrices, one set per head (section 3.2.2). Scores are dot products of queries and keys divided by the square root of the key length (section 3.2.1). The paper writes the attention projections as matrices without biases; our model's projections have biases.

    Does not prove: How a particular trained model uses its projections.

  • Ba, Kiros and Hinton 2016, Layer Normalization. Ba, J. L., Kiros, J. R., Hinton, G. E. (2016). Layer Normalization. arXiv:1607.06450. https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.06450

    Used for: Layer normalisation shifts each input's numbers to mean zero and scales them to unit spread, then applies a learned gain and bias, so the output's spread is set by the learned gain.

    Does not prove: Why it helps in a particular model.

  • Hendrycks and Gimpel 2016, Gaussian Error Linear Units. Hendrycks, D., Gimpel, K. (2016). Gaussian Error Linear Units (GELUs). arXiv:1606.08415. https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.08415

    Used for: GELU is a smooth nonlinearity, x times the standard normal cumulative distribution at x, so it treats large, small and negative inputs differently. Our model uses the paper's tanh approximation of GELU.

    Does not prove: That GELU is the best choice.

What this lesson leaves out

Real models use matrices thousands of numbers wide, and what a trained query matrix has learned is far harder to read than a crane's turn. The lesson shows one head of a two-layer toy model on one sentence.

The bends between matrices (GELU, softmax, layer normalisation) get one picture here; how a model learns the numbers in its matrices is the next lessons' subject.

Before this: Vectors (F1). Next along the hill: gradients, which way is downhill (F3), planned.

items.title: Mixed precision
items.description: Run a model with 16-bit numbers: where fp16 and bf16 can put a value, why sums stall, and what keeping the sums in 32 bits buys on held-out rows.
items.excerpt: Skip to content Zain Dana Harpernight school / K24 Mixed precision. Graphics chips multiply 16-bit numbers fastest. Tallow measures where fp16 and bf16 can put a value, adds 1 to a running total until it stops moving, and scores the whole model with 16-bit inputs and with 16-bit sums. The film About 4:23, hosted by Tallow. It asks you one question and waits
items.body_html:
The film

About 4:23, hosted by Tallow. It asks you one question and waits for your answer before it shows you. The guide's voice is not recorded yet, so for now the film plays with captions; the full words are also below.

Play the film

Nothing loads until you press play.

The lab: the measuring jugs

Type a number and see the values each format can store around it; run a long sum; or score the model on held-out rows in each mode. In the film, adding 1 stalled at 2,048 in fp16 and 256 in bf16; near 110, fp16's marks are 0.0625 apart. The model's loss was 0.6676 in 32 bits and 0.6679 in bf16 throughout.

Take down the jugs

Everything is computed on your computer, in this page. Nothing is sent anywhere.

Everything the film says

fp16, bf16 and tensor cores

fp16, bf16 and tensor cores.

Graphics chips multiply much faster in 16-bit numbers than in 32-bit ones. Tonight Tallow measures what a 16-bit number can hold, where it goes wrong, and why the sums are often kept in 32 bits.

Measuring jugs

Think of a number format as a measuring jug. The marks are its precision; the height is its range.

fp16 has 11 bits of significand and tops out at 65,504. bf16 keeps the range of 32-bit numbers but has only 8 bits of significand. 32-bit numbers have 24.

Near one hundred and ten

Look at the marks near 110. In fp16 they are 0.0625 apart. In bf16, 0.5. Any number in between is rounded to the nearest mark.

fp16 near 110. How far apart are the marks? (the film pauses here)

So in fp16 a number near 110 can be off by up to one thirty-second, about 0.03. That is about three parts in ten thousand. A job that needs one part in ten thousand needs a significand of 13 bits; fp16 has 11. We will need that in the next lesson.

A sum that stops

Now add 1 to a running total, five thousand times, keeping the total in fp16.

It stops at 2,048. There the marks are 2 apart, and adding 1 rounds back to where it was. In bf16 it stops at 256.

Small inputs, big sums

This is why tensor cores, the units that multiply small tables of numbers in one step, can take 16-bit inputs and keep the running sums in 32 bits. With fp16 inputs they can also sum in fp16. With bf16 inputs, the sums are always 32-bit.

Paulius Micikevicius and colleagues trained large networks this way in 2018 and kept a 32-bit master copy of the weights.

On the second floor's feed-forward table of our model, the error with fp16 inputs and 32-bit sums is about 0.0003 of the answer's size. Keep the sums in fp16 too, and it grows to about 0.001.

The whole model

Run the whole model with every stored number rounded to 16 bits and score it on 1,024 held-out rows.

The loss barely moves. It stays at 0.6676 with fp16 inputs and 32-bit sums, and rises to 0.6679 with bf16 throughout. Its numbers stay far below fp16's limit, so nothing overflows. Its sums are short, at most 64 terms, so the rounding hardly shows.

We only ran this model in 16 bits; we did not train it that way. When large models are trained in 16 bits, the rounding can show. Micikevicius and colleagues needed three fixes to stop it.

Goodnight

Small inputs, big sums: the marks you can afford for the parts, and the marks you need for the total.

Next, at the prism: one glint of light that 16 bits could not hold precisely enough. Goodnight.

Sources

Every claim in the film, with where it comes from and what that source does not prove. The numbers about the model are computed from its weights, which you can load and check: facts.json.

  • Night School's precision measurements, computed for this film. media/school/precision/facts.json, written by tools/school/fill_precision.mjs from system/school/precision*.mjs: exact fp16 and bf16 rounding checked on every bit pattern; spacing and error by magnitude; long sums; the attention model's layers and the whole model run with 16-bit storage and 32-bit or 16-bit accumulation, scored on 1,024 held-out rows with paired intervals. https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/precision

    Used for: Near 110: fp16 spacing 0.0625, worst rounding 0.03125; 13 significand bits needed for 1e-4, fp16 has 11. Adding 1 stalls at 2,048 in fp16 and 256 in bf16. Whole-model loss changes under 1e-3 nats in every 16-bit mode.

    Does not prove: Anything about large models trained in 16 bits.

  • IEEE 754-2019 binary16. IEEE (2019). IEEE Standard for Floating-Point Arithmetic, IEEE 754-2019 (binary16 parameters, checked against ISO/IEC TS 18661-3). https://standards.ieee.org/ieee/754/6210/

    Used for: binary16: 11-bit significand, 5-bit exponent, largest finite 65,504.

    Does not prove: Anything about bf16.

  • Micikevicius and others 2018, Mixed Precision Training. Micikevicius, P., Narang, S., Alben, J., and others (2018). Mixed Precision Training. ICLR 2018. arXiv:1710.03740. https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.03740

    Used for: Train in fp16 with an fp32 master copy of weights, loss scaling, and fp32 accumulation of products.

    Does not prove: Anything about this model.

  • NVIDIA CUDA Programming Guide, tensor core element types. NVIDIA (2026). CUDA Programming Guide 13.4.2, section 5.4.11.6, Element Types and Matrix Sizes. https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-programming-guide/

    Used for: Tensor core operations take fp16 inputs with fp16 or fp32 accumulators, and bf16 inputs with fp32 accumulators.

    Does not prove: Anything about other vendors.

  • raw-native evidence note on the denoiser's tensor-core parity, 15 October 2026. HarperZ9/raw-native, evidence/rr-tc-note-2026-10-15.json. https://github.com/HarperZ9/raw-native/blob/main/evidence/rr-tc-note-2026-10-15.json

    Used for: A value near 110 needs about 1e-4 relative precision; fp16 holds about 1e-3 there (order of magnitude).

    Does not prove: Anything about this film's arithmetic beyond the stated figures.

What this lesson leaves out

The 16-bit formats are emulated by rounding in the main processor; no graphics chip and no tensor core ran these numbers.

One small model; its scores are small enough that fp16 never overflows here, which large models cannot count on.

Scores on 1,024 held-out rows; differences from 32 bits are paired on the same rows.

items.title: Next-word prediction and the loss
items.description: How a language model guesses the next word as a spread of belief, how softmax makes it, and how the loss scores it as surprise.
headings: Next-word prediction. One guess, spread over every word.
items.excerpt: Skip to content Zain Dana Harpernight school / L9 Next-word prediction. One guess, spread over every word. A language model is first trained to say what comes next. Its answer is never one word: it is a share of belief for every word. Tallow cuts that belief into a wheel, and scores it by how surprised it was. The film About 6:08, hosted by Tallow. It asks y
items.body_html:
The film

About 6:08, hosted by Tallow. It asks you two questions and waits for your answer before it shows you. The guide's voice is not recorded yet, so for now the film plays with captions; the full words are also below.

Play the film

Nothing loads until you press play.

The lab: the scoring wheel

Type a line from the guides' world and step through it: the model's spread for each next word, the rules' own odds beside it, and the surprise of the word that came. On 6,144 held-out next words the model is torn between 1.99 words; the rules themselves, 1.93.

Turn the wheel

Everything is computed on your computer, in this page. Nothing is sent anywhere.

Everything the film says

Next-word prediction

Next-word prediction. One guess, spread over every word.

A language model is first trained on one job: read some words, and say what comes next. Tonight, what that guess looks like, and how it is scored.

A guess is a spread

Take the small model from the attention lesson, give it one word, pylon, and ask what comes next.

It does not answer with one word. It cuts the wheel into a slot for every word, some wider than others: found gets 50 percent of its belief, painted about 9, and the rest is shared out thinner.

We know the rules that wrote these sentences, so we can check it. After pylon, the rules choose found 42 percent of the time. From examples alone, the model got close.

From scores to shares

Inside, the model ends with one score per word. Scores can be any number, even below zero, so they are not yet a share of belief.

Take four words with scores 2, 1, 0 and minus 1. Raise e to each score, which makes every one positive, then divide by their total.

The shares come out 64, 24, 9 and 3 percent. A score one higher means about 2.7 times the share. This step is called the softmax.

The loss is surprise

Then the real next word arrives. Say it was lamp, the word with 64 percent.

The score for the guess is the surprise: minus the log of the share it gave the word that came. Here that is 0.44.

Give the right word half, and the surprise is about 0.69. Give it all of its belief, and the surprise is zero. Give it almost nothing, and the surprise grows without limit. This number is the loss, and training is the work of making it small.

If the model had given the right word every bit of its belief, what would the loss be? (the film pauses here)

The slope of the loss for each score is that word's share, minus one for the word that came. Training steps the other way: the right word's score goes up, and every other score comes down, each by an amount set by its share. We checked that rule against tiny test nudges, and they agree. A version with the minus one left out fails the same check.

Torn between how many?

A loss in logs is hard to picture, so turn it back. Raise e to the average surprise, and you get how many words the guesses are torn between, as if they were all equally likely. That is called perplexity. The same count can be read off a single guess, before any word arrives.

After rerun knocked, the rules allow two words, on or twice, half each: torn between exactly 2. The model's guess there: torn between 2.04.

After tallow found a, the rules allow 10 things, all equally. The model is torn between 10.07, but it leans: it gives kettle 14 percent where the rules give 10.

What context buys

Now score it properly, on 6,144 next words from rows it never trained on, against simpler guessers. The rows are new; the sentences in them are not, because the rules can only make so many.

A blind guess is torn between all 46 words. Counting how often each word appears gets that down to 26.37. Counting which word follows which: 3.60. Which word follows each pair: 2.91.

The attention model: torn between 1.99.

The gap is widest where a word must come back from far earlier, like the cone going on the thing found seven words before. There, counting which word follows which is torn between 7.11 and the model between 1.06. That is what attention is for.

Can any guesser get to torn between one, never surprised at all? (the film pauses here)

The floor

No. Some next words are a coin toss in the rules themselves. Even the rules, scoring their own sentences, are torn between 1.93. That is the floor.

Over 2,000 training steps, the model's loss on those held-out rows fell from 3.84 to 0.69. The floor is 0.66. What is left above it is 0.03.

We can say that only because we wrote the rules. For real text nobody knows exactly where the floor is, so nobody can say how much lower a loss could go.

Goodnight

A guess is a spread of belief over every word. The loss is the surprise when the real word arrives, and training makes the surprise small.

Next in the lighthouse: how the attention lamp chooses what to look at. Goodnight.

Sources

Every claim in the film, with where it comes from and what that source does not prove. The numbers about the model are computed from its weights, which you can load and check: facts.json.

  • Night School's attention model, scored for this film. media/school/nextword/facts.json, written by tools/school/fill_nextword.mjs from system/school/nextword.mjs and corpus-grammar.mjs: the attention lab's trained model (seed 7, data seed 11, 2,000 steps) scored on the corpus's 256 held-out rows against a uniform guess, the untrained model, unigram, bigram and trigram counts of the exact training tokens, and the corpus generator's own odds. https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/nextword

    Used for: Held-out perplexity over 6144 positions: model 1.9886, trigram 2.9133, bigram 3.5989, unigram 26.3654, uniform 46, generator (floor) 1.932. On the 506 copy positions: bigram perplexity 7.1101, model 1.0576. Worked example: scores 2, 1, 0, -1 give softmax shares 0.644, 0.237, 0.087, 0.032 and loss 0.440 for the first; the gradient p minus one-hot matches finite differences (relative error about 1e-10) and the control without the minus one fails. After 'pylon' the model gives found 0.498; the generator 0.421. After 'rerun knocked' the generator allows on and twice at 0.5 each; the model's perplexity there is 2.04. After 'tallow found a' the generator allows 10 things at 0.1 each; the model gives kettle 0.143. Held-out loss fell from 3.8414 at step 0 to 0.6874 at step 2,000 (curve recorded in model.json); the generator's loss is 0.6585.

    Does not prove: Anything about real text, where the floor is unknown; or that a lower loss means better text.

  • Bengio and others 2003, A Neural Probabilistic Language Model. Bengio, Y., Ducharme, R., Vincent, P., Jauvin, C. (2003). A Neural Probabilistic Language Model. Journal of Machine Learning Research 3, 1137 to 1155. https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume3/bengio03a/bengio03a.pdf

    Used for: A neural network outputs one score per vocabulary word and a softmax turns the scores into next-word probabilities; models are compared by perplexity on held-out text.

    Does not prove: Anything about this model.

  • Jurafsky and Martin, Speech and Language Processing, chapter 3 (N-gram Language Models). Jurafsky, D., Martin, J. H. Speech and Language Processing, 3rd edition draft, chapter 3: N-gram Language Models. https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/3.pdf

    Used for: Perplexity is the exponent of the average negative log probability per word; it can be read as a weighted average branching factor, the number of possible next words. Unigram, bigram and trigram models predict from counts of words, pairs and triples.

    Does not prove: Anything about this model.

  • Shannon 1951, Prediction and Entropy of Printed English. Shannon, C. E. (1951). Prediction and Entropy of Printed English. Bell System Technical Journal 30(1), 50 to 64. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1951.tb01366.x

    Used for: Predicting the next letter of text measures how much information the text carries; predictions improve as more preceding text is used.

    Does not prove: Anything about this model.

What this lesson leaves out

The held-out rows are new, but the sentences in them all occur somewhere in training: a 46-word grammar can only make so many. Real held-out text is far less forgiving.

We can show the floor only because we wrote the rules; for real text the floor is unknown, so no one can say how much lower a loss could go.

Before this: Embeddings (L8). Next: Attention (L10), then The transformer block (L11). Later: Decoding (L15).

items.title: Optimisers: momentum, Adam and the step size
items.description: Careful steps, a heavy ball and Adam race down the same valleys, then train a real network: who wins depends on the hill.
items.excerpt: Skip to content Zain Dana Harpernight school / F5 Optimisers. Better ways to step. Plain gradient descent crawls along narrow valleys. Pylon gives her walker weight, then a pair of shoes, and races all three on hills where each one wins. The film About 5:50, hosted by Pylon. It asks you one question and waits for your answer before it shows you. The narrated
items.body_html:
The film

About 5:50, hosted by Pylon. It asks you one question and waits for your answer before it shows you. The narrated cut runs 4:30, voiced by Pylon in a synthesized voice made from the author's own voice; the author approved these cuts for publishing. Captions are on by default. The live version under it draws the same film in your browser, waits for your answer at each question, and runs a little longer; the full words are also below.

Play the film

Nothing loads until you press play.

The lab: Pylon's race

Race careful steps, the heavy ball and Adam on three hills, each with the step you give it, from wherever you click. On the long narrow valley, at the steps the film chose, the heavy ball got down to stay in 285 updates, careful steps in 6,217 and Adam in 16,790. Then train the spiral network from the bucket chain with any walker and step, and compare the runs.

Line them up

Everything is computed on your computer, in this page. Nothing is sent anywhere.

Everything the film says

Optimisers

Optimisers. Better ways to step.

Last time I walked downhill one careful step at a time. Tonight the walker gets weight, and then a pair of shoes.

The trouble with careful steps

Remember the long, narrow valley. Steep across, nearly flat along.

Careful steps have to stay small for the steep way, so along the floor they crawl. At the best step we tried, it takes 6,217 steps to get the loss under a ten-thousandth and keep it there.

Give the walker weight

Now make the walker heavy. Each step keeps 90 percent of the last step's motion and adds the new slope on top.

Across the valley, the slopes keep flipping, so they cancel. Along the floor they all point the same way, so they add up. The walker picks up speed exactly where it was crawling.

Boris Polyak described it in 1964. It's known as the heavy ball method.

Shoes for every direction

The other idea is shoes that adjust to the ground. Adam keeps a running average of each slope, and a running average of each slope squared.

It divides the first by the square root of the second. So a direction with a steady slope gets a step of about the same size, however steep or gentle it is: steep directions are slowed down, gentle ones sped up. A direction whose slope keeps flipping gets a short step.

Both averages start at zero, so at first they're too small. Adam scales them back up, so its very first step is the step size you chose, to within a hair, in every direction that has any slope at all.

The race

Same valley, same start. Each walker gets the best step from a few we tried.

Which walker gets down this valley first? (the film pauses here)

The heavy ball, by a mile: 285 steps. Careful steps take 6,217. Adam dips under the line at step 10,346, keeps wandering around it, and only stays under after 16,790.

And on the gentle bowl from last time, careful steps win: 33 steps, against 146 for the other two. No walker is best on every hill.

Past the edge

Remember the edge on the bowl: past a step of 0.5, careful steps fly off. Try 0.6.

Careful steps fly off, as before. The heavy ball's edge here is 0.95, so it gets down. Adam's steps don't grow with the slope, so it doesn't fly off, and here it gets down too.

Changing the step as you go

The step size doesn't have to stay fixed. Many models start with a warmup, small steps while everything is new, then let the step size fall away along a smooth curve.

And AdamW adds one more thing: almost every number shrinks by a small fraction at each step, kept separate from Adam's own step. It pulls numbers that aren't earning their keep back towards zero.

On real networks

On the spirals from the bucket chain, with each walker's step chosen on a separate set of points, careful steps first pass 95 percent on new points at step 2,000, the heavy ball at 1,300, and Adam at 900.

But run five different starting networks and batch orders, and Adam's final score ranges from 91.8 to 99.3 percent, while careful steps stay between 99.0 and 99.8. Fast, and on this network, less steady.

The language model from the attention lesson trains with AdamW. For its first 400 steps, with the same start and the same sentences, AdamW reaches a held-out loss of 0.85, the heavy ball 0.89, and careful steps 0.96.

What a race can't tell you

Every number tonight depends on the hill and on the handful of steps we tried for each walker. Try more, or a different hill, and the order can change.

And four hundred steps is the first fifth of the language model's training. It has barely started to copy, so this shows who gets off the line fastest, not who finishes best.

Goodnight

Weight carries you through the zigzags. Shoes give every direction its own stride. Neither wins every hill.

Next along the hill: learning a harbour by heart, and why that's a trap. Goodnight.

Sources

Every claim in the film, with where it comes from and what that source does not prove. The numbers about the model are computed from its weights, which you can load and check: facts.json.

  • Night School's surfaces and optimiser races, computed for this film. media/school/optimisers/facts.json, written by tools/school/fill_optimisers.mjs from system/school/optimisers.mjs and gradients.mjs. https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/optimisers

    Used for: Rosenbrock from (-1.2, 1), threshold 1e-4 and staying under: plain descent (best of 5 steps, 0.0015) 6,217 updates; heavy ball (beta 0.9, best step 0.003) 285; Adam (best step 0.001) first under at 10,346, stays under from 16,790. Tilted bowl, threshold 1e-6: plain descent (0.4) 33 updates; heavy ball and Adam 146 each. At step 0.6 on the bowl: plain descent diverges; the heavy ball's measured edge is 0.95 (predicted 0.95) and it converges; Adam converges.

    Does not prove: Anything general about optimisers; the order depends on the surface and on the step grids tried.

  • Polyak 1964, the heavy ball method. Polyak, B. T. (1964). Some methods of speeding up the convergence of iteration methods. USSR Computational Mathematics and Mathematical Physics 4(5), 1-17. https://doi.org/10.1016/0041-5553(64)90137-5

    Used for: The heavy ball method adds a multiple of the previous step to the gradient step: x(k+1) = x(k) - a g(k) + b (x(k) - x(k-1)); it is widely known as the heavy ball method.

    Does not prove: That momentum helps on every problem.

  • Kingma and Ba 2015, Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization. Kingma, D. P., Ba, J. (2015). Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization. ICLR 2015. arXiv:1412.6980. https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.6980

    Used for: Adam keeps exponential moving averages of the gradient and of its elementwise square, corrects both for their initialisation at zero, and divides the first by the square root of the second (Algorithm 1). With bias correction, the first step is alpha times g / (|g| + eps) in each coordinate: alpha to within eps wherever the gradient is non-zero; with a steady gradient the step is about alpha whatever the gradient's scale (section 2.1).

    Does not prove: That Adam generalises as well as other methods on every task.

  • Loshchilov and Hutter 2017, SGDR: Stochastic Gradient Descent with Warm Restarts. Loshchilov, I., Hutter, F. (2017). SGDR: Stochastic Gradient Descent with Warm Restarts. ICLR 2017. arXiv:1608.03983. https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.03983

    Used for: Cosine annealing lowers the learning rate along half a cosine from its maximum to its minimum.

    Does not prove: That cosine decay is the best schedule.

  • Loshchilov and Hutter 2019, Decoupled Weight Decay Regularization. Loshchilov, I., Hutter, F. (2019). Decoupled Weight Decay Regularization. ICLR 2019. arXiv:1711.05101. https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.05101

    Used for: AdamW applies weight decay directly to the weights, separately from the adaptive gradient step and scaled by the schedule multiplier, instead of adding an L2 term to the gradient. In our model the decay applies to the matrices and embeddings (20,096 of 20,864 numbers), not to gains and biases.

    Does not prove: That decoupled decay is better for every model.

  • Goyal and others 2017, Accurate, Large Minibatch SGD. Goyal, P., et al. (2017). Accurate, Large Minibatch SGD: Training ImageNet in 1 Hour. arXiv:1706.02677. https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.02677

    Used for: A gradual warmup of the learning rate over the first 5 epochs made large-minibatch training work at a high learning rate (section 2.2).

    Does not prove: That warmup is needed for every model, or how common it is.

  • Night School's spiral network, retrained with each optimiser. media/school/optimisers/facts.json (spiral section): the F4 network, 4,000 updates, batch 32; steps chosen on a separate validation draw (seed 4), never on the held-out set. https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/optimisers

    Used for: First update at 95% held-out accuracy: plain descent 2,000, heavy ball 1,300, Adam 900. Over 5 network and batch-order seed pairs, final held-out accuracy ranges: Adam 0.9175 to 0.9925, plain descent 0.99 to 0.9975, heavy ball 0.995 to 0.9975 (facts.json, spiral.seedSpread).

    Does not prove: That Adam is less stable in general; one small network, five seeds.

  • Night School's tiny transformer, retrained for 400 updates with three optimisers. media/school/optimisers/facts.json (transformer section): same initial weights, batches, warmup and clipping as the lab trainer; only the update rule differs; AdamW is the trainer's own and reproduces model.json's curve. https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/optimisers

    Used for: After 400 updates, held-out loss: AdamW 0.8456, heavy ball 0.8925, plain descent 0.9608 (each at its best step from a 3 or 4 point grid, chosen on 64 validation rows). Besides the update rule, the AdamW arm differs in its weight decay and its second-moment average; at 400 updates copy accuracy is 0.32 (AdamW) against a chance level of about 0.10.

    Does not prove: Anything about full training: at 400 updates no arm has learned the copy skill yet.

What this lesson leaves out

Which walker wins depends on the hill and on the handful of steps tried for each; comparisons between optimisers are sensitive to how carefully each one is tuned, and these are small, chosen surfaces.

The language model comparison covers its first 400 updates only, a fifth of its training, before it has properly learned to copy; it shows who gets off the line fastest, not who finishes best.

Before this: Backpropagation (F4). Next: The held-out set (F6).

items.title: Quantisation: fewer bits per number
items.description: Store a model's weights in 8, 6, 4, 3 or 2 bits and measure what it loses: scales per table, per output and per group, and GPTQ's careful rounding.
items.excerpt: Skip to content Zain Dana Harpernight school / S18 Quantisation. Fewer bits per number. Every weight is stored in 32 bits. Tallow stores them in fewer, with one scale per table, per output or per group, rounds them plainly or with GPTQ, and scores each version on the same held-out rows. The film About 4:52, hosted by Tallow. It asks you one question and wait
items.body_html:
The film

About 4:52, hosted by Tallow. It asks you one question and waits for your answer before it shows you. The guide's voice is not recorded yet, so for now the film plays with captions; the full words are also below.

Play the film

Nothing loads until you press play.

The lab: the palette

Pick the bits, the scale and the rounding; the page quantises the model, scores it on held-out rows against the full one and repaints one table. In the film, 4 bits with one scale per output raised the loss by 0.0078 by plain rounding and 0.0028 by GPTQ, at 18% of the size.

Open the palette

Everything is computed on your computer, in this page. Nothing is sent anywhere.

Everything the film says

Quantisation

Quantisation. Fewer bits per number.

Every number in our model is stored in 32 bits. Big models have billions of numbers, so the memory adds up fast. Tonight Tallow stores the weights in fewer bits and measures what the model loses.

A smaller palette

Think of a painter with fewer paints. With 255 shades a picture looks smooth. With 15, you start to see bands. With 3, you see mostly bands.

Quantising a table of weights is the same move. Pick a scale, divide every number by it, and round to the nearest of a few levels. At 4 bits our scheme has 15 levels; at 2 bits, only 3.

To use the table again, multiply back by the scale. Every number comes back to its nearest level, off by up to half a step.

What it saves

Our model takes 83,456 bytes in 32-bit numbers. At 4 bits, with one scale for each output of each table, it takes 15,376: 18 percent of the size.

What it costs

Score every version on the same 1,024 held-out rows. The full model's loss is 0.6676.

At 8 bits per number, one scale per output: 0.6677. At 6: 0.6685. At 4: 0.6754. At 3: 0.7249. At 2 bits: 3.48, and the model is broken.

Four bits instead of thirty-two. How much worse is the loss? (the film pauses here)

With one scale for each whole table instead of each output, it breaks sooner: 1.59 already at 3 bits.

Where it hurts

One scale has to cover a table's biggest number. If a few numbers are much bigger than the rest, the steps get wide, and every small number is rounded coarsely.

Quantise one table at a time to 4 bits, with one scale for the whole table, and see which one hurts. The readout, the table that turns the model's last list of numbers into word scores, costs the most: 0.0276 nats on its own.

Tim Dettmers and colleagues found in 2022 that in large models, once the activations are stored in 8 bits too, the trouble comes from a few huge values in them. Activations are the numbers flowing between tables. We left those in full precision here, so that part of the story does not show.

Rounding with care

Rounding each number on its own throws away the fact that they work together. GPTQ, from Elias Frantar and colleagues in 2023, rounds the numbers of a table one input column at a time and nudges the ones not yet rounded to make up for the error. It uses a small sample of text to see which errors matter.

At 4 bits with one scale per output, plain rounding raises the loss by 0.0078. GPTQ raises it by 0.0028, roughly a third as much.

It is not magic. At 2 bits with one scale per table, both versions are broken, and GPTQ comes out worse.

Goodnight

Fewer bits per number is how large models fit on smaller machines. Our model has only 83,456 bytes of numbers, and large ones behave differently, so how few bits you can get away with has to be measured on the model you have.

Next, in the cannery: the sums these tables are used for, and how a chip does them fast. Goodnight.

Sources

Every claim in the film, with where it comes from and what that source does not prove. The numbers about the model are computed from its weights, which you can load and check: facts.json.

  • Night School's quantisation runs, computed for this film. media/school/quant/facts.json, written by tools/school/fill_quant.mjs from system/school/quant.mjs and quant-gptq.mjs: the attention model's weights quantised by round-to-nearest and GPTQ at 8, 6, 4, 3 and 2 bits, per tensor, per output channel and per group, scored on 1,024 held-out rows with bootstrap intervals; one tensor at a time; controls. https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/quant

    Used for: Float loss 0.6676; per channel round-to-nearest 8/6/4/3/2 bits: 0.668, 0.668, 0.675, 0.725, 3.483. 4 bits per channel: 15,376 bytes (18 percent); rise +0.0078 (round-to-nearest) and +0.0028 (GPTQ). Readout alone at 4 bits: +0.0276.

    Does not prove: Anything about large models; activations stay in float.

  • Jacob and others 2018, Quantization and Training of Neural Networks for Efficient Integer-Arithmetic-Only Inference. Jacob, B., Kligys, S., Chen, B., and others (2018). CVPR 2018. arXiv:1712.05877. https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.05877

    Used for: Real values are represented by an integer and a scale (and zero point): r = S (q - Z).

    Does not prove: Anything about this model.

  • Dettmers and others 2022, LLM.int8(). Dettmers, T., Lewis, M., Belkada, Y., Zettlemoyer, L. (2022). LLM.int8(): 8-bit Matrix Multiplication for Transformers at Scale. NeurIPS 2022. arXiv:2208.07339. https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.07339

    Used for: Large-magnitude outlier features in activations emerge in large transformers and break naive 8-bit quantisation.

    Does not prove: Anything about this model.

  • Frantar and others 2023, GPTQ. Frantar, E., Ashkboos, S., Hoefler, T., Alistarh, D. (2023). GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-trained Transformers. ICLR 2023. arXiv:2210.17323. https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.17323

    Used for: Quantises weights column by column, updating the not-yet-quantised weights to compensate, using second-order information from calibration data.

    Does not prove: Anything about this model.

What this lesson leaves out

One model of 83,456 bytes; large models behave differently, and their activation outliers do not show here because activations stay in full precision.

Symmetric round-to-nearest without a zero point, and GPTQ with a symmetric grid and calibration text from the lesson's own generator.

Scores on 1,024 held-out rows; differences from the full model are paired on the same rows.

Before this: Threads, workgroups and memory (K21). Next, in the cannery: Matmul tiling (K22).

items.title: Scaling: bigger, longer, how much
items.description: Twelve small models of different sizes trained on the same text: what size buys, what more work buys, and what the scaling-law papers found.
items.excerpt: Skip to content Zain Dana Harpernight school / L14 Scaling. Bigger, longer, how much. Making models bigger and training them longer kept making them better. Tallow builds a shelf of small ones and measures how far each gets toward the floor its text allows. The film About 3:45, hosted by Tallow. It asks you one question and waits for your answer before it sh
items.body_html:
The film

About 3:45, hosted by Tallow. It asks you one question and waits for your answer before it shows you. The guide's voice is not recorded yet, so for now the film plays with captions; the full words are also below.

Play the film

Nothing loads until you press play.

The lab: the shelf

Pick a width and a number of floors, train the model in this page, and watch its gap above the floor against the work done, over the film's frontier. The film's twelve models run from 616 to 100,544 numbers outside their word and place tables.

Open the shelf

Everything is computed on your computer, in this page. Nothing is sent anywhere.

Everything the film says

Scaling

Scaling. Bigger, longer, how much.

Large language models are large because, for years, making them bigger and training them longer kept making them better. Tonight we try that on a shelf of small ones, and we are honest about what a shelf this small can show.

The shelf

We built 12 versions of the attention model: 8 to 64 numbers per word, one to three floors. The smallest has 616 numbers outside its word and place tables; the largest, 100,544.

Each trained for 4,000 steps on the same text, and each is scored by how far its held-out loss sits above the floor, 0.6585, the loss of the rules themselves.

Bigger

The smallest ends 0.15 above the floor and gets 36 percent of look-back words right. Two floors of 16: 0.0161 above the floor, and 99.6 percent.

Over twenty times more numbers than the two-floor model of 16. How much closer to the floor? (the film pauses here)

Past that, for the models with two or three floors, the gap barely moves. The lesson's own recipe, trained twice as long, ends 0.0150 above the floor, and the largest 0.0225.

Three runs of the same model with different seeds spread about as much as that. So on this text, at this length, we cannot see any gain from size above about 4,480 numbers.

Longer, and the frontier

Now count the work instead: the arithmetic each training run has done, in floating-point operations.

At every amount of work, take the lowest loss any model on the shelf had reached. Plotted on a log-log chart, their gaps above the floor fall on a straight line, with a slope of -0.65. More work, a smaller gap, at a steady rate.

And the best model for each amount of work mostly grows as the work grows: small models win the small budgets and bigger ones the big ones, though not at every step.

The real curves

Kaplan and colleagues, in 2020, found curves like this over models from hundreds of numbers to more than a billion, and over a much wider range of work.

Hoffmann and colleagues, in 2022, found that most large models of the time were too big for their training text. Their Chinchilla had 70 billion numbers, a quarter of Gopher's, trained on more than four times the text, and beat it.

Our shelf is far too small to test their numbers. What it can show is the shape: a floor, a gap that shrinks with work, and a best size that grows with the budget.

Goodnight

Bigger and longer help until a model gets close to what its text allows. On our shelf, that comes early.

Goodnight.

Sources

Every claim in the film, with where it comes from and what that source does not prove. The numbers about the model are computed from its weights, which you can load and check: facts.json.

  • Night School's shelf of small models, trained for this film. media/school/scaling/facts.json, written by tools/school/fill_scaling.mjs from system/school/scaling.mjs: 12 models (width 8 to 64, depth 1 to 3) trained 4,000 steps on the same text, scored by held-out loss above the generator's floor; fits on log-log axes; the frontier over compute; three seeds at two grid points. https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/scaling

    Used for: Excess over the floor (0.6585): smallest 0.15426, d16 L2 0.016079, d32 L2 0.014979, d64 L3 0.022533. Seed spread of log10 excess: 0.13761 (d16 L2), 0.11772 (d32 L2). Frontier slope of excess against compute: -0.64767 (R2 0.97109); best size against budget slope 0.41372.

    Does not prove: The papers' exponents; one learning rate and schedule for every size is a confound.

  • Kaplan and others 2020, Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models. Kaplan, J., McCandlish, S., Henighan, T., Brown, T. B., Chess, B., Child, R., Gray, S., Radford, A., Wu, J., Amodei, D. (2020). Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models. arXiv:2001.08361. https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361

    Used for: Loss falls as a power law in non-embedding parameters, data and compute over about 768 to 1.5e9 parameters and several orders of magnitude of compute.

    Does not prove: Anything about this model.

  • Hoffmann and others 2022, Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models (Chinchilla). Hoffmann, J., Borgeaud, S., Mensch, A., and others (2022). Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models. arXiv:2203.15556. https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556

    Used for: Parameters and training tokens should grow in equal proportion with compute; many large models of the time were undertrained; Chinchilla (70B parameters, 1.4T tokens) outperforms Gopher (280B, 300B tokens) at the same compute.

    Does not prove: Anything about this model.

What this lesson leaves out

The shelf is tiny next to the papers' models and one learning rate serves every size; it shows the shape of scaling, not their exponents.

Above about 4,500 numbers, the differences between sizes are within the spread of three seeds.

Before this: Data (L13). Later: Decoding (L15).

items.title: Search and sorting: the cost of looking
items.description: Count the comparisons: knocking along a row against halving it, insertion sort against merge sort, and why halving only works on a row in order.
headings: Search and sorting. The cost of looking.
The lab: the row of shells
Search and sorting: the cost of looking
Only if they are in order
items.excerpt: Skip to content Zain Dana Harpernight school / A26 Search and sorting. The cost of looking. Looking things up and putting them in order are two of the commonest jobs a computer does. Rerun counts every knock: one shell at a time, halving a sorted row, and two ways to sort it first. The film About 4:30, hosted by Rerun. It asks you one question and waits for
items.body_html:
The film

About 4:30, hosted by Rerun. It asks you one question and waits for your answer before it shows you. The guide's voice is not recorded yet, so for now the film plays with captions; the full words are also below.

Play the film

Nothing loads until you press play.

The lab: the row of shells

Pick a sort, a kind of row and a size, and watch it sort with every comparison counted; then look for a shell by knocking along or by halving. In the film's measurements, a jumbled row of 1,024 took 260,740 comparisons by insertion and 8,952 by merging; halving found any shell among 65,536 in at most 17 knocks.

Walk the row

Everything is computed on your computer, in this page. Nothing is sent anywhere.

Everything the film says

Search and sorting: the cost of looking

Search and sorting: the cost of looking.

Looking things up and putting them in order are two of the commonest jobs a computer does. Tonight Rerun counts the cost, one knock at a time.

One shell at a time

Rerun is looking for one shell in a row of 65,536. The plain way is to knock on each in turn until he finds it.

On average that took 32,921 knocks, about half the row. If the shell is not there, he knocks on all 65,536.

Halve the beach

Now suppose the shells are in order, smallest to largest. Knock on the middle one. If it is too big, the shell must be in the left half; too small, the right. Half the beach is gone in one knock.

Keep halving. For 65,536 shells it takes at most 17 knocks, and about 15 on average.

Sixty-five thousand shells, in order. How many knocks at most? (the film pauses here)

Only if they are in order

Halving only works because the shells are in order. Try it on a jumbled row of the same size and it still stops within 17 knocks, but even in its best run it missed 65,515 of the 65,536 shells that are there.

Fewer knocks is no good if the answer is wrong. So first, the shells have to be put in order.

Sorting by insertion

The simplest way: pick up each shell in turn and slide it left past every bigger one, the way many people sort a hand of cards.

On a row that is already in order, that is 65,535 comparisons for 65,536 shells, one for each shell after the first. On a row in reverse order it is 2,147,450,880. On a jumbled row, about 1,074,190,182.

Sorting by merging

A better way: split the row in half, sort each half, then merge the two sorted halves by walking along both and always taking the smaller front shell.

Each half is sorted the same way, down to single shells. On jumbled rows of 65,536, that took about 965,755 comparisons on average. Insertion took more than a thousand times as many.

How the cost grows

Double the row and see what happens. Knocking along it doubles. Halving adds one knock. Insertion sort on a jumbled row about quadruples. Merge sort a little more than doubles.

On this computer, sorting 65,536 jumbled shells took 1,151 milliseconds by insertion and 7.34 by merging.

What the count leaves out

These are counts of comparisons, not times. A real computer also pays for moving things and for memory, and the built-in sort that comes with the JavaScript engine, which counts nothing, took 2.99 milliseconds on the same row and the same computer.

But the counts tell you which way it grows, and that matters more as the row gets longer.

Goodnight

Put the shells in order once, and then halve the beach every time you look.

Goodnight.

Sources

Every claim in the film, with where it comes from and what that source does not prove. The numbers about the model are computed from its weights, which you can load and check: facts.json.

  • Night School's counts of comparisons. media/school/search/facts.json, written by tools/school/fill_search.mjs from system/school/search.mjs: linear and binary search, insertion and merge sort with counters, on sizes 8 to 65,536 and seeds 1 to 10, with 134 closed-form checks, a binary-search-on-unsorted control and Node timings. https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/search

    Used for: Every count in the film, the closed-form checks and the control.

    Does not prove: Times on other machines or engines; counts are of comparisons only.

  • Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, vol. 3, 2nd ed. (1998). Donald E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 3: Sorting and Searching, 2nd edition, Addison-Wesley, 1998; sections 5.2.1 (insertion), 5.2.4 (merging), 6.2.1 (binary search).

    Used for: The standard treatment of these algorithms and their costs.

    Does not prove: The film's exact counts, which are measured here; the section text was not read for this film.

  • Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, Introduction to Algorithms, 4th ed. (2022), chapter 2. MIT Press, 2022; 2.1 Insertion sort, 2.3 Designing algorithms (merge sort).

    Used for: Insertion sort and merge sort as described.

    Does not prove: The film's counts; the book uses its own cost model.

What this lesson leaves out

Counts of comparisons, not times; real costs also depend on moves, memory and the machine.

The timings in the film are one computer's, with counting switched on.

Every closed form the film uses was checked against the counters at every size; the textbook sections were checked only by their tables of contents.

Next, on the same beach: Dynamic programming (A27).

items.title: The held-out set: learning, or remembering?
items.description: A curve that passes through every point and fails on new ones: overfitting, the held-out set, a leash, and how even a held-out score is one draw.
headings: The held-out set. Learning, or remembering?
The spirals, with too few points
items.excerpt: Skip to content Zain Dana Harpernight school / F6 The held-out set. Learning, or remembering? A model can learn its training examples by heart and still be lost on new ones. Pylon fits curves at her desk, keeps some points back, and shows what they reveal. The film About 5:18, hosted by Pylon. It asks you one question and waits for your answer before it show
items.body_html:
The film

About 5:18, hosted by Pylon. It asks you one question and waits for your answer before it shows you. The narrated cut runs 4:07, voiced by Pylon in a synthesized voice made from the author's own voice; the author approved these cuts for publishing. Captions are on by default. The live version under it draws the same film in your browser, waits for your answer at each question, and runs a little longer; the full words are also below.

Play the film

Nothing loads until you press play.

The lab: practice and test

Fit a curve of any flexibility to 16 points, with or without a leash, and see its error on them and on 500 held-out points; draw new training points and watch the best flexibility move. Then train the spiral network on 10 to 400 points. In the film, 40 points gave 78.2% on new points and 400 gave 99.5%.

Open the chart

Everything is computed on your computer, in this page. Nothing is sent anywhere.

Everything the film says

The held-out set

The held-out set. Learning, or remembering?

I could learn this harbour by heart, every crate in its place. Then one night they send me to a different harbour.

Sixteen points

Here are 16 points. They come from a smooth curve, plus a little noise, the way real measurements do.

Let's fit a curve through them. A straight line misses the bend. A gentle curve follows it. And a wild one, with enough freedom, passes through every single point.

Which curve will do best on points it has never seen? (the film pauses here)

The wild one gets every point right: its error on them is about one part in a hundred billion. That's zero, apart from rounding in the arithmetic.

Points kept back

So keep some points back. 500 of them, drawn the same way, never used for fitting. That's the held-out set.

On those, the gentle curve's error is 0.33. The wild one's is 3,936. Between the points it learned it swings wildly, and past the outermost ones it shoots off the chart.

Make the curve more flexible, step by step, and the error on the training points only ever goes down. The error on the held-out points goes down, then turns around and climbs, with a few bumps on the way.

A leash

One fix is a leash: keep the wild curve, but charge it for every large number it uses.

A moderate charge brings its held-out error down from 3,936 to 0.43. That's the best of seven charges we tried, picked by looking at these same held-out points, so it flatters the leash a little. Pull too hard and it gets worse again: at the heaviest pull we tried, 0.70.

The spirals, with too few points

The bucket chain from last time learned two spirals from 400 points. Give it only 40.

It still gets every training point right. On new points it's right 78.3 percent of the time, against 99.5 with all 400.

Watch the held-out loss. It's lowest early, at step 300, and then climbs while the training loss keeps falling. Its score on new points still creeps up for a while, to 80 percent by step 1,000, but it grows ever more sure of itself, wrong answers included. After that the score stops improving, and training only tightens its grip on these forty points.

One draw is one draw

And a score from one training set is one draw. Pick five different sets of 40 training points, and the held-out score runs from 75.5 to 86.0 percent.

Even which curve looks best depends on the draw. Over two hundred draws of sixteen points, the gentle curve came out best 113 times, not every time.

The language model

The language model from the attention lesson was trained on a stream of freshly made sentences, a new batch every step. Its little grammar does repeat itself: 507 of its 32,000 training rows were exact copies of earlier ones. But no row came round more than 5 times, so it had little chance to learn its training rows by heart.

Score the finished model on rows it trained on, and its loss is about 0.63. On the next stretch of the same stream, which it didn't train on, 0.67. A small gap, not a chasm.

And its own held-out set turns out to be a little hard: 0.69, higher than five fresh draws of the same size, which range from 0.65 to 0.67.

Keep it held out

One rule makes all of this work. Once you use the held-out points to choose anything, how flexible the curve is, how long to train, they stop being held out.

So careful work keeps a third set locked away until the very end, and looks at it once.

Goodnight

Getting the practice right is not the test. Keep points back, and check on those.

That's the hill done. Next, down at the dock, we cut words into crates. Goodnight.

Sources

Every claim in the film, with where it comes from and what that source does not prove. The numbers about the model are computed from its weights, which you can load and check: facts.json.

  • Night School's curve fits, computed for this film. media/school/heldout/facts.json (poly section), written by tools/school/fill_heldout.mjs from system/school/heldout.mjs: least squares by Householder QR; ridge by QR on the design matrix stacked over sqrt(lambda) times the identity. https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/heldout

    Used for: 16 training points from sin(pi x) with noise sigma 0.2; 500 held-out points. Degree 3 held-out RMSE 0.330; degree 15 train RMSE 1.4e-11 and held-out RMSE 3,936. Ridge at degree 15: held-out RMSE 3,936 at lambda 0, 0.429 at 0.01 (the best of 7), 0.703 at 100. Over 200 training draws, degree 3 is the best degree on held-out data 113 times. Degree 3 and the penalty 0.01 were picked on the same held-out points they are scored on, which flatters them a little. The wild curve's held-out error is 2.99 on points inside the training range and far larger past the outermost training points.

    Does not prove: Anything about real data; a toy curve chosen to show one effect.

  • Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville 2016, Deep Learning. Goodfellow, I., Bengio, Y., Courville, A. (2016). Deep Learning. MIT Press. Chapter 5.2 (capacity, overfitting and underfitting) and 5.3 (hyperparameters and validation sets). https://www.deeplearningbook.org/

    Used for: Training error falls as capacity grows, while test error typically falls and then rises (overfitting). Choosing hyperparameters on the test set biases it; a separate validation set is used for choices, and the test set only to estimate generalisation at the end.

    Does not prove: Anything about a particular model.

  • Hoerl and Kennard 1970, Ridge Regression. Hoerl, A. E., Kennard, R. W. (1970). Ridge Regression: Biased Estimation for Nonorthogonal Problems. Technometrics 12(1), 55-67. https://doi.org/10.1080/00401706.1970.10488634

    Used for: Ridge regression adds a penalty on the size of the coefficients (lambda times their sum of squares) to least squares.

    Does not prove: Which lambda to use.

  • Night School's spiral network on 40 points against 400. media/school/heldout/facts.json (spiral section): the F4 network, plain descent at 0.3, 10,000 updates, on the first 40 of the 400 training points and, as the control, on all 400. https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/heldout

    Used for: Both reach training accuracy 1. Held-out accuracy 0.7825 with 40 points, 0.995 with 400. With 40 points the held-out loss is lowest at update 300 (0.648) and ends at 1.487. Over five different 40-point draws, held-out accuracy ranges from 0.755 to 0.86. After the held-out loss minimum at update 300, held-out accuracy still rises, to 0.8025 at update 1,000, while the held-out loss climbs.

    Does not prove: Anything general about how many points a task needs.

  • Night School's tiny transformer, its training and held-out losses. media/school/heldout/facts.json (attention section): model.json's own curves, and the final weights rescored on rows they were trained on, on unseen rows of the same stream, on the lab's 256 held-out rows and on five fresh 256-row draws. https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/heldout

    Used for: The trainer draws a fresh batch every update; the generator repeats rows by chance: 507 of the 32,000 training rows were exact copies of earlier rows, and no row came round more than 5 times. 8 of the 256 'unseen' rows and 3 of the lab's 256 held-out rows also occur in training (facts.json, attention.repeats). Final weights: loss 0.626 on the last 16 trained batches, 0.668 on the next 16 unseen batches, 0.687 on the lab's held-out rows, 0.650 to 0.672 on five fresh draws.

    Does not prove: That the model would not memorise with repeated data; it never had any.

What this lesson leaves out

The curve and the spirals are toy problems with known answers, so overfitting is easy to see; in real work the truth is unknown and the held-out set is the only window onto it.

Some choices in the film (the best degree, the best leash) were picked on the same held-out points they are scored on, which flatters them a little; the film says so, and the closing rule (a third set, looked at once) is the fix.

Before this: Optimisers (F5). Next, at the dock: Tokens (L7).
