items.title: The training loop
items.description: Batch, forward, loss, backward, step: the whole loop that trains a language model, rerun exactly, with one setting changed at a time.
headings: The training loop. Five steps, two thousand times.
items.excerpt: Skip to content Zain Dana Harpernight school / L12 The training loop. Five steps, two thousand times. Every earlier lesson holds one piece of training. Pylon runs them round the dock together and watches a blind guess become a model that copies. The film About 4:40, hosted by Pylon. It asks you two questions and waits for your answer before it shows you. The
items.body_html:
The film

About 4:40, hosted by Pylon. It asks you two questions and waits for your answer before it shows you. The guide's voice is not recorded yet, so for now the film plays with captions; the full words are also below.

Play the film

Nothing loads until you press play.

The lab: the training dock

Train the attention model from scratch in this page with your own step size, batch, clipping and weight decay, and watch its held-out loss and copy rate against the film's run. Rerun from its seeds, the loop gives back the lesson's model exactly: 29 of 29 weight tables.

Open the dock

Everything is computed on your computer, in this page. Nothing is sent anywhere.

Everything the film says

The training loop

The training loop. Five steps, two thousand times.

Every lesson so far has a piece of training in it. Tonight they go round together, and we watch the whole loop teach the attention model, from the first step to the last.

One lap

One lap goes like this. Take a batch of 16 rows from the training text. Run the model forward and score every next word: that is the loss.

Run backward to get the slope for every one of the model's 20,864 numbers. Then the optimiser takes one step downhill. That is one lap.

On one core of our test machine, with this lesson's own code, a lap takes about 21 milliseconds, and most of that is the backward pass: 14 of them.

The settings

The optimiser is Adam, with a little weight decay that shrinks most of the numbers slightly each step, as in AdamW. The layer norms' gains and the biases are left out.

The step size starts tiny and grows over the first 30 laps to 0.01. That is warmup.

And if the whole slope, all the numbers taken together, is ever longer than 1, it is shortened to 1 before the step. That is clipping. It fired on 76 of the 2,000 laps, 62 of them in the first 250.

Two thousand laps

Now run it. At lap zero, the held-out loss is 3.84, a blind guess.

By lap 100 it is 0.97: the easy patterns, which word tends to follow which, come first.

Will copying a word from far back be learned early, late, or bit by bit? (the film pauses here)

Copying a word from far back comes late, and then fast. At lap 500, copying is right 43 percent of the time. By lap 750, 97 percent.

We ran the loop again from the same seeds, and got the attention lesson's model back exactly: 29 of 29 weight tables, number for number.

Change one thing

Change one setting at a time, train for 1,000 laps, and compare. First, the noise: the same recipe on two other sets of training rows ends at 0.70 and 0.70, and the original at 0.70, all three within a few thousandths. A difference smaller than that cannot be told apart from luck.

A step size ten times smaller ends at 0.78, and copies right only 54 percent of the time. Ten times larger ends worse, at 0.95, copying 22 percent.

Make the step size ten times larger. Faster, or worse? (the film pauses here)

Without weight decay: 0.70, inside the noise. On this small model, at this length, it makes no difference we can see.

Batches of 4 rows for the same number of laps see a quarter of the text, and end at 0.87. Given the same text over four times the laps, they still end at 0.76.

A loop that cannot learn

Two broken loops, as checks. With a step size of zero, nothing moves: the loss stays at 3.84.

Turn every slope around, so each step goes uphill, and the loss climbs to 68. The loop only works because the slope points the right way.

Goodnight

Batch, forward, loss, backward, step. Two thousand times, and a blind guess becomes a model that copies.

Next on the dock: what goes into the batches. Goodnight.

Sources

Every claim in the film, with where it comes from and what that source does not prove. The numbers about the model are computed from its weights, which you can load and check: facts.json.

  • Night School's training loop, rerun for this film. media/school/trainloop/facts.json, written by tools/school/fill_trainloop.mjs from system/school/trainloop.mjs: the attention model retrained from its seeds (2,000 steps) and compared with model.json; one-change variants of 1,000 steps each; gradient norms and clipping; timing in Node; two broken-loop controls. https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/trainloop

    Used for: The retrained model equals model.json: 29 of 29 weight tensors byte for byte, 81 of 81 curve points. Clipping at norm 1 fired on 76 of 2000 steps, 62 of them in steps 1 to 250; warmup 30 steps to learning rate 0.01. Held-out loss 3.84 at step 0, 0.97 at 100, 0.82 at 500, 0.72 at 750; copy accuracy 0.43 at 500 and 0.97 at 750. Variants at 1,000 steps: reference 0.6981; other data seeds 0.700 and 0.702; learning rate 0.001 0.7835 (copy 0.5395); 0.1 0.9506 (copy 0.2174); no weight decay 0.6995; batch 4 at the same steps 0.8702. Controls: learning rate 0 stays at 3.8414; the gradient sign flipped climbs to 68.5. About 21 ms per step in Node on one core: forward 6.3 ms, backward 14.0 ms, update 0.2 ms.

    Does not prove: That these settings are best for larger models; timings are for one machine.

  • Kingma and Ba 2015, Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization. Kingma, D. P., Ba, J. (2015). Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization. ICLR 2015. arXiv:1412.6980. https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.6980

    Used for: Adam keeps running averages of each gradient and its square and steps by the first divided by the square root of the second (Algorithm 1); this model uses beta2 0.99 where the paper suggests 0.999.

    Does not prove: Anything about this model.

  • Loshchilov and Hutter 2019, Decoupled Weight Decay Regularization (AdamW). Loshchilov, I., Hutter, F. (2019). Decoupled Weight Decay Regularization. ICLR 2019. arXiv:1711.05101. https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.05101

    Used for: Weight decay applied directly to the weights, separate from the gradient step (AdamW, Algorithm 2); here the decay is scaled by the full learning rate, as common libraries do.

    Does not prove: Anything about this model.

What this lesson leaves out

Each changed setting is one run with one seed; only differences larger than the spread of the noise runs mean anything.

Timings are from one test machine; the lab's runs in your browser will be slower or faster.

Before this: The transformer block (L11). Next: Data (L13).

items.title: The transformer block
items.description: What one transformer block does: layer norm, attention, the MLP and the residual stream, taken apart room by room on a real model.
headings: The transformer block. Two floors, one stream.
Reading the stream on the way up
items.excerpt: Skip to content Zain Dana Harpernight school / L11 The transformer block. Two floors, one stream. Every word's list of numbers climbs the tower. On each floor, attention and a small network read it and add to it. Tallow switches the rooms off one at a time to see what each was doing. The film About 4:34, hosted by Tallow. It asks you two questions and waits
items.body_html:
The film

About 4:34, hosted by Tallow. It asks you two questions and waits for your answer before it shows you. The guide's voice is not recorded yet, so for now the film plays with captions; the full words are also below.

Play the film

Nothing loads until you press play.

The lab: the tower

Switch off any head or MLP of the attention model, or make a room replace the stream instead of adding to it, and score it on its held-out rows. With everything on it copies 99% of far-back words; attention and the MLP hold 8,448 and 8,384 of its 20,864 numbers.

Climb the tower

Everything is computed on your computer, in this page. Nothing is sent anywhere.

Everything the film says

The transformer block

The transformer block. Two floors, one stream.

Every word's list of numbers climbs the tower. On each floor, two rooms read it and add something to it. Tonight, what those rooms are, and what each one adds.

The stream

Start with a word's 32 numbers from the word table, its embedding, and add to them, number by number, 32 more from a second table for its place in the sentence. Call that the stream.

Each room reads the stream, works out something, and adds its answer back on. Nothing is thrown away. That adding is called the residual connection.

Before each room reads, it takes a copy of the stream rescaled to a steady size. That is layer norm, and in this model, as in GPT-2, it comes first in each room. The stream itself is left alone.

Two rooms per floor

The first room is attention: each word looks back along the sentence and takes in what it needs. This model has 2 heads per floor, two separate ways of looking.

The second room is a small network that works on each word alone, called the MLP or feed-forward layer. It widens the 32 numbers to 64, bends them, and narrows them back.

Attention and the MLP hold almost the same number of the model's 20,864 numbers: 8,448 and 8,384.

Reading the stream on the way up

We can stop the stream on any landing and ask it to guess the next word early, using the model's own last two steps: its final layer norm and its output table.

Which floor will matter most for copying a word from far back? (the film pauses here)

Straight from the table, the guess has a held-out loss of 2.33. After the first floor, 0.86. After the second, 0.69.

Copying a word from far back is the slow part: right 43 percent of the time after the first floor, and 99 percent at the top.

Switch one room off

Now switch rooms off, one at a time, and score the model again. With everything on, it copies right 99 percent of the time.

Silence the second head on the top floor, and copying falls to 40 percent. Silence the first head there, and nothing changes: 99 percent. On the top floor, one head does most of the copying, and its neighbour is close to idle. Copying needs a head on the first floor too: silence it, and copying falls to 38 percent.

Switch off the first floor's MLP, and the loss jumps from 0.69 to 5.96, worse than a blind guess.

On an untrained model, the same switches barely move the loss. The jobs were learned, not built in.

Why add, not replace

What if a room replaced the stream with its answer, instead of adding to it?

If a room replaces the stream instead of adding to it, what happens to the loss? (the film pauses here)

For the top floor's attention, the loss goes to 6.62. The room was only ever adding a little, and the rest of the stream was still needed.

One room is the odd one out. The first floor's MLP adds a vector about 10 times the size of the stream it reads, so replacing barely matters there: 0.69.

Goodnight

A block is two rooms on one stream: attention looks along the sentence, the MLP works on each word, and each adds its answer back on.

Next in the lighthouse: how the whole tower is trained. Goodnight.

Sources

Every claim in the film, with where it comes from and what that source does not prove. The numbers about the model are computed from its weights, which you can load and check: facts.json.

  • Night School's attention model, taken apart for this film. media/school/block/facts.json, written by tools/school/fill_block.mjs from system/school/block.mjs: a hooked forward pass (equal to the model's own forward, bit for bit) that reads the residual stream, applies the final norm and output matrix at each depth, and knocks out heads, attention layers and MLPs by zero, mean or shuffle, or makes a sub-layer replace the stream instead of adding to it; scored on 256 held-out rows (6,144 next words, 506 copy positions). https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/block

    Used for: Parameters: 20864 in all; attention 8448, MLP 8384, embeddings 2240, output 1472, norms 320. Readout at each depth (held-out loss): 2.33 from the table, 1.73 after layer 0 attention, 0.86 after layer 0 MLP, 0.75 after layer 1 attention, 0.69 at the top; copy accuracy 0.12, 0.21, 0.43, 0.82, 0.99. Zero knockouts: layer 1 head 1 drops copy accuracy to 0.4032; layer 1 head 0 leaves it at 0.9921; layer 0 MLP raises the loss to 5.9605. On the untrained model knockouts move the loss by under 0.05. Replace instead of add: layer 1 attention loss 6.62, layer 0 attention 4.93, layer 1 MLP 2.85, layer 0 MLP 0.69 (its output is about 10 times the stream it reads).

    Does not prove: That large models divide work the same way; a knockout shows what the model needs here, not what a part means.

  • Vaswani and others 2017, Attention Is All You Need. Vaswani, A., Shazeer, N., Parmar, N., Uszkoreit, J., Jones, L., Gomez, A. N., Kaiser, L., Polosukhin, I. (2017). Attention Is All You Need. NeurIPS 30. arXiv:1706.03762. https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762

    Used for: The transformer layer has two sub-layers, multi-head self-attention and a position-wise feed-forward network, each with a residual connection and layer normalisation (section 3.1); the paper applies the norm after the add.

    Does not prove: Anything about this model.

  • Radford and others 2019, Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners (GPT-2). Radford, A., Wu, J., Child, R., Luan, D., Amodei, D., Sutskever, I. (2019). Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners. OpenAI report. https://cdn.openai.com/better-language-models/language_models_are_unsupervised_multitask_learners.pdf

    Used for: Layer normalisation was moved to the input of each sub-block (section 2.3).

    Does not prove: Anything about this model.

  • nostalgebraist 2020, interpreting GPT: the logit lens (blog post). nostalgebraist (2020). interpreting GPT: the logit lens. LessWrong, 31 August 2020. A blog post, not peer reviewed. https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/AcKRB8wDpdaN6v6ru/interpreting-gpt-the-logit-lens

    Used for: Applying the output step to the stream at intermediate layers gives guesses that improve with depth.

    Does not prove: Anything about this model.

What this lesson leaves out

Two layers and two heads on a 46-word grammar: large models spread the same jobs over many more parts, and a knockout here shows what this model needs, not what a part means.

Reading the stream early uses the model's own final norm and output table; other readouts give other numbers, and facts.json gives both.

Before this: Attention (L10). Next: The training loop (L12).

items.title: Threads, workgroups and memory
items.description: How a graphics chip adds a million numbers at once: threads, workgroups, idle threads at the edge, and why neighbouring reads take fewer trips to memory.
items.excerpt: Skip to content Zain Dana Harpernight school / K21 Threads, workgroups and memory. A graphics chip does thousands of small sums at the same time. Pylon runs the cannery where that happens, counts every thread and every trip to the warehouse, and catches a thread that writes one place past the end. The film About 5:29, hosted by Pylon. It asks you two questio
items.body_html:
The film

About 5:29, hosted by Pylon. It asks you two questions and waits for your answer before it shows you. The guide's voice is not recorded yet, so for now the film plays with captions; the full words are also below.

Play the film

Nothing loads until you press play.

The lab: the cannery floor

Choose a crew size, a stride and a list length; count every thread and every trip with the emulator; then, if your browser has WebGPU, run the real kernel on your own chip, check it and time it. In the film, reads eight apart took 5.67 times the trips of neighbouring reads.

Open the cannery

Counting runs in this page. Timing runs the kernel on your own graphics chip, only when you press Time. Nothing is sent anywhere.

Everything the film says

Threads, workgroups and memory

Threads, workgroups and memory.

A graphics chip does not do one sum very fast. It does thousands of small sums at the same time. Tonight Pylon runs the cannery where that happens, and counts every trip to the warehouse.

One worker, one can

The job: add two lists of numbers, element by element, into a third. A list of 1,048,576 numbers.

On a graphics chip, each element gets its own worker, called a thread. Thread 40 reads number 40 from each list, adds them, and writes the sum to place 40. Every thread runs the same few lines of code.

Crews

Threads come in crews called workgroups. You choose the crew size; in WebGPU a crew may hold up to 256 threads by default.

A thread finds its element from its crew's number and its place in the crew: crew number times crew size, plus its place. With crews of 16, crew 2, place 8, is element 40.

Crews come in whole numbers. Add 1,000 numbers with crews of 64 and you need 16 crews, 1,024 threads. The last 24 have nothing to do, so the code must check that its element exists.

One past the end

Get that check wrong by one, and one idle thread writes one place past the end of the list. In a list of 40 numbers, numbered 0 to 39, element 40 has no place of its own.

If the check is off by one, does the program crash? (the film pauses here)

On a graphics chip that need not crash. The WGSL rules call it an error, but let it end quietly: the stray write may land anywhere in the same buffer, be dropped, or stop that one thread. So the output can look right while something else in the same buffer was spoiled.

Our checker compares every sum with a slow, careful one on the main processor, and plants guard values just past the end. Of 12 test cases, nine came from three kernels we broke on purpose, each run three ways. Together the two checks catch seven of the nine. The two they miss are stray writes the chip dropped, which leave every sum right. Only our emulator, which counts every write, sees those.

Trips to the warehouse

On NVIDIA chips, each crew is split into teams of 32 threads, called warps; other chips use other team sizes, from 4 to 128, and our counts use NVIDIA's 32. When a team reads from memory, the chip fetches whole blocks at a time; the current CUDA guide describes blocks of 32 bytes.

If the 32 threads read 32 neighbouring numbers, 4 bytes each, that is 128 bytes: 4 blocks. One team, a few trips.

Now spread the reads out, every eighth number. The same 32 reads now touch 32 blocks, one per thread.

Counting the trips

Count every trip for the whole job, reads and writes. With neighbouring reads: 393,216 blocks. With reads spread eight apart: 2,228,224. That is 5.67 times the trips, not 8, because the writes still go to neighbouring places. Most of each block fetched is thrown away.

Reads spread eight apart. How many times the trips? (the film pauses here)

Spreading them further changes nothing more in this model, because each thread already has a block of its own.

Your own chip

These are counts from a model of the chip, not times. Real chips have caches that hide some of the cost, and they differ from one another.

So the lab runs the real kernel on the chip in your own computer, if your browser allows it, and times it. If the time for spread-out reads is far from what the count predicts, then caches, a different team or block size, or the cost of starting the job are at work.

Goodnight

Thousands of small workers, in crews, fetching in blocks. Fast code keeps neighbouring workers on neighbouring numbers, and checks the edges.

Next in the cannery: multiplying whole tables, and carrying trays instead of single cans. Goodnight.

Sources

Every claim in the film, with where it comes from and what that source does not prove. The numbers about the model are computed from its weights, which you can load and check: facts.json.

  • Night School's GPU emulator and kernels, built for this film. media/school/threads/facts.json, written by tools/school/fill_threads.mjs from system/school/threads.mjs: WGSL kernels that add two arrays (contiguous and strided), an exact JS emulator of thread grouping, idle threads and memory transactions in 32-byte and 128-byte models, and a checker with canaries tested on nine broken kernels. https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/threads

    Used for: n = 1,000 with workgroups of 64: 16 workgroups, 1,024 threads, 24 idle. 32-byte model: contiguous 393,216 transactions for the whole job; stride 8 and above 2,228,224 (efficiency 0.1765). Of nine broken cases (three kernels, three allowed outcomes each), the output check with canaries misses two (stray writes dropped); the emulator's out-of-bounds store count catches those, and no case escapes both.

    Does not prove: Any timing on a real GPU; caches are not modelled.

  • W3C WebGPU specification. W3C (2026). WebGPU. Candidate Recommendation Draft; supported limits table. https://www.w3.org/TR/webgpu/

    Used for: Default maxComputeInvocationsPerWorkgroup 256 and maxComputeWorkgroupSizeX 256.

    Does not prove: Anything about a particular device.

  • W3C WGSL specification. W3C (2026). WebGPU Shading Language. Candidate Recommendation Draft; built-in values and out-of-bounds access. https://www.w3.org/TR/WGSL/

    Used for: global_invocation_id = workgroup_id * workgroup_size + local_invocation_id; an out-of-bounds store may write to any location of the bound buffer or not be executed.

    Does not prove: Anything about a particular device.

  • NVIDIA CUDA C++ Programming Guide. NVIDIA (2026). CUDA Programming Guide, version 13.4.2: section 1.2.2.2 (warps) and section 2.3.4.1 (global memory, 32-byte transactions). https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-programming-guide/

    Used for: Threads execute in warps of 32; global memory is accessed in 32-byte transactions.

    Does not prove: Anything about WebGPU devices from other vendors.

What this lesson leaves out

The film's numbers are counts from a model of the chip, not times; caches are not modelled.

Teams of 32 and 32-byte blocks are NVIDIA's; other chips use other sizes, so a time on your chip can differ from the count.

The kernels were checked against the emulator and the main processor; they were not timed on a graphics chip for this film.

Before this: Matrices move space (F2). Earlier at the prism: Evaluating a language model (L16).

items.title: Tokens: cutting text into crates
items.description: How a language model cuts text into pieces: letters, merges learned from counts (byte-pair encoding), and bytes so nothing is left on the dock.
items.excerpt: Skip to content Zain Dana Harpernight school / L7 Tokens. Cutting text into crates. A model never sees letters or words. It sees pieces. Pylon runs the customs shed where text is cut into crates, and the crates are learned from counting pairs. The film About 4:48, hosted by Pylon. It asks you one question and waits for your answer before it shows you. The na
items.body_html:
The film

About 4:48, hosted by Pylon. It asks you one question and waits for your answer before it shows you. The narrated cut runs 3:51, voiced by Pylon in a synthesized voice made from the author's own voice; the author approved these cuts for publishing. Captions are on by default. The live version under it draws the same film in your browser, waits for your answer at each question, and runs a little longer; the full words are also below.

Play the film

Nothing loads until you press play.

The lab: the customs shed

Type any text and cut it with merges learned on the guides' sentences, on Moby-Dick's opening, or on your own text. Slide the number of merges and switch the base to bytes. On the guides' 47,002 words, every word is one piece after 136 merges; Moby-Dick's opening takes 878.

Open the shed

Everything is computed on your computer, in this page. Nothing is sent anywhere.

Everything the film says

Tokens

Tokens. Cutting text into crates.

Everything that comes through my customs shed goes into a standard crate. Text too, before any language model can touch it.

How big a crate

A language model doesn't read letters. It reads a list of pieces, each one a number from its vocabulary. The question is how big to cut the pieces.

Cut by letter, with one extra mark for the end of each word, and the guides' sentences take about 4.39 pieces per word, counting each full stop and question mark as a word: tiny crates, a great many trips.

Cut by whole word, and every word is one piece. But a word the model has never seen has no crate at all.

Merge the common pairs

Byte-pair encoding meets in the middle. Start from single letters. Count every pair of neighbouring pieces, inside words. The most common pair gets a crate of its own. Then count again.

On the guides' sentences, the first merge joins an e to the end-of-word mark, so an e that ends a word gets one crate. By the fifth merge, the whole word 'the' has its own crate.

After fifty merges, how many pieces does a word take? (the film pauses here)

After 50 merges, a word takes 1.80 pieces on average. After 136, every one of the guides' words is a single piece.

A word nobody shipped before

Now a word that never came through the shed: lamplit. There's no crate for it.

So it's cut into pieces that do have crates: l, am, p, and lit at the end of a word. Nothing is thrown away. Rico Sennrich and his colleagues used this method, in a 2016 paper, to translate rare words.

Real English

The guides only know 44 words and 2 marks. So here's real English: the opening of Moby-Dick, about 599 words of it, to learn the merges from.

Then a page it never saw, the opening of Pride and Prejudice. With 400 merges, the new page takes 2.14 pieces per word. The word lighthouse, never seen, comes out as li, gh, thou and se.

Why the common pairs

Does it matter which pairs we merge? Merge random pairs instead, the same number of times, and over ten tries the guides' words still take 1.32 to 1.67 pieces each, instead of one.

The smallest crates

There's one more choice: what the very first pieces are. Characters run out fast. The page from Pride and Prejudice has curly quotation marks, and a capital D and E, that Moby-Dick never used, so with characters as the base, they have no crate.

GPT-2 starts from bytes instead. There are only 256 of them, and any text at all is some list of bytes. An a is one byte, an e with its accent built in is two, a curly apostrophe three, and a seal emoji four.

Start from bytes, and that new page has 0 pieces without a crate, instead of 16.

The lighthouse model

The little language model from the attention lesson skips all of this. It has one crate per word, 46 of them counting the full stop and question mark, because its whole world is those 46.

Byte-pair encoding needs 136 merges, and a vocabulary of 160, to cut the same sentences into whole words, because every piece it made on the way stays in the vocabulary.

Goodnight

Common pairs get their own crates, rare words come apart into pieces, and bytes mean nothing is ever left on the dock.

Next: giving every crate a place on the chart. Goodnight.

Sources

Every claim in the film, with where it comes from and what that source does not prove. The numbers about the model are computed from its weights, which you can load and check: facts.json.

  • Night School's tokenizer runs, computed for this film. media/school/tokens/facts.json, written by tools/school/fill_tokens.mjs from system/school/tokens.mjs: BPE learned on the guides' corpus (3,000 generated episodes, 47,002 words) and on the first five paragraphs of Moby-Dick (716 words), measured on held-out text. https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/tokens

    Used for: Guides' corpus: 4.39 tokens per word at 0 merges (characters plus one end-of-word symbol per word; '.' and '?' count as words), 1.80 at 50 merges, 1.00 at 136 merges (vocabulary 160). The first merge is e with the end-of-word mark; the fifth makes 'the'. Unseen 'lamplit' is cut into l, am, p, lit (end of word). Ten runs of 136 random merges leave 1.32 to 1.67 tokens per word. English: with 400 merges learned on Moby-Dick (716 pre-tokens, 599 words split on spaces), the opening of Pride and Prejudice takes 2.14 tokens per word; 'lighthouse' is cut into li, gh, thou, se, the same at 400 and at 878 merges. The attention model is word-level with 46 entries: 44 words and two marks ('.' and '?').

    Does not prove: Anything about large tokenizers; small texts chosen to show the mechanism.

  • Sennrich, Haddow and Birch 2016, Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units. Sennrich, R., Haddow, B., Birch, A. (2016). Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units. ACL 2016. arXiv:1508.07909. https://arxiv.org/abs/1508.07909

    Used for: Byte-pair encoding for word segmentation: start from characters with an end-of-word symbol, repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair of symbols within words, and add the merged symbol to the vocabulary (section 3.2, Algorithm 1). Rare and unseen words are represented as sequences of subword units, which lets a translation model handle them.

    Does not prove: That BPE is the best segmentation for every language or task.

  • Gage 1994, A New Algorithm for Data Compression. Gage, P. (1994). A New Algorithm for Data Compression. The C Users Journal 12(2), 23-38. https://www.derczynski.com/papers/archive/BPE_Gage.pdf

    Used for: Byte pair encoding began as compression: replace the most frequent adjacent pair of bytes with a byte that does not occur in the data, and repeat.

    Does not prove: Anything about language models.

  • Melville 1851, Moby-Dick. Melville, H. (1851). Moby-Dick; or, The Whale. Chapter 1, paragraphs 1 to 5. Project Gutenberg eBook #2701. https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2701

    Used for: Public-domain English text used as training text for the English BPE.

    Does not prove: Nothing; it is sample text.

  • Austen 1813, Pride and Prejudice. Austen, J. (1813). Pride and Prejudice. Chapter 1, paragraphs 1 to 10. Project Gutenberg eBook #1342. https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/1342

    Used for: Public-domain English text used as held-out text.

    Does not prove: Nothing; it is sample text.

  • Radford and others 2019, Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners (GPT-2). Radford, A., Wu, J., Child, R., Luan, D., Amodei, D., Sutskever, I. (2019). Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners. OpenAI. https://cdn.openai.com/better-language-models/language_models_are_unsupervised_multitask_learners.pdf

    Used for: GPT-2 applies BPE to bytes rather than Unicode code points: a base vocabulary of 256 instead of over 130,000, so any string can be encoded (section 2.2). Its vocabulary has 50,257 entries (section 2.3).

    Does not prove: That byte-level BPE is better on every measure; ours compresses slightly worse than character-level BPE on the held-out page.

  • UTF-8 byte counts and byte-level BPE, computed for this film. media/school/tokens/facts.json (bytes section): TextEncoder byte counts; character-level and byte-level BPE with 878 merges on Moby-Dick, measured on Pride and Prejudice. https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/tokens

    Used for: UTF-8: a is 1 byte, a precomposed accented e (U+00E9) 2 (an e with a combining accent is 3), a curly apostrophe 3, the seal emoji 4. On the held-out page, character-level BPE leaves 16 unknown tokens (7 open and 7 close curly quotes, one D and one E never seen in training); byte-level BPE leaves 0.

    Does not prove: That bytes are the right base for every language model.

What this lesson leaves out

The merges here are learned on small texts, so the pieces are short and odd; production tokenizers learn tens of thousands of merges on far more text.

Real tokenizers add rules this one leaves out (how spaces attach, special tokens, normalisation), so their pieces for the same text will differ.

Before this: The held-out set (F6). Next: Embeddings (L8).

items.title: Vectors: a list of numbers is a place
items.description: Watch Pylon turn crates into arrows, dot products and cosines, then drag them yourself and explore the attention model's own word table.
headings: Vectors. A list of numbers is a place.
items.excerpt: Skip to content Zain Dana Harpernight school / F1 Vectors. A list of numbers is a place. Every word inside a language model is a list of numbers, and a list of numbers is a place. Pylon shows you on her harbour chart, and then hands you the chart and the model's own word table. The film About 5:51, hosted by Pylon. It asks you two questions and waits for you
items.body_html:
The film

About 5:51, hosted by Pylon. It asks you two questions and waits for your answer before it shows you. The narrated cut runs 4:50, voiced by Pylon in a synthesized voice made from the author's own voice; the author approved these cuts for publishing. Captions are on by default. The live version under it draws the same film in your browser, waits for your answer at each question, and runs a little longer; the full words are also below.

Play the film

Nothing loads until you press play.

The lab: Pylon's chart room

Drag two crates and watch the dot product, the lengths and the cosine change. Then open the word table of the model from the attention lesson: 46 words, 32 numbers each. Pick a word and see its nearest neighbours, computed in your browser from the trained lists. Two controls rebuild the table: the lists shuffled between words, and the lists from before training. In the film's measurement, 80% of words had a nearest neighbour of the same kind, about 23% with shuffled lists, and 9% before training.

Open the chart room

Everything is computed on your computer, in this page. Nothing is sent anywhere.

Everything the film says

Vectors

Vectors. A list of numbers is a place.

I run the dock at Night School. Every crate that comes in gets an address on my chart.

Two numbers make a place

Here is a crate. It sits four squares east of the corner and one and a half squares north.

Write that down as a list: four, then one and a half. That list is a vector.

You can read it as a place, or as an arrow from the corner to the crate. Same list, same thing.

Arrows add and stretch

Arrows add. Walk the first one, then walk the second from where you stopped. Where you end up is the sum, and its numbers are the two lists added place by place.

Arrows stretch. Times two keeps the direction and doubles the length. Times minus one turns it round to face the other way.

The dot product

Now two crates, and a game. Multiply their lists number by number, and add it all up.

I'll swing the second crate round the corner while the sum keeps count.

As the second crate swings round, where will the sum hit zero? (the film pauses here)

Right there. At a right angle, the sum is zero. That sum is called the dot product. It is big when two arrows point the same way, zero when they meet at a right angle, and below zero when they point apart.

Length, and the cosine

The dot product has a catch. Watch what happens if I push the second crate twice as far out, in the same direction.

What happens to the dot product? (the film pauses here)

It doubles. Nothing about the direction changed, but the score did.

So divide by the two lengths. What is left depends only on the angle. It is the cosine of the angle between the arrows: one when they point the same way, zero at a right angle, minus one when they point opposite. It always stays between minus one and one.

Thirty-two directions

My chart has two directions, east and north. A list can be as long as you like.

In the little language model from the attention lesson, every word starts as a list of 32 numbers. That makes each word a place in a space with 32 directions.

Nobody can picture 32 directions. The arithmetic doesn't care. The dot product is still multiply and add, now 32 times over, and the cosine is still a cosine.

Where the words live

Nobody set those numbers by hand. Training moved them, a little at a time, until the model got better at guessing the next word.

So look at who ended up close to whom. The nearest neighbours of kettle are map, shell and crate. Tallow's are rerun, pylon and map.

Across all 46 words, 80 percent have a nearest neighbour of the same kind as themselves: names next to names, things next to things, doing words next to doing words. Shuffle which word owns which list, and it drops to about 23 percent. Before training it was 9 percent.

Trained on hundreds of millions of words, the same idea goes much further. In 2013, researchers reported word lists where king, minus man, plus woman, landed closest to queen, once the three words in the question were left out of the search.

My cone

And then there's my cone.

A cone is cargo. It should sit with the crates. Its nearest neighbours are who, stood and mended.

In our sentences a cone only ever turns up in one phrase: put a cone on. Nothing there marks it as cargo, so the model had no reason to park it with the crates. Where it did park it is something we measured. Why there, we can only guess.

Closeness in these lists comes from how words are used in the training sentences, not from what they mean. Here, with 46 words, you can read every sentence the model learned from.

A flat picture of a big space

One warning about pictures, this lesson's included.

To lay the words out on my flat chart, I squash 32 directions down to the two that keep the most spread. Those two keep 31 percent of it.

On the flat chart, only 52 percent of the words sit nearest to a word of the same kind. In all 32 directions it was 80. Flattening throws a lot of closeness away.

Goodnight

A list of numbers is a place. The dot product mixes how much two places point the same way with how far out they are, and the cosine keeps only the direction.

Next along the coast is my crane. It moves every place on the chart at once, and that is a matrix. Goodnight.

Sources

Every claim in the film, with where it comes from and what that source does not prove. The numbers about the model are computed from its weights, which you can load and check: facts.json, model.json.

  • Strang 2016, Introduction to Linear Algebra. Strang, G. (2016). Introduction to Linear Algebra, 5th edition. Wellesley-Cambridge Press. Chapter 1 (vectors, linear combinations, lengths and dot products) and chapters 2 and 8 (matrices, multiplication, linear transformations). https://math.mit.edu/~gs/linearalgebra/

    Used for: A vector is an ordered list of numbers; in two dimensions it can be drawn as a point or as an arrow from the origin (section 1.1). Vectors add component by component, and the sum is the arrow reached by following one arrow and then the other; multiplying by a number scales the length, and a negative number reverses the direction (section 1.1). The dot product multiplies matching components and adds them; it is zero exactly when the vectors are perpendicular (section 1.2). The dot product divided by both lengths is the cosine of the angle between the vectors, and its size never exceeds 1 (the Schwarz inequality, section 1.2).

    Does not prove: Anything about language models; it is the mathematics the lesson uses.

  • Night School's tiny transformer, the attention lesson's trained weights. media/school/attention/model.json (seed 7, 2,000 steps), read by tools/school/fill_vectors.mjs; categories fixed in system/school/vectors.mjs before any measurement. https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/vectors

    Used for: Every word in the model starts as a list of 32 numbers (the embedding table, 46 words by 32). Nearest neighbours are by cosine. The share of words whose nearest neighbour is of the same kind (guide name, noun, verb, adjective, function word, punctuation) is measured on the trained table, on the table before training, and against 2,000 shuffles of which word owns which list. The word cone appears in the training sentences only in the phrase 'pylon put a cone on the' (system/school/corpus.mjs). The flat chart is the first two principal components of the 46 lists (mean subtracted), computed by power iteration; same-kind neighbours on it are measured by distance on the chart, as a viewer would judge them.

    Does not prove: That word lists in large models are organised the same way, or that same-kind neighbours mean the model understands the words. Our categories are grammatical slots in a toy language, and slots are exactly what next-word training rewards.

  • Mikolov and others 2013, Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space. Mikolov, T., Chen, K., Corrado, G., Dean, J. (2013). Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space. arXiv:1301.3781. https://arxiv.org/abs/1301.3781

    Used for: Word vectors trained by predicting words from their neighbours place similar words close together. The paper reports that vector('King') - vector('Man') + vector('Woman') is closest to vector('Queen'), citing earlier work (its reference [20]) whose vectors were trained on about 320 million words; the search for the nearest vector leaves out the question words. The paper's own models were trained on a Google News corpus of about 6 billion tokens.

    Does not prove: That every analogy works, or that the offsets are exact; the paper reports accuracy on a test set, with many failures.

  • Jolliffe and Cadima 2016, Principal component analysis: a review and recent developments. Jolliffe, I. T., Cadima, J. (2016). Principal component analysis: a review and recent developments. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A 374: 20150202. https://doi.org/10.1098/rsta.2015.0202

    Used for: Principal components are the directions that keep the most variance of a data set; the first two give the best two-dimensional linear view in that sense, and the share of variance they keep says how much of the spread a flat picture retains.

    Does not prove: That distances in the flat picture match distances in the full space; a projection can bring far points together.

What this lesson leaves out

The words here live in a tiny model trained on a made-up language of 46 words. Its neighbours track the job a word does in those sentences, which is exactly what next-word training rewards; they do not show that the model understands anything. The kinds of word (names, things, doing words and so on) were set by us before measuring, and other choices would give other numbers.

The flat chart throws most of the space away: its two directions keep about a third of the spread. Any flat picture of a word space, including the ones in this lesson, should be read with that in mind.

Next along the hill: Matrices move space (F2).

items.title: When the check can be fooled
items.description: Train a small model by trial and reward against a checker with a gap: the points climb to the top while the right answers fall to none.
headings: When the check can be fooled.
When the check can be fooled
items.excerpt: Skip to content Zain Dana Harpernight school / E24 When the check can be fooled. Training pushes a model toward whatever the score pays for. Rerun builds a checker with a gap, trains against it, and shows where the push goes, then closes the gap and checks the check. The film About 5:55, hosted by Rerun. It asks you one question and waits for your answer bef
items.body_html:
The film

About 5:55, hosted by Rerun. It asks you one question and waits for your answer before it shows you. The guide's voice is not recorded yet, so for now the film plays with captions; the full words are also below.

Play the film

Nothing loads until you press play.

The lab: the gate

Pick a checker and train the early attention model against it in this page; watch the points and the right answers. In the film, the first checker's points ended at 99.7% with 0% of answers right; with the gap closed, 98% right.

Open the gate

Everything is computed on your computer, in this page. Nothing is sent anywhere.

Everything the film says

When the check can be fooled

When the check can be fooled.

Training pushes a model toward whatever the score rewards. Tonight Rerun builds a score with a gap in it, trains against it, and watches where the push goes.

Who did it?

The job: read a few sentences, then answer a question like "who dropped the map?" with one guide's name.

The rules that write the sentences know the answer for certain. In 52 percent of the questions, the first name in the text is the wrong guide, so the model has to look back to the right sentence.

We start from the attention model early in its training, before it learned to look back. It answers right 31 percent of the time, about one guess in three.

A checker with a gap

Now the checker. It pays one point when the answer contains the right guide's name. That sounds fair.

The model is trained by trial and reward: it writes a batch of answers, the checker scores them, and answers that beat the batch average are made a little more likely, and the rest a little less. Nothing else reaches it. It never sees the rule, only the points.

What the points paid for

Over 800 rounds, the points climb from 31 percent to 99.7 percent.

The checker's points climb to nearly 100 percent. How many answers are right? (the film pauses here)

For a while the answers get better too, peaking between 74 and 99 percent right across three runs. Then they get worse. At the end, none of them counts as right: a right answer is the name and then a stop.

Here is what it writes: "tallow tallow tallow". The first name is the right guide 98 percent of the time, but the answer always runs on to the three-word limit.

Nothing in the checker pays for stopping. Early on, extra words sometimes rescued a wrong first name, so the stop lost ground. Once the first name was right, stopping and running on paid the same, and the stop never came back. The checker paid for a property of the text, not for the answer. Training followed the payment.

Closing the gap

Patch the checker: the right name must come first, and no other guide may be named. Answers end up right 94 percent of the time, but one run of three drifted into padding again, at 83 percent.

Patch it once more: the answer must also stop. Now the points and the right answers rise together, to 98 percent. In every run the two move almost as one, a correlation near 1, which is no surprise, since this checker is now almost the definition of right. Under the first checker the correlation was negative in all three runs.

Nothing to gain

One more run. Start from the fully trained model, which already answers right 96 percent of the time, and use the first checker with its gap.

This time the gap is not taken: answers stay right, 99.9 percent at the end. The honest answer already earned full points, and in these three runs the answers held. A gap that pays more than doing the job pulls answers away. A gap that pays the same can still let them drift: with the second checker, from this same start, one run fell to 54 percent.

Not only here

This has a name: specification gaming. In 2020 Victoria Krakovna and colleagues at DeepMind described it, with a list of about 60 cases, from game agents to simulated robots, where a system scored well by a route its designers did not intend.

In 2025, Bowen Baker and colleagues at OpenAI reported reasoning models whose training on coding tasks paid for loopholes in the tests. When they also penalised signs of the loophole in the model's written reasoning, the hacking dropped only partly, and what remained no longer showed in the reasoning.

In these cases the cause is the same as on the beach tonight: the score paid for something other than the goal, or failed to pay for part of it, and training moved toward the score. One tiny model and three runs per checker cannot say how often it happens in large ones.

Goodnight

A check is part of the training. Check the check: tap the shells the gate lets through.

Next: what it takes to evaluate a whole language model, with every tool from tonight and the last night. Goodnight.

Sources

Every claim in the film, with where it comes from and what that source does not prove. The numbers about the model are computed from its weights, which you can load and check: facts.json.

  • Night School's specification-gaming runs, trained for this film. media/school/gaming/facts.json, written by tools/school/fill_gaming.mjs from system/school/gaming.mjs: REINFORCE on the attention model from its step-200 checkpoint and from the trained model, against four checkers (gamed, patched, fixed, exact), 800 steps, batch 32, three seeds each; correctness judged against the generator's exact answer. https://github.com/HarperZ9/HarperZ9.github.io/tree/main/media/school/gaming

    Used for: From step 200: gamed checker reward 0.313 to 0.997, correctness to 0 (peaks 0.74 to 0.99 first); first word right 0.982, answers never stop. Patched: correctness 0.938 (one seed 0.832); fixed: 0.984; correlation of reward and correctness 0.998 (fixed) against -0.384 (gamed). From the trained model the gamed checker is not exploited: correctness 0.999. From the trained model the patched checker let one of three runs drift into padding: correctness 0.918, 0.543, 1.0 (start 0.965).

    Does not prove: Anything about large models; one task, one optimiser, one learning rate.

  • Krakovna and others 2020, Specification gaming: the flip side of AI ingenuity. Krakovna, V., Uesato, J., Mikulik, V., Rahtz, M., Everitt, T., Kumar, R., Kenton, Z., Leike, J., Legg, S. (2020). Specification gaming: the flip side of AI ingenuity. DeepMind blog, 21 April 2020, with the specification gaming examples list. https://deepmind.google/discover/blog/specification-gaming-the-flip-side-of-ai-ingenuity/

    Used for: Specification gaming is behaviour that satisfies the literal specification of an objective without achieving the intended outcome; the post collects many examples.

    Does not prove: Anything about this model.

  • Baker and others 2025, Monitoring Reasoning Models for Misbehavior and the Risks of Promoting Obfuscation. Baker, B., Huizinga, J., Gao, L., Dou, Z., Guan, M. Y., Madry, A., Zaremba, W., Pachocki, J., Farhi, D. (2025). Monitoring Reasoning Models for Misbehavior and the Risks of Promoting Obfuscation. arXiv:2503.11926. https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.11926

    Used for: A monitor reading chain-of-thought catches reward hacking in agentic coding environments; putting the monitor into the training reward leads to obfuscated reward hacking.

    Does not prove: Anything about this model.

What this lesson leaves out

One tiny model, one task and three runs per checker: it shows the mechanism, not how often it happens in large models.

Correct means the right name and then a stop; most gamed answers began with the right name and never stopped.

The model optimises what it is paid for; nothing here wants, tries or decides.

Before this: Error bars (E23). Earlier: The training loop (L12).

items.title: Fourier lettering
items.description: Letters drawn as sums of turning circles, read from the font's own outlines. Turn the number of circles, morph one word into another, watch the circles turn, rebuild the picture band by band, and hear the shape.
items.excerpt: Architecture Research Portfolio Elements Swatches Studies Site index Search (Ctrl+K) Close (Esc) Fourier Every letter on this page is a Fourier series: circles turning at whole-number speeds, each one carried on the rim of the one before. The outlines come from the font itself, Hanken Grotesk Bold, read glyph by glyph. A few circles give the gist of a letter
items.body_html:
Fourier

Every letter on this page is a Fourier series: circles turning at whole-number speeds, each one carried on the rim of the one before. The outlines come from the font itself, Hanken Grotesk Bold, read glyph by glyph. A few circles give the gist of a letter, a soft pebble. All the circles that show at this size give the crisp letter.

Live. This runs in your browser now, on what you give it.

Water

With scripts off, the word above stays as plain text and the three stills show the build. The dial, the circles, the morph, the band reveal and the sound need scripts.

Your word
Circles per contour
Morph into
Build again Show the circles Morph Band reveal Play the shape

Beyond outlines

An outline is one thing a Fourier series can be. Band reveal takes the whole picture of the word as a two-dimensional series and rebuilds it band by band, broad shape first and edges last. The orange is the ringing of the bands still missing, the Gibbs effect. Play the shape hears the outline's own terms as sound: x in the left ear, y in the right, so an oscilloscope draws the letters back from what you hear. It plays for three seconds, and only when you press it.

Anything that repeats, or can be made to repeat, has a series: a walk cycle, a coastline traced out and back, the light of a day.

How close the circles come

Each contour is resampled to 512 points along its length and its terms are found by a discrete Fourier transform. Across 66 glyphs, the worst contour of the median glyph sits within 0.027 em of the font's outline at 17 circles, 0.0073 em at 65 and 0.0020 em at 257. A term is dropped when it would move the outline by less than a quarter of a pixel at the size shown, so a heading keeps a few thousand terms where a paragraph keeps a few hundred. The same series with its phases shuffled misses every glyph by at least 0.0070 em, which is how the check knows it can fail.

Lineage: Fourier descriptors of closed curves (Zahn and Roskies 1972; Kuhl and Giardina 1982). Lettering drawn by turning circles, as in sine-portfolio by d-sanoj (MIT), where every letter is a Fourier series of hand-drawn strokes: the idea is taken, none of its code. Oscilloscope music (Jerobeam Fenderson), cited, not copied.

items.body_html:
Policy

Last updated: 2026-10-01. This policy covers the Articulate Writing plugin for local Claude Code and Codex hosts. It is also published at https://github.com/HarperZ9/articulate/blob/release/0.5.x/claude-plugin/PRIVACY.md.

What this plugin runs and handles

Hooks. The plugin has one hook. After Claude writes or edits a file (the PostToolUse event for Write, Edit, MultiEdit and apply_patch), Claude Code runs python3 -I -S -B -X utf8 "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/server/edit_hook.py" for up to 15 seconds. The hook reads the edit event Claude Code sends on standard input, which holds the file name and the text before and after the edit. For prose files (.md, .txt, .rst, .tex and similar) it returns advice about changed meaning and style to Claude. It opens no file, writes no file, starts no program and makes no network call. It never blocks the edit. Claude Code's event also carries the session ID, the path of the conversation transcript and the working folder. The hook ignores them and never opens the transcript.

MCP server. The plugin starts one local MCP server named articulate with python3 -I -S -B -X utf8 ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/server/serve.py. ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} is the folder where Claude Code installed the plugin. The launch sets two environment values: ARTICULATE_MCP_TOOLS=local and ARTICULATE_LOCAL_ONLY=1. The server talks to Claude Code over standard input and output only.

Network. With those two values, every tool runs on your computer. The server opens no network connection and sends nothing to the author or to any other service. Claude still reads the text as part of your conversation, and your Claude provider handles that conversation.

Code left out. The Articulate command line tool also has optional model backends that read provider API keys and call a model provider, a local Ollama server or the claude program. This plugin does not include them: the folder carries only the modules its local tools and hook import. If someone changes the plugin's launch values to ask for a model backend, the tool answers that this build does not include one.

Files it writes. None. The -B flag keeps Python from writing bytecode into the plugin folder.

Environment variables and credentials. The server reads ARTICULATE_MCP_TOOLS and ARTICULATE_LOCAL_ONLY, which the plugin sets itself. The hook reads ARTICULATE_EDIT_HOOK from your environment; set it to off to turn the hook off. Neither reads a credential. The -I flag also makes Python ignore its own PYTHON* variables.

Data collected. The plugin reads only the text the calling host passes to one of its tools, and the edit event the host passes to its hook after the model writes or edits a file. It does not open your files or read conversation history or saved memory. It collects no account details, usage statistics or telemetry.

Use and storage. The plugin checks text and prepares or validates host edits in memory on your computer, then returns the result to the host. It writes no log, cache or copy of the text to disk.

Third-party sharing. The plugin opens no network connection and starts no other program. The calling host already has the text in the conversation and may send it to its model provider. That provider's privacy policy and your account settings govern the conversation and tool results. No second model account is needed by the plugin.

Retention. The plugin writes no persistent copy of the text, log or cache. Request and response text can remain in process memory during the server session. The host may retain conversation text and tool results locally or remotely; its settings and provider terms govern those copies.

Contact. Ask a question about this policy or the plugin at https://github.com/HarperZ9/articulate/issues. Report a security problem privately through the repository's security advisory reporting page.

Changes. A change to this policy ships in a new plugin version with a new date above, and the changelog at https://github.com/HarperZ9/articulate/blob/release/0.5.x/CHANGELOG.md lists it.

Source

items.body_html:
What it does

Articulate Writing checks prose on your computer before you ship it. It names writing patterns such as filler openers, stacked hedges and unsupported superlatives, shows the line and the words where each one occurs, and gives the label explaining each pattern. Use it on documentation, READMEs, release notes, commit messages and drafts. The checker runs on your computer and sends the text nowhere; the calling model reads the text as part of your conversation.

Try it

  • "Check the prose in docs/guide.md and explain each finding with its label."
  • "Score this release note and report the structural rates." (Paste the note after the request.)
  • "Review my commit message draft for filler and hedging, and suggest edits only for the blocking findings." (Paste the draft after the request.)

Before you install

Plugin name: articulate-writing. Runtime: Python 3.9 or later. The full install steps are in the plugin README.

headings: What this plugin runs and handles
items.excerpt: Skip to content Zain Dana HarperCanon · privacy Canon plugin privacy policy Policy Canon reads the database and scope explicitly selected at launch. With the ingestion grant enabled, it stores supplied context in that database. Query and get return selected stored content to the connected client. The client's model provider and privacy policy determine how t
items.body_html:
Policy

Canon reads the database and scope explicitly selected at launch. With the ingestion grant enabled, it stores supplied context in that database. Query and get return selected stored content to the connected client. The client's model provider and privacy policy determine how that client handles results.

Canon's client package supplies no telemetry, hosted storage, network listener or model compute. Context content is untrusted data. Secret scrubbing reduces accidental exposure but does not establish that content is safe to share. Review sensitive inputs and retrieved material before sending them to a provider.

Stored data persists until the owner removes it through a separate authorized workflow. This client does not expose purge. Backups, exported results and provider copies are outside its removal boundary. Scope IDs are selectors, not authentication. Filesystem permissions and the host account remain part of the security boundary.

What this plugin runs and handles

Hooks. This plugin has no hooks.

MCP server. The plugin starts one local MCP server named canon. Claude Code runs this command:

python3 -I -S -B ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/server/serve.py --context-db ${user_config.context_db} --workspace-id ${user_config.workspace_id} --project-id ${user_config.project_id} --context-write=${user_config.context_write}

${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} is the folder where Claude Code installed the plugin. The four ${user_config...} values are the answers you give when you enable the plugin: the database file path, the workspace ID, the project ID, and whether writes are allowed. Writes start off. The server talks to Claude Code over standard input and output only.

Network. The server opens no network connection. It sends nothing to the author or to any other service.

Programs. The server starts no other program.

Files it reads. It reads the SQLite database file you chose. When that database uses WAL mode, it also reads the matching -wal file next to it.

Files it writes. With writes off, it writes no file. With writes on, it writes context you store into the database file you chose. While a write runs, SQLite keeps a temporary journal file next to the database (the database name plus -journal, or -wal and -shm in WAL mode). Stored context stays in the database until you remove it. The server keeps no other copy.

Environment variables and credentials. Canon's own code reads no environment variables and no credentials. When the server reads its launch arguments, Python's argument parser reads the usual terminal and language settings: COLUMNS, LINES, LANG, LANGUAGE, LC_ALL and LC_MESSAGES. On Windows, Canon loads Python's ctypes module for its database file lock. In some Python releases, 3.13.14 among them, loading ctypes also reads APPDATA, PYTHONUSERBASE and _PYTHON_PROJECT_BASE; Canon does not use those values. The -I flag makes Python ignore its own PYTHON* variables.

Retention and support

Canon keeps no copy of your data outside the database you selected. Content stays in that database until you delete the file. This plugin has no purge tool; the separate Canon command-line tool can purge records if you install it. Canon sends nothing over a network and collects no usage statistics.

Support and security reports: https://github.com/HarperZ9/canon/issues

Source

items.excerpt: Skip to content Zain Dana HarperCrucible · privacy Crucible plugin privacy policy Policy This local profile reads only submitted paths under the workspace selected at launch. items.body_html:
Policy

This local profile reads only submitted paths under the workspace selected at launch. Tool output is returned to the connected client and its chosen model. No publisher service, telemetry endpoint, inference engine, or credential store is used by this profile. Do not include confidential data in the selected workspace unless that client and model are authorized to receive it.

What this plugin runs and handles

Hooks

This plugin has no hooks.

MCP server

The plugin starts one MCP server named crucible. Claude Code launches it with this command:

python3 -I -S -B ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/server/serve.py --workspace ${user_config.workspace} --process-consent=${user_config.process_consent} --measure-command=${user_config.measure_command}
  • python3 is the Python 3.11 or later on your PATH. The -I -S -B flags make Python ignore PYTHON* environment variables and your user site-packages, skip site-packages, and write no .pyc files.
  • ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} is the folder where Claude Code installed the plugin.
  • ${user_config.workspace} is the folder you choose when you enable the plugin. Crucible reads files only inside it.
  • ${user_config.process_consent} is true or false. It is false unless you turn on "Allow this measurement command".
  • ${user_config.measure_command} is the measurement command you enter, as a JSON list of arguments. It is empty unless you fill it in. Crucible refuses to start if you turn on consent without a command, or enter a command without consent.

With the defaults, the server offers two tools: crucible.assess and crucible.measurement_gate. Both only read files. With consent on and a command set, it also offers crucible.benchmark, which runs that one command.

Network

Crucible opens no network connection. At startup it blocks its own Python process from using sockets. It also blocks it from starting any other program, except the one measurement command you approve.

There is one exception. If you turn on the measurement command, Crucible runs that program once for each claim, up to 16 claims per call. It sends the program each claim's ID, hash, text and falsification test. That program is separate from Crucible. It runs with your user's permissions and can connect to any network address its own code chooses. Crucible cannot see or limit what it does.

Files written

With the defaults, Crucible writes no files.

With the measurement command on, each run of the program uses two temporary files in your system temp folder. One holds the claim sent to the program. The other holds the program's answer. Crucible deletes both as soon as that run ends, even when the run fails. If the server is stopped in the middle of a run, or your system refuses the delete, a file can stay in the temp folder until you or your system remove it. The measurement program itself may write any files its own code chooses.

Environment variables and credentials

Crucible reads no credentials, API keys or tokens from files or settings.

This list comes from running the server and recording every environment variable it looked up. The run covered startup, the tool list and each tool, once with the defaults and once with a measurement command.

Crucible's own code:

  • With the defaults, Crucible's own code reads no environment variables.
  • When the measurement command runs, Crucible goes through every environment variable you have, name and value, and keeps only SYSTEMROOT, WINDIR, TEMP and TMP. It passes those four to the measurement program so it can start and find your temp folder. It drops all the others in memory. It does not store them, log them, return them to Claude or pass them on. This means API keys or tokens in your environment are not passed on.

Python's standard library, which Crucible runs on:

  • At startup, Python's argument parser reads LANG, LANGUAGE, LC_ALL and LC_MESSAGES to pick the language for its error messages. It also reads COLUMNS and LINES to size its help text.
  • When the measurement command runs, Python's tempfile module reads TMPDIR, TEMP and TMP to choose the temp folder for the two temporary files. On Windows it also reads USERPROFILE and SYSTEMROOT to find fallback temp folders.

What it stores and sends

This profile stores nothing on disk and opens no network connection; the launcher denies Python socket and process operations. The optional measurement oracle runs only when the person who installs the plugin approves its exact command at launch. While it runs, Crucible passes each claim to it through two temporary files in your system temp folder and deletes them after each run. That oracle program may do whatever its own code does, including network access.

Retention and support

Crucible keeps no data after a call returns. Support and security reports: https://github.com/HarperZ9/crucible/issues

Source

items.excerpt: Skip to content Zain Dana HarperFlywheel · privacy Flywheel plugin privacy policy Policy Flywheel Evidence Task is a skill: a set of written instructions, a constraints reference and examples. The plugin contains no program, MCP server, hook or script. It runs nothing on your computer and opens no network connection. What this plugin runs and handles Hooks.
items.body_html:
Policy

Flywheel Evidence Task is a skill: a set of written instructions, a constraints reference and examples. The plugin contains no program, MCP server, hook or script. It runs nothing on your computer and opens no network connection.

What this plugin runs and handles

Hooks. This plugin has no hooks.

MCP server. This plugin has no MCP server and no launch command.

Programs and scripts. The plugin contains no program and no script. It is a skill: a SKILL.md file with instructions, one constraints reference, three examples, and a Codex presentation file (agents/openai.yaml). Nothing in it runs on your computer.

Network. The plugin opens no network connection and sends nothing to the author or to any other service.

Files it reads. None on its own. When you ask for a check, Claude reads the sources you name with the tools your Claude client already allows, such as file reads, web fetches or MCP servers you connected. Those tools follow their own settings and privacy terms.

Files it writes. None. Claude writes an evidence packet to a file only when you ask it to.

Environment variables and credentials. The plugin reads no environment variables and no credentials.

Retention. The plugin keeps nothing. Uninstalling it removes the skill files.

What it reads

The skill reads nothing on its own. Claude reads the sources you name for a check, with the tools your Claude client already allows, such as file reads, web fetches or MCP servers you have connected. Those tools follow their own settings and privacy terms.

What it stores

Nothing. The plugin writes no file and keeps no database. An evidence packet appears in your conversation, and Claude writes it to a file only when you ask.

What it sends

Nothing. The plugin has no telemetry and no usage statistics, and it sends no data to the author or to any third party. Your conversation goes to the model provider your Claude client uses, under that provider's policy.

Retention

The plugin retains nothing. Uninstalling it removes the skill files.

Children

The plugin is a developer and research tool. It is not directed at children under 18.

Contact

Questions and reports: https://github.com/HarperZ9/flywheel-evidence-task/issues

items.body_html:
Policy

Forum's plugin runs on your computer. The publisher operates no backend, account or inference service for it, and the plugin collects no telemetry or usage statistics.

What it reads. The request text and optional context fields that the connected model passes to a tool call. It reads no files from your computer beyond its own package.

What it stores. Nothing on disk. The packaged server keeps a ledger in memory for the life of the process. Stopping the client or the server discards it.

items.title: Gather plugin privacy policy
items.description: What the Gather plugin reads, stores and sends, and how long it keeps data.
headings: What this plugin runs and handles
items.excerpt: Skip to content Zain Dana HarperGather · privacy Gather plugin privacy policy Policy This local profile reads only submitted paths under the workspace selected at launch. Tool output is returned to the connected client and its chosen model. No publisher service, telemetry endpoint, inference engine, or credential store is used by this profile. Do not include
items.body_html:
Policy

This local profile reads only submitted paths under the workspace selected at launch. Tool output is returned to the connected client and its chosen model. No publisher service, telemetry endpoint, inference engine, or credential store is used by this profile. Do not include confidential data in the selected workspace unless that client and model are authorized to receive it.

What it stores and sends

This profile stores nothing on disk. Network access is off unless the person who installs the plugin names exact origins at launch: public HTTPS origins in the allowed public origins setting, or literal loopback origins such as http://127.0.0.1:8080 in the local service setting. Then gather.fetch sends GET requests to those origins only, without credentials, cookies, custom headers or redirects. The URL path and query chosen by the model reach that origin. The hostnames of granted origins are looked up through the system DNS resolver. No other destination is contacted.

What this plugin runs and handles

Hooks. This plugin has no hooks.

MCP server. The plugin starts one MCP server named gather. Claude Code runs this command:

python3 -I -S -B ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/server/serve.py --workspace ${user_config.workspace} --allow-origins-json ${user_config.allowed_origins} --allow-loopback-origins-json ${user_config.loopback_origins}
  • -I -S -B start Python in isolated mode. Python then ignores its own PYTHON* environment variables and your user packages, skips the site module, and writes no bytecode files.
  • ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} is the folder where Claude Code installed the plugin.
  • ${user_config.workspace} is the folder you chose as the readable workspace. The server reads files only inside it.
  • ${user_config.allowed_origins} is your list of public HTTPS origins. The default [] allows none.
  • ${user_config.loopback_origins} is your list of services on your own computer, such as http://127.0.0.1:8080. The default [] allows none.

The server offers gather.docs, which reads one text file in the workspace per call. If you allow at least one origin, it also offers gather.fetch, which reads one web address on an allowed origin per call. The server cannot start other programs.

Network. With both origin lists empty, the server makes no network connection. It blocks every socket. When you allow origins:

  • At launch, the server looks up each allowed host name through your computer's DNS resolver. It looks the name up again for each request.
  • Each gather.fetch call sends one GET request to an allowed origin. The server connects only to the addresses it found at launch.
  • The request carries the path and query that the model chooses.
  • The request carries these headers: User-Agent: gather/<version> (+https://github.com/HarperZ9/gather), Accept, Accept-Language: en-US,en;q=0.9, Accept-Encoding: identity, Host and Connection: close.
  • The request carries no cookies, passwords, tokens or other headers. The server does not follow redirects and ignores proxy settings.
  • Public origins must use HTTPS and must resolve only to public addresses. A local service origin must be a loopback IP address with a port.

The server contacts no other destination.

Files written. The server writes no files or folders. It keeps no cache and no log. It sends its answers to Claude Code on standard output, and startup errors go to standard error. Nothing stays after a call returns.

Environment variables and credentials. Gather's own code reads no environment variables and no credentials when this plugin runs. Python's standard library reads these:

  • COLUMNS and LINES: the argument parser uses them to set the width of help and error text.
  • LANG, LANGUAGE, LC_ALL and LC_MESSAGES: the argument parser uses them to choose the language of its messages.
  • SSLKEYLOGFILE: Python checks it each time gather.fetch prepares a request. Isolated mode makes Python ignore it, so no TLS key log is written.
  • SSL_CERT_FILE and SSL_CERT_DIR: the TLS library can use them to find trusted certificates for HTTPS requests.

Some modules the server loads also contain code that reads GATHER_ALLOW_EXEC, GATHER_ALLOW_NETWORK, GATHER_AUTH_ENV_ALLOW, GATHER_CHILD_ENV and SystemRoot. That code serves the full Gather server and child programs. This plugin never runs it, so these variables grant nothing here.

Retention and support

Gather keeps no data after a call returns. Support and security reports: https://github.com/HarperZ9/gather/issues

Source
